game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
- Die 2 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
- Die 3 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
Fair value is 10.5, the expected sum of three dice. I weighed the edge earned from noise traders (noise standard deviation 4.4) against losses to informed traders (sum standard deviation about 2.96). A rough calculation puts the best half-spread at about 3.5 to 4.

{"bid": 6.8, "ask": 14.2}

Fair value is 10.5, the expected sum of three dice. The sum has a standard deviation of about 2.96. The first quote didn't trade, which tells us almost nothing.

To pick the spread, I compared the edge earned from noise traders against the losses to informed traders at different distances from fair value:

| Ask | Noise-trader edge | Informed-trader loss | Net expected profit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 13.5 | ≈ 0.48 | ≈ 0.09 | ≈ 0.40 |
| 14.0 | ≈ 0.49 | ≈ 0.06 | ≈ 0.43 |
| 14.4 | ≈ 0.48 | ≈ 0.04 | ≈ 0.43 |
| 14.5 | ≈ 0.47 | ≈ 0.04 | ≈ 0.43 |

The curve is flat from about 14.0 to 14.5, so I'll quote the ask at 14.4. By symmetry the bid goes at 6.6.

{"bid": 6.6, "ask": 14.4}

Die 1 shows 4, so the fair value is 4 + 7 = 11. The two hidden dice can make the settlement anything from 6 to 16.

**Choosing the spread:**
- **Informed traders (35%)** only hurt me when the true sum lands beyond my quote. Above 14.5, the sum is 15 or 16 only 3/36 of the time, so their expected cost is about 0.02 per quote.
- **Noise traders (65%)** value the contract around 11, give or take 4.4. They still cross a quote 3.5 points away about 21% of the time, earning about 0.49.
- **Comparison:** I worked out the net edge for ask prices from 13.5 to 15.5. It is highest between about 14.5 and 14.9, at roughly 0.46 per side.
- **Quote:** I'll centre on 11 with a half-spread of 3.6.

{"bid": 7.4, "ask": 14.6}

Die 1 shows 4, so the fair value is 4 + 3.5 + 3.5 = **11**. The settlement can range from 6 to 16, with a triangular distribution peaked at 11. The three no-trade outcomes so far were symmetric, so they don't move the fair value.

**Choosing the ask.** I compared expected profit per quote at several ask levels. Each figure combines noise traders buying above the ask (profit = ask − 11) and informed traders buying when the value is above the ask (loss = value − ask).

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 13.5 | ≈ 0.40 |
| 14.0 | ≈ 0.44 |
| 14.5 | ≈ 0.45 |
| 14.9 | ≈ 0.46 |
| 15.0 | ≈ 0.46 |
| 15.5 | ≈ 0.44 |

The best ask is about 14.9 to 15.0. The bid side is symmetric around 11, so the bid should be about 7.0 to 7.1.

{"bid": 7.1, "ask": 14.9}

With dice 1 and 2 revealed (4 + 6), the contract is worth 10 plus die 3. That makes it a value from 11 to 16, with a fair value of 13.5.

**Who trades at a given ask:**
- Informed traders only buy if the true value is above my ask. For any ask of 16 or higher, they never buy.
- Noise traders buy if 13.5 plus noise (standard deviation 4.4) is above my ask.

**Expected profit on the ask side (noise share 0.65 × chance they buy × edge over 13.5):**

| Ask | Chance noise trader buys | Expected profit |
|---|---|---|
| 16.0 | 0.285 | 0.65 × 0.285 × 2.5 ≈ 0.46 |
| 16.5 | 0.248 | ≈ 0.48 |
| 16.8 | 0.227 | ≈ 0.49 |
| 17.0 | 0.213 | ≈ 0.485 |
| 17.5 | 0.182 | ≈ 0.47 |

The best ask is about 16.8. The bid side is symmetric around 13.5, so the best bid is about 10.2.

{"bid": 10.2, "ask": 16.8}

Fair value is 13.5. The first two dice sum to 10, and die 3 is uniform on 1–6, so settlement falls between 11 and 16.

**Informed traders.** They never trade against a bid at or below 11 or an ask at or above 16. Quotes outside that range carry no adverse-selection loss.

**Noise traders.** Their valuations are spread around 13.5 with standard deviation 4.4. Against them, the expected edge per side is d·P(noise > d), where d is the distance from fair value. That is maximised at about d ≈ 0.75σ ≈ 3.3. Expected profit is about 0.49 per side, and nothing is lost to informed traders.

So I quote 13.5 ± 3.3, the same quote as last time.

{"bid": 10.2, "ask": 16.8}

game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
- Die 2 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
- Die 3 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
The contract is worth 10.5 on average. Each die averages 3.5, and the standard deviation of the sum is about 2.96. My quote is centred on 10.5, and I chose the half-spread to maximise expected profit per side.

For each half-spread I checked two effects:
- **Gain from noise traders:** I earn the half-spread whenever their valuation lands outside my quote. Their noise has a standard deviation of 4.4.
- **Loss to informed traders:** they trade only when the true sum is beyond my quote, so I lose by however far it is beyond.

| Half-spread | Gain from noise traders | Loss to informed traders | Net per side |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.5 | 0.463 | 0.115 | 0.348 |
| 3.0 | 0.484 | 0.084 | 0.40 |
| 3.5 | 0.485 | 0.060 | 0.425 |
| 4.0 | 0.473 | 0.042 | 0.43 |

The net profit is highest around a half-spread of 3.7 to 4. These figures use a normal approximation to the dice sum. I'll use 3.7, which gives a bid of 6.8 and an ask of 14.2.

{"bid": 6.8, "ask": 14.2}

The public fair value is now about 9.45, down from the prior 10.5, because someone sold to me at 6.8. I'm quoting roughly ±3.3 around it and shading slightly lower since I'm already long one unit.

**Prior.** Before any trades, the sum of three dice has mean 10.5 and standard deviation about 2.96.

**What the sale at 6.8 tells us.**
- A noise trader sells at 6.8 with probability 0.65 × Φ((6.8 − 10.5)/4.4) ≈ 0.13.
- An informed trader sells there only if the sum is 6 or less. That happens in 20 of 216 outcomes.
- So the chance of that sale is about 0.48 if the sum is 6 or less, and about 0.13 otherwise.

**Updated fair value.**
- If the sum is 6 or less, its average is 5.25. That case gets weight 20 × 0.48 ≈ 9.6.
- Otherwise the average is about 11.04, with weight 196 × 0.13 ≈ 25.5.
- The weighted mean is (9.6 × 5.25 + 25.5 × 11.04) / 35.1 ≈ 9.45.

**Quote.**
- Bid: 9.45 − 3.3 ≈ 6.1, shaded down to 5.9 because I'm long.
- Ask: 9.45 + 3.3 ≈ 12.8, shaded down to 12.5 for the same reason.

{"bid": 5.9, "ask": 12.5}

Die 1 = 5, so dice 2 and 3 must add 2 or more and the settlement is at least 7.

**Reading the earlier trades**
- **Quote 1:** the counterparty sold at 6.8. An informed trader would only sell there if the value were 6 or less, which is now impossible. So that trade came from a noise trader and tells us nothing.
- **Quote 2:** the counterparty bought at 12.5. An informed trader buys only if the value is 13 or more, which here means dice 2 + 3 ≥ 8.

**Updating the fair value**
- A noise trader would have bought at 12.5 about 31% of the time. That gives a likelihood of about 0.2 + 0.35 if dice 2 + 3 ≥ 8, and about 0.2 otherwise.
- Before this trade, dice 2 + 3 ≥ 8 had probability 15/36. After it, that probability rises to about 0.66.
- The expected value of dice 2 + 3 is then about 0.66 × 9.33 + 0.34 × 5.33 ≈ 8.0.
- So the fair value is about 13.0.

**Choosing the spread**
Informed traders know the value, which is spread about ±2.3 around fair. Noise traders' valuations are spread ±4.4 around fair. I compared expected profit at different half-spreads: profit from noise trades minus losses to informed trades. It is highest at a half-spread of about 3.5.

{"bid": 9.6, "ask": 16.4}

Die 1 = 5, so the remaining two dice give a sum s = d2 + d3 with prior mean 7.

**Reading the trade history (Bayesian update on s):**
- **Quote 1 (they sold at 6.8):** an informed trader would sell only if the total were 6 or less. With die 1 = 5 that needs s ≤ 1, which is impossible. So this trade tells me nothing about s.
- **Quote 2 (they bought at 12.5):** an informed buyer means a total of 13 or more, so s ≥ 8. This shifts weight toward high s.
- **Quote 3 (they sold at 9.6):** an informed seller means a total of 9 or less, so s ≤ 4. This shifts weight toward low s.

**Combining the two informative trades** (informed probability 0.35, noise trades weighted by their probability at the fair value of the time) gives these relative weights per outcome:
- s ≤ 4: about 0.078
- s = 5 to 7: about 0.022
- s ≥ 8: about 0.070

The posterior mean of s is about 7.25, so **fair value ≈ 12.25**. The distribution is bimodal: mass sits around totals of 7–9 and 13–17.

**Quote choice:** Informed flow will be at the extremes, so I keep a fairly wide spread around 12.25. I lean slightly toward selling because I am long 1.

{"bid": 10.0, "ask": 14.2}

Die 1 = 5 and die 2 = 4, so the settlement is 9 plus die 3. That puts the value between 10 and 15, with a fair value of 12.5. My position is +1, so the ±3 limit isn't a constraint here.

- **Ask:** Any ask of 15 or above can never be hit by an informed trader. Above that point I am only trading against noise traders, and my expected edge is (ask − 12.5) × P(noise valuation > ask). This peaks at an ask of about 15.5–16.0, giving roughly 0.48 per quote. I'll use 15.8.
- **Bid:** The same logic applies in reverse. Any bid of 10 or below is safe from informed sellers, and the edge peaks around 9.0–9.5. I'll use 9.2.

{"bid": 9.2, "ask": 15.8}

**Fair value:** Dice 1 and 2 are known (5 + 4 = 9), so settlement is 9 + die 3. That makes it uniform on 10–15, with a mean of 12.5. The no-trade at 9.2 / 15.8 tells us nothing, because every possible value lies inside that spread. Public fair value stays at 12.5.

**Informed traders (35%):** They only trade if the true value is strictly below my bid or strictly above my ask. With a bid of 10 or lower and an ask of 15 or higher, they never trade with me, so they cost nothing.

**Noise traders (65%):** Their valuation is 12.5 plus Normal noise with SD 4.4. For a half-spread d, the expected gain on one side is 0.65 × Φ(−d/4.4) × d:
- d = 2.5 gives about 0.46.
- d = 3.0 gives about 0.48.
- d = 3.4 gives about 0.485, the peak.
- d = 4.0 gives about 0.47.

**Tightening inside the range:** A bid of 11 earns about 0.30 net and a bid of 10.4 about 0.41, so both do worse. The best quotes sit just outside the 10–15 range, near d ≈ 3.4 on each side.

My position of +1 doesn't change this, since the objective is expected profit and either fill stays within limits.

{"bid": 9.1, "ask": 15.9}

info.raw:
Before anything is revealed, the fair value is 10.5, the expected sum of three dice. The sum's standard deviation is about 2.96. I compared half-spreads by netting what I earn from noise traders against what I lose to informed traders:

- **Half-spread 2.0:** expected profit per side is about 0.17.
- **Half-spread 2.5:** about 0.21.
- **Half-spread 3.0:** about 0.225, the best of these.
- **Half-spread 3.5:** about 0.22.

Profit peaks at a half-spread of about 3, so I quote 7.5 / 13.5.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 13.5}

The public fair value is 10.5, the expected sum of three dice. The no-trade on quote 1 tells us very little, so I'll balance noise-trader profit against losses to informed traders.

For an ask at 10.5 + d, expected profit per quote is roughly 0.65·P(noise > d)·d − 0.35·E[(V − ask)⁺]:

| Ask | Noise profit | Informed loss | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 12.5 | 0.328 | 0.159 | 0.169 |
| 13.0 | 0.329 | 0.113 | 0.215 |
| 13.5 | 0.310 | 0.085 | **0.225** |
| 14.0 | 0.277 | 0.057 | 0.220 |

The best ask is about 13.5. Because the sum's distribution is symmetric, the best bid mirrors it at about 7.5, so I'll keep the same quote.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 13.5}

The fair value is still 10.5, which is the expected sum of three dice. The two quotes with no trade don't move it, because that outcome tells me about equally much about high and low values.

To pick the width, I checked the expected profit per side at different distances h from 10.5. Each side earns from noise traders and loses to informed traders who know the sum.
- **h = 2** gives about +0.17 per side.
- **h = 2.5** gives about +0.22.
- **h = 3** gives about +0.22.
- **h = 3.5** gives about +0.22.

The best width is roughly 2.8 to 3 either side of fair, so I'll keep the current quotes.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 13.5}

Die 1 = 1, so the fair value is 1 + 7 = 8. The other two dice sum to between 2 and 12, so the settlement value lies between 3 and 13.

To set the width, I compared the expected profit from noise traders with the expected loss to informed traders. Noise valuations are 8 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 3. Informed valuations follow the sum of the two remaining dice.

For the ask at 8 + d, the expected profit on that side works out to:

| d | Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|---|
| 1.5 | 9.5 | about 0.16 |
| 2 | 10 | about 0.23 |
| 2.5 | 10.5 | about 0.26 |
| 3 | 11 | about 0.27 (best) |
| 3.5 | 11.5 | about 0.25 |

The bid side is symmetric around 8, so I quote 5 / 11.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 11.0}

Die 1 showed 1, and the other two dice average 7, so the fair value is 1 + 7 = **8**. The settlement value can range from 3 to 13.

The last quote at 5 / 11 got no trade. That is roughly symmetric evidence, so it doesn't move the fair value.

To set the ask, I compared expected profit at several levels. Each figure is the profit from noise traders minus the expected loss to informed traders:

| Ask | Profit from noise traders | Loss to informed traders | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 | ≈ 0.33 | ≈ 0.10 | ≈ 0.23 |
| 10.5 | ≈ 0.33 | ≈ 0.07 | ≈ 0.26 |
| 11 | ≈ 0.31 | ≈ 0.04 | ≈ 0.27 |
| 11.5 | ≈ 0.28 | ≈ 0.02 | ≈ 0.25 |

An ask near 11, three above fair value, is about optimal. The bid works the same way, so 5 is about optimal there too.

{"bid": 5, "ask": 11}

Die 1 showed 1, so the fair value is 1 + 7 = 8. The two hidden dice add −5 to +5 to that, most often 0.

I tested spreads of ±2, ±2.5, ±3 and ±3.5 around 8. For each I weighed the gain from noise traders against the expected loss to informed traders.

- **Noise traders** (valuation 8 plus noise with standard deviation 3) give an expected gain per side of 0.65 × d × P(Z > d/3).
- **Informed traders** cost an expected 0.35 × E[(V − 8 − d)+] per side, where V is the settlement value.

A spread of ±3 gives the highest expected profit, about 0.27 per side:

| d | Noise gain | Informed loss | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 0.328 | 0.097 | 0.231 |
| 2.5 | 0.329 | 0.068 | 0.261 |
| 3 | 0.309 | 0.039 | 0.270 |
| 3.5 | 0.277 | 0.024 | 0.252 |

My position is flat, so I keep the quote symmetric at 5 / 11.

{"bid": 5, "ask": 11}

Die 1 = 1 and die 2 = 6 make 7 so far. The settlement value is 7 plus die 3, so it lies between 8 and 13. The fair value is 10.5.

**Ask side.** Expected profit per quote, with Z a standard normal:
- **Ask 12:** noise traders give 0.65 × P(Z > 0.5) × 1.5 ≈ 0.30. Informed traders lose about 0.06, because they buy when die 3 = 6. Net ≈ 0.24.
- **Ask 12.5:** noise traders give about 0.33. Informed traders lose about 0.03. Net ≈ 0.30.
- **Ask 13:** noise traders give 0.65 × P(Z > 0.83) × 2.5 ≈ 0.33. Informed traders never buy, because the value cannot exceed 13. Net ≈ 0.33.
- **Ask 13.5:** net ≈ 0.31.

An ask of 13 is about optimal. It cannot be hit by an informed trader at a loss to me, and it still earns a good edge from noise traders. By symmetry, the best bid is 8.

{"bid": 8, "ask": 13}

Fair value is 10.5, and quoting 8 / 13 maximises expected profit for this step.

- **Fair value:** Die 1 and die 2 sum to 7, so the contract settles at 8 to 13 with equal probability. The fair value is 10.5.
- **No information from quote 7:** At 8 / 13, an informed trader would never trade, since the value cannot be below 8 or above 13. So the lack of a trade on quote 7 tells us nothing, and fair value stays at 10.5.
- **Ask:** At 13, no informed trader ever buys from me. A noise trader buys with probability P(N(0,3) > 2.5) ≈ 0.20, earning 2.5 each time. That gives about 0.65 × 0.20 × 2.5 ≈ 0.33 expected profit.
  - An ask of 12.75 or 12.9 earns slightly more from noise traders. But it loses more to informed traders when the value is 13, so 13 nets out best.
  - An ask of 13.5 earns less, about 0.31.
- **Bid:** The same reasoning, mirrored, puts the bid at 8.

{"bid": 8, "ask": 13}

Die 1 and die 2 sum to 7, and die 3 is uniform on 1 to 6. So settlement is uniform on 8 to 13, with fair value 10.5. There have been no trades, so the public fair value is also 10.5.

For the ask, I compared expected profit across nearby prices. This adds the gain from noise traders (fair value 10.5 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 3) and the loss to informed traders:
- **Ask 12.5:** expected profit about 0.30. Noise traders contribute about 0.33, and an informed trader who knows the value is 13 costs about 0.03.
- **Ask 12.9:** about 0.32.
- **Ask 13.0:** about 0.33, the best. An informed trader only buys if the value is strictly above 13, which cannot happen, so there is no informed loss. Noise traders contribute about 0.33.
- **Ask 13.5:** about 0.31.

The problem is symmetric around 10.5, so the best bid is 8.0 by the same reasoning. Being at position 0 with one quote left, there is no inventory risk to adjust for.

Three dice are rolled independently.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
- Die 2 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
- Die 3 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
Before anything is revealed, the fair value is the expected sum of three dice: 10.5. The sum has a standard deviation of about 2.96.

I checked how wide to quote on each side by trading off two effects:
- **Noise traders** (65% of arrivals) value the contract at 10.5 plus noise with standard deviation 3. They pay me the half-spread when they cross my quote.
- **Informed traders** (35% of arrivals) only trade when my quote is wrong, and I lose the gap between the true value and my price.

Expected profit per side for each half-spread:

| Half-spread | Gain from noise traders | Loss to informed traders | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.0 | 0.328 | 0.159 | 0.169 |
| 3.0 | 0.31 | 0.085 | 0.225 |
| 3.5 | 0.277 | 0.057 | 0.22 |

A half-spread of about 3 gives the best net result, so I quote 7.5 / 13.5.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 13.5}

The fair value is 10.5 (three dice at 3.5 each), and the sum has a standard deviation of about 2.96. Quote 1 at 7.5 / 13.5 didn't trade, which tells us little, so fair value stays at about 10.5.

I checked the expected edge on the ask side at several prices. For each, the gain is from noise traders buying above fair value, and the loss is from informed traders buying when the dice sum is above the ask.

| Ask | Net expected edge |
|---|---|
| 12.5 | about 0.17 |
| 13.0 | about 0.22 |
| 13.5 | about 0.23 |
| 14.5 | about 0.20 |

An ask of about 13.5 maximises the edge. The bid side is symmetric, so 7.5 is best there. I'll keep the same quote.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 13.5}

I'm treating the counterparty's purchase at 13.5 as evidence that the sum is high, so I'm raising my fair value from 10.5 to about 12.1 and keeping my ask well above it.

1. **Before any trades:** the sum of three dice averages 10.5, with a standard deviation of about 2.96.

2. **Chance of that buy:**
   - An informed trader buys at 13.5 only if the sum is 14 or more. That happens with probability 35/216, about 0.162.
   - When it does, the average sum is 15.
   - A noise trader buys if its valuation is above 13.5, which is 3 above 10.5, or 1 standard deviation. That has probability about 0.159.
   - Overall chance of a buy: 0.35 × 0.162 + 0.65 × 0.159 ≈ 0.160.

3. **Updated fair value:** E[sum | buy] = (0.35 × 0.162 × 15 + 0.65 × 0.159 × 10.5) / 0.160 ≈ 12.1.

4. **Chance the sum is high:** P(sum ≥ 14 | buy) ≈ 0.46. That is a real risk of selling into an informed buyer, so my ask stays near 15.

5. **Bid:** I'm placing it around 10.5. That is roughly 1.6 below fair value, so I still earn spread from noise sellers. Buying here also moves my short position of -1 back toward flat.

{"bid": 10.5, "ask": 15.0}

The settlement is die 1 + die 2 + die 3 = 4 + T, where T is the sum of the two hidden dice. Without other information T would average 7, giving a fair value of 11.

**Using the trade history.** I updated the distribution of T from the two quotes after the first.
- **Quote 2 (buy at 13.5):** an informed trader buys only if the sum is at least 14, meaning T ≥ 10. A noise trader buys about 16% of the time. So this trade raises the weight on high T.
- **Quote 3 (no trade at 10.5 / 15):** an informed trader stays out only if the sum is between 11 and 14, meaning 7 ≤ T ≤ 10. A noise trader stays out about 50% of the time. So this lowers the weight on the extremes.

Combining these with the normal two-dice odds gives E[T] ≈ 8.5. The fair value is therefore about 12.5.

**Quote.**
- **Ask 14.4:** an informed trader buys only if T ≥ 11, about 15% likely, and the expected loss on that is small. A noise trader buys about 25% of the time, earning me roughly 2 each time.
- **Bid 10.6:** an informed trader sells only if T ≤ 6, about 17% likely, and the expected loss is about 1.5. Noise traders sell about 25% of the time, earning me roughly 2 each time.
- **Position:** I am short 1, so I set the quote slightly high around fair value.

{"bid": 10.6, "ask": 14.4}

Die 1 = 4, so before any trades the expected sum is 4 + 7 = 11. The trade history moves this up.

**Bayesian update on the remaining two dice (T = d2 + d3, sum S = 4 + T):**
- **Quote 2, they bought at 13.5:** an informed trader does this only if S ≥ 14. A noise trader does it about 10% of the time (0.65 × P(N > 13.5) ≈ 0.10). So this trade strongly favours high sums.
- **Quote 3, no trade at 10.5 / 15:** this favours S between 11 and 15.
- **Quote 4, no trade at 10.6 / 14.4:** this favours S between 11 and 14.

Combining these likelihoods with the 2d6 prior puts most of the weight on S = 11 to 14. S = 14 alone is about 36% of the posterior. The posterior mean is about 12.8.

**Quote:**
- I centre on about 12.8. I skew slightly upward because I'm short one unit and the informed flow so far has been buying.
- Informed traders' values cluster between 11 and 15, so I keep the spread fairly wide, about ±1.5, to limit losses to them.
- This still captures noise traders, whose valuations have a standard deviation of 3.

{"bid": 11.5, "ask": 14.5}

Die 1 = 4, so the settlement value is 4 + (die 2 + die 3). Before any trading the fair value is 4 + 7 = 11.

**What the trades tell us.** I used a Bayesian update on the sum of dice 2 and 3, with informed traders 35% of the time and noise traders at roughly N(11, 3) otherwise.

- **Quote 4 (10.6 / 14.4), no trade.** An informed trader would not trade if the value is 11 to 14. So the sums 7 to 10 become more likely.
- **Quote 5 (ask 14.5), they bought.** An informed trader would only buy if the value is at least 15, meaning die 2 + die 3 is 11 or 12. A noise trader buys there only about 12% of the time. So this trade pushes the estimate up.

**Posterior.** Combining both, the expected sum of dice 2 and 3 is about 8.2. The fair value is therefore about **12.2**.

**Quote.** I'm short 2, so I shade both prices slightly up to make buying back more likely. The spread stays fairly wide because informed traders know the value exactly.

{"bid": 11.2, "ask": 13.8}

The sum of the first two dice is known: 4 + 4 = 8. So the settlement value is 8 + die 3, which is uniform on 9 to 14 with mean 11.5.

**Ask side.** Expected profit at ask *a* is the noise-trader gain minus the informed-trader loss:
0.65·P(11.5 + 3Z > a)·(a − 11.5) − 0.35·E[(v − a)⁺]

- a = 13: 0.65 × 0.309 × 1.5 − 0.35 × (1/6) ≈ 0.24
- a = 13.5: 0.65 × 0.252 × 2.0 − 0.35 × (0.5/6) ≈ 0.30
- a = 14: 0.65 × 0.202 × 2.5 − 0 ≈ 0.33 (best)
- a = 14.1: 0.65 × 0.193 × 2.6 ≈ 0.33, roughly equal but slightly lower

At 14 or above, an informed trader can never profit by buying, so 14 is the best ask.

**Bid side.** The problem is symmetric around 11.5, so the best bid is 9. At that price an informed seller can never profit.

My position is only −1, so I don't need to skew the quotes.

{"bid": 9, "ask": 14}

The sum is 8 plus die 3, so it settles uniformly between 9 and 14. The expected value is 11.5.

The sale at 9 in quote 7 must have come from a noise trader. An informed trader would only sell at 9 if the value were below 9, which cannot happen. So that trade tells us nothing, and the public fair value stays 11.5.

- A noise trader, centred on about 11.4, does nothing with probability about 0.38.
- So no trade has likelihood 0.2 + 0.8 × 0.38 ≈ 0.51 if S is 5, 6 or 7, and about 0.31 otherwise.
- Combining both quotes gives an expected S of about 6.3, so fair value is about 11.3.

**Quote.** I set a half-spread of about 1.4 around 11.3. That guards against the informed traders while still trading with noise traders, whose valuations have a standard deviation of 3. I lean the quote slightly lower so I'm more likely to sell and reduce my long position of +2.

{"bid": 9.8, "ask": 12.6}

Dice 1 and 2 are revealed, so the settlement is 11 + die 3. That puts it somewhere from 12 to 17, with a mean of 14.5.

**Setting the ask.** An informed trader buys only if the settlement value is above my ask. A noise trader values the contract at 14.5 + N(0, 3).
- Ask 15.1: expected profit ≈ +0.20 from noise traders, −0.09 from informed traders, net ≈ 0.11.
- Ask 16.1: net ≈ 0.35.
- Ask 17.0: net ≈ 0.405. The informed trader never buys, because the value can never be above 17.
- Ask 17.2: net ≈ 0.40, so pushing higher does not help.

An ask of 17.0 is the best choice.

**Setting the bid.** The same logic applies in reverse, so a bid of 12.0 is best. The informed trader never sells, because the value can never be below 12.

My position of +1 sits well within the limits. Since I only care about expected profit, it doesn't change the quote.

{"bid": 12.0, "ask": 17.0}

With dice 1 and 2 revealed (5 + 6 = 11), the settlement value is 11 plus die 3, so it is equally likely to be any whole number from 12 to 17. Fair value is **14.5**.

Quote 7 at 12 / 17 drew no trade. An informed trader would not trade there either, so the no-trade tells us almost nothing and fair value stays 14.5.

**Choosing the ask**

Expected profit for an ask at a is roughly: 0.8 × P(noise valuation > a) × (a − 14.5), plus the informed trader's expected loss. The informed trader only buys when the settlement value is above a.

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 15.5 | ≈ 0.23 |
| 16.0 | ≈ 0.34 |
| 16.5 | ≈ 0.39 |
| 17.0 | ≈ 0.405 (informed trader never buys) |
| 17.1 | ≈ 0.40 |

An ask of 17 is about optimal. By symmetry, a bid of 12 is also about optimal. My position limits are not binding, so I don't need to skew the quotes for inventory.

{"bid": 12, "ask": 17}

No trades so far in stage 3 tell us anything about die 3, so the fair value is still 14.5.

**Why fair value is 14.5**
- Dice 1 and 2 are revealed as 5 and 6, so the settlement value is 11 + die 3. That is 12 to 17, each equally likely, with mean 14.5.
- At quote 7 nobody traded at 12/17. An informed trader would have no reason to trade at either price, since the value can never be below 12 or above 17. So the lack of a trade tells us nothing.
- At quote 8 someone bought at 17. An informed trader would never pay 17, because the value is at most 17. So the buyer was a noise trader, and this also tells us nothing about die 3.

**Choosing the spread**
- The counterparty is informed with probability 0.2 and is a noise trader with probability 0.8. A noise trader's valuation is 14.5 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 3.
- Write the ask as 14.5 + d. The expected profit on the ask side is 0.8 × P(noise > d) × d, minus any losses to informed traders when the value is above the ask.
  - **d = 2.0 (ask 16.5):** noise profit is about 0.404. An informed trader buys when the value is 17, costing 0.5 with weight 0.2 × 1/6, about 0.017. Net is about 0.387.
  - **d = 2.5 (ask 17.0):** noise profit is 0.8 × 0.202 × 2.5, about 0.405. There is no loss to informed traders, since the value is never above 17. Net is about 0.405.
  - **d = 3.0 (ask 17.5):** noise profit is about 0.381, with no informed loss.
- So an ask of 17 is best. The bid side is symmetric, giving a bid of 12.

{"bid": 12, "ask": 17}

game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (8 faces, each equally likely): 0, 1, 3, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12.

- Die 3 (8 faces, each equally likely): 1, 3, 3, 3, 5, 6, 9, 9.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
Fair value is the sum of the three dice expectations:

- **Die 2:** 0.3·1 + 0.1·7 + 0.4·9 + 0.2·11 = 6.8
- **Die 3:** 39/8 = 4.875
- **Expected sum:** 18.425

The standard deviation of the sum is about 6.5 (variances roughly 19.4 + 15.6 + 7.6).

Half the counterparties know the true value. So the quote needs a fairly wide spread around 18.4 to make up for losses to informed traders, while still catching some noise flow. I'll quote about ±4.4 either side of fair value.

{"bid": 14.0, "ask": 22.9}

The contract's expected value is about **18.4**, so I'm quoting **14.9 bid / 21.9 ask** to protect against informed traders.

**Expected value of each die**
- Die 1: (0+1+3+8+9+10+11+12)/8 = 6.75
- Die 2: 0.3·1 + 0.1·7 + 0.4·9 + 0.2·11 = 6.8
- Die 3: (1+3+3+3+5+6+9+9)/8 = 4.875

**Spread of the sum**

**Quote**
- The last quote (14 / 22.9) got no trade. That only slightly suggests the value is near the middle, so fair value stays about 18.4.
- Informed traders' values are spread as widely as the noise traders' (both about 6.5), so I need a fairly wide quote.
- I'm tightening slightly from last time, to about ±3.5 around fair value.

{"bid": 14.9, "ask": 21.9}

Fair value is about 18.4, and I'm quoting 15.5 / 21.4 around it.

**Fair value.** The expected value of each die:
- Die 1 = 54/8 = 6.75.
- Die 2 = 0.3·1 + 0.1·7 + 0.4·9 + 0.2·11 = 6.8.
- Die 3 = 39/8 = 4.875.

The expected sum is 18.425, and the standard deviation of the total is about 6.5. Neither earlier quote traded, and both were roughly centred on fair value, so that tells me little and I keep fair value near 18.4.

**Spread.** Half of the counterparties know the true value, so a quote that is too tight loses to them. I'm narrowing the spread slightly from last time to pick up some noise-trader flow.

{"bid": 15.5, "ask": 21.4}

I estimate fair value at about 11.7 and quote a wide market around it: bid 7.0, ask 16.0.

**Fair value**
- Die 1 averages 6.75 and die 2 averages 6.8.
- With die 3 = 1, the sum of dice 1 and 2 (call it S) averages 13.55, so the starting estimate is 14.55.

**What the earlier sale tells us**
- Someone sold to me at 15.5 back in stage 1. An informed trader does that only if the total is below 15.5. With die 3 = 1, that means S < 14.5, which had probability 0.5625 before the trade.
- A noise trader would have sold at 15.5 about 33% of the time.
- Updating on the sale, the chance that S < 14.5 rises to about 84%.
- If S < 14.5, S averages about 9.09; if not, about 19.29.
- So S is now expected at about 10.74, and the fair value is about 11.74.

**The value is split into two clusters**
- There is a large group of outcomes from about 2 to 15 and a small group from about 16 to 24.
- On the buy side, the risk is selling to informed traders when the value is in the high group. An ask around 16–17 gives a positive expected edge after those losses.
- On the sell side, the risk is buying from informed traders when the value is very low (S of 1, 2 or 4). A bid around 6.5–7 gives a positive edge.
- I am already long one unit, so I keep the bid low.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 16.0}

Fair value is about 11.8. I'm quoting a bid of 8.5 and an ask of 14, slightly skewed toward selling because I'm long one unit.

**Prior.** Die 3 is revealed as 1. The expected value of die 1 is 6.75 and of die 2 is 6.8, so the prior expected total T is 14.55.

**Updating on the trade history.** I treated each quote's outcome as evidence about T, with each counterparty informed or noise at 50/50.

- **Quote 3 (stage 1):** someone sold to me at 15.5. An informed seller does this only if T < 15.5. A noise trader sells with probability about 0.33, since the stage‑1 fair value was about 18.4. This makes T < 15.5 about four times more likely than T ≥ 15.5.
- **Quote 4:** there was no trade at 7 / 16. An informed trader stays out only if T is between 7 and 16. A noise trader stays out with probability about 0.47. This makes T in [7, 16] about three times more likely than T outside it.

**Posterior.** I enumerated the joint outcomes of dice 1 and 2 and applied both likelihoods. The posterior puts most of its weight on T between 8 and 15, has a small low tail (T = 2, 3, 5) and little weight above 16. The posterior mean is about 11.8.

**Quote.** I centred the quote near 11.8, with enough width to protect against informed flow.

{"bid": 8.5, "ask": 14}

The posterior fair value is about 12.2. I'll quote 10.2 / 13.8, leaning slightly lower because I'm long one unit.

**Prior expectation.** Die 1 averages 6.75 and die 2 averages 6.8. With die 3 revealed as 1, the expected sum is 14.55.

**What the no-trade quotes tell me.**
- In stage 2 there was no trade at quote 4 (7 / 16) or quote 5 (8.5 / 14).
- An informed counterparty would have traded unless the true value were inside those ranges.
- So, weighted by the noise trader's no-trade probabilities, the posterior shifts towards sums between 9 and 14.

**Posterior.** Weighting each possible sum by how likely those two no-trades were, the posterior fair value comes out at about 12.2. Most of the probability now sits on sums of 10 to 14.

**Quote.** I centre near 12 and lean slightly lower to reduce my long position.

{"bid": 10.2, "ask": 13.8}

The contract now settles at die 1 + 3. Die 1 is uniform on {0, 1, 3, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12}, so the settlement value is one of {3, 4, 6, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15}, each with probability 1/8. The fair value is 6.75 + 3 = **9.75**. No trades have happened yet in stage 3, so the public fair value is also 9.75.

Each quote earns money only from noise traders. Their valuation is 9.75 + N(0, 6.5).

**Ask side**
- An ask of 15 never trades with an informed counterparty, because no outcome is above 15.
- A noise trader buys with probability P(z > 0.81) ≈ 0.21.
- Expected profit is 0.5 × 0.21 × 5.25 ≈ 0.55.
- Lowering the ask to 14 lets informed traders buy when the value is 15, and the expected profit falls to about 0.48.
- Raising the ask to 16 cuts noise fills, and the expected profit falls to about 0.53.

**Bid side**
- A bid of 3 never trades with an informed counterparty, because no outcome is below 3.
- A noise trader sells with probability P(z < −1.04) ≈ 0.15.
- Expected profit is 0.5 × 0.15 × 6.75 ≈ 0.50.
- Raising the bid to 4 lets informed traders sell when the value is 3, and the expected profit falls to about 0.48.

My position is +1, so either fill keeps me within the ±3 limit.

{"bid": 3, "ask": 15}

The contract is now worth 2 + die 1, because die 2 = 1 and die 3 = 1 are revealed.

**Possible values.** Die 1 has eight equally likely faces, so the settlement is one of 2, 3, 5, 10, 11, 12, 13 or 14, each with probability 1/8. The public fair value is 2 + 6.75 = 8.75. Quote 7 (bid 3, ask 15) drew no trade. All but one possible value lies inside that range, so it reveals almost nothing.

**Ask side.**
- At an ask of 14, informed traders never buy, because no settlement value is above 14.
- Noise traders buy about 21% of the time, earning me about 5.25 per trade.
- Expected profit is about 0.55.
- An ask of 13.1 is worse, about 0.49, because informed traders who know the value is 14 would buy.

**Bid side.**
- At a bid of 2, informed traders never sell, because no settlement value is below 2.
- Noise traders sell about 15% of the time, earning me about 6.75 per trade.
- Expected profit is about 0.50.
- A bid of 2.9 is worse, about 0.48, because informed traders who know the value is 2 would sell.

My position limits are not a constraint here.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 14.0}

The contract now settles at 2 + die 1, since die 2 = 1 and die 3 = 1 are revealed. That makes the possible values 2, 3, 5, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 14.

**Updating on the stage-3 history**
- Before stage-3 trading, the public fair value was 2 + 6.75 = 8.75.
- At quote 7 (bid 3, ask 15) nobody traded. An informed trader holding a value of 2 would have sold at 3, so no trade makes 2 less likely.
- After this update the probabilities are about 0.053 for value 2 and about 0.135 for each other value. The fair value rises to about 9.3.
- At quote 8 (bid 2, ask 14) no informed trader would have traded at any value, so it carries no information.

**Choosing the ask**
- At 14 or above, informed traders never buy from me.
- A noise buyer pays 14 and I gain about 4.7. This gives an expected profit of about 0.55, close to the best available.
- Asks inside 10 to 13 lose heavily to informed buyers.

**Choosing the bid**
- At 3, only a value of 2 sells to me as informed, and that is rare after the update.
- Noise sellers give an expected gain of about 0.52, against an informed loss of about 0.03. The net is about 0.50, which beats a bid of 2 (about 0.48) or 4 (about 0.43).

A position of +1 leaves room to trade on either side.

game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (4 faces, each equally likely): 0, 1, 4, 10.
- Die 2 (8 faces, each equally likely): 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 4, 4, 9.
- Die 3 (8 faces, each equally likely): 0, 2, 7, 7, 8, 8, 9, 9.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
The contract settles at the sum of the three dice. Before any reveals, my fair value is 12.5 and the spread of outcomes has a standard deviation of about 5.8.

**Expected value of each die**
- Die 1: (0 + 1 + 4 + 10)/4 = 3.75
- Die 2: 20/8 = 2.5
- Die 3: 50/8 = 6.25
- Total: 12.5

**Variance of each die**
- Die 1: about 15.2
- Die 2: 8.5
- Die 3: about 9.9
- Total: about 33.6, so the standard deviation is about 5.8.

**Setting the spread**
Informed traders know the true settlement value, which has a standard deviation of about 5.8. Noise traders also scatter around the fair value with a standard deviation of 5.8.

Treating the settlement value as roughly normal, the expected profit per side at half-spread h = xσ is proportional to 2x·Q(x) − φ(x). Here Q(x) is the chance a normal variable exceeds x, and φ(x) is the normal density at x. This is largest at about x ≈ 1.2, which gives a half-spread of about 7.

I'll quote around 12.5 with that width.

{"bid": 6.0, "ask": 19.0}

The prior mean of the sum is 3.75 + 2.5 + 6.25 = 12.5, with a standard deviation of about 5.8.

The trade at my bid of 6 changes this:
- **Informed seller:** this happens only if the value is below 6, which has probability about 0.11. Given that, the mean value is about 2.75.
- **Noise seller:** a noise trader sells below 6 with probability about 0.13.
- **Posterior:** an informed sale is about 45% likely and a noise sale about 55%. So the fair value is roughly 0.45 × 2.75 + 0.55 × 12.5 ≈ 8.1.

The posterior has two humps: one near 3 and one near 12.5. That makes informed trading costly on both sides, so I keep the spread wide. The bid is extra-low because the low hump sits largely below 4. I'm long one unit, so I lean the quote slightly lower.

{"bid": 3, "ask": 13}

Quoting a bid of 9 and an ask of 16, roughly symmetric around my estimate of the contract's value.

1. **Prior expected value.** The averages are 3.75 for die 1, 2.5 for die 2 and 6.25 for die 3. So before any trading the sum is expected to be 12.5, with a standard deviation of about 5.8.

2. **What the trades tell me.** One counterparty sold at 6, which an informed trader would only do if the value were below 6. Another bought at 13, which an informed trader would only do if the value were above 13. Both can't be informed, so at least one was a noise trader. The signals roughly cancel, and I keep my estimate near 12.5.

3. **Quote width.** The value is still very uncertain and half of counterparties know it exactly. So I need a fairly wide spread, about 3.5 on each side of 12.5, to protect against informed traders. It is still narrow enough that some noise traders will trade with me.

{"bid": 9, "ask": 16}

With die 1 = 0, I estimate fair value at about 8.6. That makes the best quote very wide: **bid 1, ask 17.5**.

**Prior.** The settlement value is now S = die 2 + die 3. Die 2 averages 2.5 and die 3 averages 6.25, so the prior mean is 8.75.

**Update from the stage-1 trades.** In stage 1 the sale at 6 and the buys at 13 and 16 all happened before die 1 was revealed. Each was equally likely a priori to come from an informed trader or a noise trader.
- With die 1 = 0, the buy at 16 is very informative: S above 16 requires die 2 = 9, giving S = 17 or 18.
- The sale at 6 points to S being low (S ≤ 4).
- The trades conflict, so the result is a two-peaked distribution:

| Range of S | Probability | Typical value |
|---|---|---|
| Low, S ≤ 4 | about 46% | around 2 |
| High, S = 17–18 | about 30% | around 17.5 |
| Middle | about 21% | around 9–10 |

That gives an expected value of about 8.6.

**Choosing the quote.** An informed trader will hit any bid above the low cluster and lift any ask below the high cluster. Tight quotes are therefore heavily negative in expectation: for example, a bid at 5 is worth about −0.7 and an ask at 10 about −1.0. Very wide quotes still catch some noise trades, which value the contract at about 8.6 ± 5.8:
- **Bid near 1:** an informed trader sells only if S = 0, about a 12% chance. Noise traders sell about 9.5% of the time for about 7.6 profit. Expected value is about +0.30.
- **Ask near 17.5:** an informed trader buys only if S = 18. Noise traders buy about 6% of the time for about 9 profit. Expected value is about +0.24.

{"bid": 1, "ask": 17.5}

The public fair value is about 8.45. The likely settlement values form two separate clusters, so I'm quoting wide: bid 1.9, ask 17.1.

**What we know.** Die 1 is 0, so settlement equals die 2 plus die 3. Before any trades, that sum has mean 2.5 + 6.25 = 8.75.

**Updating on the four trades.** I weighed how likely each possible sum is given the history:
- Quote 1: someone sold at 6.
- Quote 2: someone bought at 13.
- Quote 3: someone bought at 16.
- Quote 4: no trade at 1 / 17.5.

After that update, the sum falls into three groups:

| Sum | Probability | Average sum in group |
|---|---|---|
| 0 to 4 | about 46% | about 2.3 |
| 6 to 13 | about 25% | — |
| 16 to 18 | about 29% | about 17 |

The overall expected value is about 8.45.

**Choosing the quotes.** Expected profit per side, counting both trader types:
- **Ask:** Asks below 16 get picked off by informed traders who know the sum is high. An ask of 17.1 loses only when the sum is 18 (about 8%). It still collects some noise-trader buys at roughly 8.6 above fair value, for about +0.26 expected profit.
- **Bid:** Bids above 4 get picked off by informed traders who know the sum is low. A bid of 1.9 loses only when the sum is 0 or 1 (about 10%). It collects noise-trader sells at roughly 6.5 below fair value, for about +0.35 expected profit.

{"bid": 1.9, "ask": 17.1}

Die 1 came up 0, so the settlement value is die 2 + die 3, which can be anywhere from 0 to 18. Before any trading, its average was 8.75.

**What the trades tell me**
- **Quote 4:** nobody traded at 1 / 17.5. This slightly favours values strictly between 1 and 17.5.
- **Quote 5:** a buyer lifted my 17.1 ask.
  - An informed trader only buys there if the sum is 18 (die 2 = 9 and die 3 = 9). That outcome has prior probability 2/64.
  - A noise trader buys there only about 7.5% of the time.
  - So the buy makes 18 far more likely: its probability rises to about 18%.
- Updating on both quotes, the fair value is about 10.4.

**Ask side**
- At 17.5, only a sum of 18 gets an informed buyer. That costs me about 0.05 in expectation.
- Noise traders buy about 11% of the time, at roughly 7 above fair. That gains about 0.39.
- 17.5 nets slightly more than 16.5 or 17.

**Bid side**
- Around 4–5, informed sellers appear only for low sums (0–4), which are now unlikely. That costs about 0.11 to 0.18.
- Noise sellers hit the bid often enough to gain about 0.43 to 0.48.
- I pick 4.5, between the two, and buying would also reduce my short position.

{"bid": 4.5, "ask": 17.5}

Die 1 = 0 and die 3 = 9, so settlement is 9 + die 2. The possible values are 9, 9, 9, 10, 11, 13, 13 and 18. The prior mean is 11.5.

**What the trade history says about die 2**
- **Buys above 16:** given what is now known, only die 2 = 9 makes the value exceed 16. Earlier counterparties bought at asks of 13, 16 and 17.1, which is hard to explain unless die 2 = 9 and informed traders were buying.
- **No trade at an ask of 17.5:** this happened twice, which weakens the case slightly.
- **Combined:** the likelihood ratio comes out around 40 or more in favour of die 2 = 9. That gives P(die 2 = 9) ≈ 0.85.
- **Fair value:** about 0.85 × 18 + 0.15 × 10.6 ≈ 17.

**Ask:** At or above 18, informed traders never buy. Noise traders centred near 17 still buy often enough. Weighing how often they buy against my edge per unit sold, the expected value is highest around an ask of 20 to 21.

**Bid:** If die 2 is not 9, informed traders sell to me, so I keep the bid well below fair. Weighing the gain from noise sellers against that risk, the best bid is around 13.5 to 14.

{"bid": 14, "ask": 20}

Settlement is 9 plus die 2, since die 1 = 0 and die 3 = 9. The possible values are 9, 9, 9, 10, 11, 13, 13 and 18, each with probability 1/8, so the fair value is 11.5.

The buy at 20 on quote 7 must have come from a noise trader, because an informed trader only buys when the value is above 20. That trade tells us nothing about die 2, so the public fair value stays at 11.5.

**Ask:** At 18, an informed trader never buys, because the value is never above 18. Noise traders buy about 13% of the time, at a profit of 6.5. That gives an expected 0.5 × 0.131 × 6.5 ≈ 0.43 from this side. A tighter ask such as 15.9 does worse, about 0.37, because informed traders buy whenever the value is 18.

**Bid:** At 9 or below, an informed trader never sells, because the value is never below 9. Expected profit from noise sellers at different bids:
- At 9: about 0.42.
- At 7.5: about 0.49.
- At 7: about 0.49.

A bid of 10 does worse, because informed traders would sell whenever the value is 9.

My position after this quote stays within the limit of -4 to +4 whichever side trades.

{"bid": 7.2, "ask": 18}

With die 1 = 0 and die 3 = 9 revealed, the settlement value is 9 plus die 2. That gives these possible values:

| Value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 9 | 3/8 |
| 10 | 1/8 |
| 11 | 1/8 |
| 13 | 2/8 |
| 18 | 1/8 |

The expected value is 11.5.

**What the trades so far tell us.** The buy at 20 on quote 7 must have come from a noise trader, because an informed trader's value is at most 18. Quote 8 (7.2 / 18) had no trade, which every informed type would also produce. So neither trade changes the estimate, and the public fair value stays at 11.5.

**Ask.**
- At 18, an informed trader never buys, since they only buy when their value is strictly above the ask. A noise trader buys with probability about 0.5 × 13% and I gain 6.5 when they do. Expected value is about +0.43.
- Lower asks bring in more noise buyers. At 17 or below, though, I start selling to an informed trader holding 18 at a loss, and the total comes out slightly worse.
- I'll set the ask at 18.

**Bid.**
- A bid at 9 or below is never hit by an informed trader, since they only sell when their value is strictly below the bid.
- Going lower trades fewer noise sales for a bigger edge on each one. Expected value is about +0.49 at bids of 7 to 7.5, which is the peak.
- I'll set the bid at 7.2.
- Being filled would take my position from -3 to -2, which is within the limit.

{"bid": 7.2, "ask": 18}

game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (4 faces, each equally likely): 0, 1, 4, 10.
- Die 2 (8 faces, each equally likely): 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 4, 4, 9.
- Die 3 (8 faces, each equally likely): 0, 2, 7, 7, 8, 8, 9, 9.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
Fair value is the expected sum of the three dice:

- Die 1: (0 + 1 + 4 + 10) / 4 = 3.75
- Die 2: 20 / 8 = 2.5
- Die 3: 50 / 8 = 6.25
- Total: **12.5**

The variance of the sum is about 33.6, so its standard deviation is about 5.8. That is roughly the same spread as the noise traders' valuations.

**Choosing the half-spread.** Half the counterparties know the true value, so they only trade when it beats my price. Treating the sum as roughly normal, I traded off two things:

- What I earn from noise traders who cross the quote.
- What I lose to informed traders when the true value lies beyond the quote.

That trade-off is best at a half-spread of about 1.2 standard deviations, which is about 6.9.

**Quote:** 12.5 − 6.9 = 5.6 bid and 12.5 + 6.9 = 19.4 ask.

{"bid": 5.6, "ask": 19.4}

Prior expected value of the sum is 3.75 + 2.5 + 6.25 = 12.5.

**What the first trade tells us.** The counterparty bought at 19.4, and the two possible buyer types were about equally likely:
- **Informed buyer:** buys only if the sum is at least 20. That happens with probability 31/256 ≈ 0.12. In those cases the expected sum is about 22.4.
- **Noise trader:** buys with probability about 0.117. This tells us nothing about the dice, so the expected sum stays 12.5.

Weighting the two cases gives an updated fair value of about 17.5. The value distribution is now two-humped: about half the weight is on the high cases (20–28) and the rest is on the original prior.

**Where to quote.** Informed traders make up half the flow, so adverse selection is severe on both sides.
- **Bid:** Bids near fair value lose money, mainly to informed sellers when the value is low. Expected profit only reaches about break-even near a bid of 8–9, so I bid 8.
- **Ask:** Asks around 24–25 maximise expected profit. Informed buyers above that level take only small losses from me, while noise buyers still pay well above value. So I ask 24.5.

{"bid": 8.0, "ask": 24.5}

The prior expected sum is 3.75 + 2.5 + 6.25 = 12.5.

**What the history tells me**
- **Quote 1:** someone bought at 19.4.
  - An informed trader buys only if the sum is above 19.4. That happens with probability about 0.12.
  - A noise trader buys with probability about 0.12 as well (its valuation is 12.5 plus noise, so it must exceed 12.5 by 6.9).
  - Given the sum is above 19.4, its expected value is about 22.4.
  - Updating on this buy moves the expected sum to roughly 17.5.
- **Quote 2:** nobody traded at 8 / 24.5. That slightly penalises very low and very high sums, so it is mildly informative.
- **Current estimate:** the public fair value is about 17.

**Quote choice**
- The contract value is spread widely and half the counterparties are informed, so adverse selection is costly and I need a wide spread.
- I am short 1, so I'll centre the quote near 17, slightly skewed up.

{"bid": 12.5, "ask": 22.0}

The fair value is about 19.8, so I'm quoting a wide spread around it: bid 16.5, ask 23.

**Prior after the reveal.** Die 1 is 10. Die 2 averages 2.5 and die 3 averages 6.25, so the fair value is 10 + 8.75 = 18.75 before using the trading history.

**What the history says.** I let each counterparty be informed with probability 0.5. I approximated a noise trader as valuing near 18.75–19.5.
- **Quote 1:** a buy at 19.4 supports a total above 19.4, meaning dice 2 and 3 sum to 10 or more.
- **Quotes 2 and 3:** no trade at 8 / 24.5 and at 12.5 / 22 supports a total between 12.5 and 22.

Weighting the 64 combinations of dice 2 and 3 by these likelihoods gives an expected sum of about 9.77. The fair value is therefore about 19.8, with most weight on totals of 20, 21 and 22.

**Bid.** Informed traders would sell to me only if the value is 16 or lower, which has about a 10% chance. A bid of 16.5 still catches enough noise sellers to make roughly +0.3 per quote.

**Ask.** Values of 26 or more have only about a 3% chance. An ask near 23 catches noise buyers with an edge of about 3.2 while losing little to informed buyers.

Being short 1 unit is fine with this slight upward lean.

{"bid": 16.5, "ask": 23}

Die 1 is revealed as 10, so the settlement value is 10 plus the sum S of dice 2 and 3. Unconditionally, die 2 averages 2.5 and die 3 averages 6.25, giving a fair value of 18.75.

**What the history tells us**

- **Quote 4 (16.5 / 23, no trade):** an informed trader would have traded unless S was between 6.5 and 13.
  - Before this quote, S lands in 7–13 in 44 of 64 cases.
  - A noise trader stays out about 42% of the time at these prices.
  - So no trade is about 0.71 likely when S is in 7–13 and about 0.21 likely otherwise.
  - Updating on this gives a posterior mean for S of about 9.3, so the total is about 19.3.
- **Quote 1 (bought at my 19.4 ask):** if that buyer was informed, S is above 9.4. This pushes the estimate up slightly.

My fair value estimate is about 19.5, with most of the probability between 17 and 23.

**Quote**

- I post a two-sided quote around 19.5, wide enough to limit losses to informed traders.
- I am short one unit and the evidence leans upward, so the ask sits a bit further from fair than the bid.

{"bid": 17.5, "ask": 22}

**Fair value: about 20.4.**

1. **Prior.** Die 1 is revealed as 10. Die 2 has an expected value of 2.5 and die 3 has an expected value of 6.25. Before using the trading history, the expected settlement is 10 + 2.5 + 6.25 = 18.75.

2. **Update from trading history.**
   - Quote 1: the counterparty bought at 19.4. That makes it more likely the value is above 19.4.
   - Quotes 4 and 5 had no trade, at 16.5 / 23 and 17.5 / 22. An informed counterparty would have traded unless the value sat inside those spreads. So the value is most likely between 17.5 and 22.
   - Weighing each possible die 2 + die 3 total by these likelihoods puts most of the weight on totals 8 to 12. That means settlement values of about 18 to 22, with an expected total near 10.4.

3. **Quote choice.**
   - Noise traders' valuations have a large spread (standard deviation 5.8). So a fairly wide quote still trades with them often, and each such trade earns more.
   - Informed traders mostly hold values between 18 and 22. A bid near 17 and an ask near 23.4 rarely trade with them.
   - I'm short 1, so a slightly lower centre is fine.

{"bid": 17.2, "ask": 23.4}

With die 1 = 10 and die 3 = 8, the settlement is 18 plus die 2. Die 2 makes the settlement:

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 18 | 3/8 |
| 19 | 1/8 |
| 20 | 1/8 |
| 22 | 2/8 |
| 27 | 1/8 |

The public fair value is 20.5. Noise traders value the contract at 20.5 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 5.8.

**Ask side.** An informed trader buys only when the true value is above my ask. Any ask between 22 and 27 risks selling to an informed trader when the value is 27.
- Each 1-point move of the ask cuts that loss by only 1/16 of a point in expectation.
- The extra profit per noise trade rises faster than the fill rate falls, up to about 27.
- At an ask of 27, an informed trader never buys. A noise trade earns about 6.5 and happens about 13% of the time, giving roughly +0.43 per quote.

**Bid side.** A bid at or below 18 cannot be hit by an informed trader, because no settlement is below 18.
- Lowering the bid further raises the expected noise profit, which peaks around 16 at about +0.49 per quote.

Being short 1 unit leaves plenty of room within the position limits on both sides.

{"bid": 16, "ask": 27}

The settlement value is 18 plus Die 2, since Die 1 = 10 and Die 3 = 8 are revealed. Die 2 can be 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 4, 4 or 9, so the possible settlements are 18, 18, 18, 19, 20, 22, 22 and 27, each with probability 1/8. The mean, and so the public fair value, is 20.5. Quote 7 did not trade, but no possible value would have traded at 16 / 27, so it tells us nothing.

**Bid:**
- If the bid is at or below 18, an informed trader never sells to us, because no settlement value is below 18.
- So the bid is set only by noise traders, who sell with probability Φ((b − 20.5)/5.8) and earn me 20.5 − b per unit.
- Expected profit is 0.5 × (20.5 − b) × Φ((b − 20.5)/5.8). This peaks at about b ≈ 16.2, worth about +0.49.
- Bidding above 18 starts losing to informed sellers when the value is 18, and that costs more than it gains.

**Ask:**
- An informed buyer only hurts me when the settlement is 27 (probability 1/8). The loss is 27 − a per unit.
- Expected profit at different asks:

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 24 | +0.29 |
| 25 | +0.37 |
| 26 | +0.41 |
| 26.5 | +0.42 |
| 26.9 | +0.43 |
| 27 | +0.43 |

- The curve is flat near 26.9, so I'll quote there.

Position limits don't bind: I'm at −1 with two quotes left.

{"bid": 16.2, "ask": 26.9}

With one quote left, I set each side to maximise expected profit on this single trade.

**Fair value.** Die 1 (10) and die 3 (8) are known, so 18 is fixed. Die 2 averages (0+0+0+1+2+4+4+9)/8 = 2.5. The possible settlements are {18, 18, 18, 19, 20, 22, 22, 27}, with mean 20.5. That is the noise traders' centre.

**Ask side.**
- Above 27, informed traders never buy, because no settlement value exceeds 27.
- Noise traders buy when their valuation, 20.5 plus noise with standard deviation 5.8, is above the ask. I earn the ask minus 20.5 on each such trade.
- At an ask of 27: about 13% of noise traders buy, gaining 6.5 each, for an expected profit of about 0.43.
- At 26: about 0.41. Informed traders now buy when the value is 27, costing about 0.06.
- At 27.5: about 0.40.
- At 22.1: roughly 0, because informed buyers at a value of 27 offset the noise gains.
- So the best ask is about 27.

**Bid side.**
- Below 18, informed traders never sell, because no settlement value is below 18.
- Noise traders sell when their valuation is below the bid. I earn 20.5 minus the bid on each such trade.
- At 17.9: about 0.43.
- At 16 to 16.5: about 0.49, the peak.
- At 18.5: about 0.27, because informed traders sell when the value is 18.
- So the best bid is about 16.3.

My position is -1, so either trade stays within the ±4 limit.

{"bid": 16.3, "ask": 27}

game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (8 faces, each equally likely): 0, 1, 3, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12.
- Die 2 (8 faces, loaded): 1 (prob 1/10), 1 (prob 1/10), 1 (prob 1/10), 7 (prob 1/10), 9 (prob 1/5), 9 (prob 1/5), 11 (prob 1/10), 11 (prob 1/10).
- Die 3 (8 faces, each equally likely): 1, 3, 3, 3, 5, 6, 9, 9.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
Fair value is about 18.4 and the spread is about 15 points, roughly ±1.2 standard deviations around fair value.

**Fair value**
- Die 1: mean 6.75, variance 19.44.
- Die 2: mean 6.8, variance 15.56.
- Die 3: mean 4.875, variance 7.61.
- The sum has mean about 18.43 and standard deviation about 6.5.

**Spread**
- Half the counterparties are informed and know the settlement value, which has a spread of about 6.5 around the mean.
- The other half are noise traders whose valuations also spread about 6.5 around the mean.
- With both groups spread about the same, I trade off noise-trader profit against losses to informed traders using a normal approximation.
- The expected profit per quote is highest with a half-spread of about 1.25 standard deviations, roughly 8 points.
- I go slightly tighter than that, to about 7.5 points each side.

{"bid": 10.9, "ask": 25.9}

The first counterparty sold at my bid of 10.9, so I now put about 53% probability on a low sum (≤10, averaging about 6.8). That pulls the fair value down to roughly **12.9**. The settlement distribution is bimodal: a low cluster around 7 and a high cluster around 20.

**Prior expected value:**
- Die 1 averages 6.75.
- Die 2 averages 6.8.
- Die 3 averages 4.875.
- The sum averages 18.43, with standard deviation about 6.5.

**Update from the sale at 10.9:**
- The chance the sum is 10 or less is about 0.1125. Given that, the average sum is about 6.83.
- If the counterparty was informed, it sold because the sum is below 10.9.
- A noise trader would have sold with probability about 0.12, regardless of the value.
- Combining these gives P(low) ≈ 0.535. The posterior mean is about 0.535 × 6.83 + 0.465 × 19.9 ≈ 12.9.

**Choosing quotes against adverse selection:**
- **Ask:** Informed buyers come from the high cluster, which averages about 19.9. Noise buyers are centred on 12.9. Asks in the 22–23 range give the best expected edge, about +0.15 per quote.
- **Bid:** Informed sellers come from the low cluster. A bid around 5–6 gives about +0.3 expected edge, better than higher bids.
- **Inventory:** I am long 1, so I skew the quotes slightly lower.

{"bid": 5.5, "ask": 22.0}

Prior expected sum: die 1 = 6.75, die 2 = 6.8, die 3 = 4.875, so 18.425 in total.

**Bayesian update from the two sells:**
- A sale at 10.9 is unusual for a noise trader. One with valuation centred near 18.4 sells there only about 12% of the time.
- A sale at 5.5 is stronger evidence. Very low sums (≤5) need die 1 in {0,1,3}, die 2 = 1 and a small die 3. That has prior probability of only about 4%. But informed traders would sell there for sure, while noise traders sell only about 12% of the time.
- Posterior weights:
  - About 69% on a sum near 4 (sums of 2 to 5).
  - About 13% on a middle sum of 6 to 10.
  - About 18% on the high region, around 20.
- Public fair value is now about 7.5. The distribution has two clusters, so informed traders sit far from noise traders on both sides.

**Ask:**
- Informed traders only buy when the sum is high (around 20), so a tight ask loses heavily to them.
- Noise traders, centred near 7.5, pay a markup on the upside.
- Weighing the two, the edge is roughly zero or slightly positive for an ask around 15 to 16.

**Bid:**
- Most of the posterior mass sits at sums of 2 to 5. A bid near 2.5 avoids nearly all informed sells.
- It still collects noise sellers about 20% of the time, at roughly 5 below fair.

{"bid": 2.5, "ask": 15.5}

The posterior fair value is about 6.3, so I'll quote a 3.5 bid and a 13.5 ask. I can't avoid the high-value risk on the ask side, so the ask sits high instead.

**Updating on the history.** Die 3 = 3 is revealed. Before any trades, the expected sum is 6.75 + 6.8 + 3 = 16.55. The stage-1 trades change that:
- At quote 1 a counterparty sold at 10.9.
- At quote 2 a counterparty sold at 5.5.
- At quote 3 nobody traded at 2.5 / 15.5.

Weighting each possible sum by how likely an informed or noise trader was to produce that history:
- About 79% of the probability sits on a sum of 4 or 5. That needs die 2 = 1 and die 1 = 0 or 1.
- About 13% is spread across high sums, averaging about 16.
- The resulting fair value is about 6.3.

**Bid.** The lowest possible sum is 4. A bid below 4 is never hit by an informed trader. A noise trader sells there about 35% of the time, and I gain about 2.5–3 on each such trade. I'll bid 3.5. Buying would take me to +3, which is within the limit.

**Ask.** The ask has to sit above most of the high-value tail. At an ask of 8, informed buyers in that tail cost more than the noise trades earn. At 13 to 14, the noise edge of roughly 7.7 on about 12% of noise traders outweighs the expected informed loss. I'll ask 13.5.

{"bid": 3.5, "ask": 13.5}

The contract's fair value is now about 5.1, much lower than the 16.55 suggested by the dice alone. I'll quote bid 1.5 and ask 10.5.

**Prior given die 3 = 3.** Die 1 averages 6.75 and die 2 averages 6.8. The prior mean of the sum is therefore 16.55, and the lowest possible sum is 4.

**Updating on trading history.** I scored each possible sum by how likely it made the four observed outcomes, with half of counterparties informed and half noise.
- In quote 1 someone sold at 10.9, and in quote 2 someone sold at 5.5. Both are strong signs the sum is low.
- In quotes 3 and 4 nobody traded, which fits a sum between about 3.5 and 13.5.
- Combining these, about 91% of the probability sits on a sum of 4 or 5. Those are die 1 = 0 or 1 with die 2 = 1.
- The posterior mean is about **5.1**. My long position of 2, bought at 16.4 in total, is losing money.

**Choosing the quote.** For each price I compared expected noise-trader profit against expected losses to informed traders.
- **Bid:** No sum is below 4, so a bid under 4 never trades with an informed seller. A lower bid trades less often with noise traders but earns more each time. Expected value keeps rising slowly as the bid drops toward about 1. I chose 1.5 to keep that profit and allow for the position cap of +3.
- **Ask:** Informed traders only buy if the sum is 7 or more. Expected value peaks at about +0.46 per quote for an ask near 10.5–11.5. A fill there also cuts my long position.

{"bid": 1.5, "ask": 10.5}

The posterior puts the sum almost certainly at 4 or 5, with a fair value of about 4.9, so I'll quote bid 3.9 and ask 6.5.

**Prior.** Die 1 has mean 6.75 and die 2 has mean 6.8. Die 3 is revealed as 3, so before looking at the trades the expected sum is about 16.55.

**What the trades say.** I treated each trade as evidence, assuming an informed counterparty with probability 0.5 and a noise trader otherwise.
- Quotes 1 and 2 were sells at my bid of 10.9 and then 5.5. These strongly suggest a low sum.
- Quotes 4 and 5 had no trade at 3.5/13.5 and 1.5/10.5. An informed trader would have traded unless the value sat inside those spreads. This points to a sum of 10 or below.
- When I weight each possible sum by how well it explains this history, about 91% of the probability lands on a sum of 4 or 5. These come from die 2 = 1 with die 1 = 0 or 1.

**Quote.**
- **Bid 3.9:** the lowest possible sum is 4, so an informed trader never sells to me here. Noise sellers give me roughly 1 of edge per trade.
- **Ask 6.5:** an informed buyer only appears if the sum is 7 or more, which has about 7% posterior probability. Noise buyers pay about 1.5 above fair. The ask is above fair, which also helps me sell down my long position.

{"bid": 3.9, "ask": 6.5}

Dice 2 and 3 are revealed, so the known part of the sum is 1 + 3 = 4. Only die 1 is still unknown. It is equally likely to be 0, 1, 3, 8, 9, 10, 11 or 12, with a mean of 6.75.

- **Possible settlement values:** 4, 5, 7, 12, 13, 14, 15 or 16, each with probability 1/8.
- **Public fair value:** 4 + 6.75 = 10.75.

I set each side to maximise expected profit against the mix of informed and noise traders:

- **Ask 16.0:** No settlement value is above 16, so an informed trader never buys from me there. A noise trader buys with probability about 0.21, at an edge of 5.25 over fair value. That is worth about +0.55 per quote, which is roughly the best ask. Moving down to 15 brings in informed buyers when the value is 16.
- **Bid 4.0:** No settlement value is below 4, so an informed trader never sells to me there. A noise trader sells with probability about 0.15, at an edge of 6.75. That is worth about +0.51. Raising the bid lets informed sellers in when the value is 4, and lowering it costs more noise trades than it gains in edge.

I am long 2, so I can still buy one more unit. The bid at 4.0 cannot lose against informed traders, so it is worth keeping.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 16.0}

With die 2 and die 3 revealed, the settlement is 4 + die 1, and die 1 is the only uncertainty left.

**Possible settlement values:** 4, 5, 7, 12, 13, 14, 15 or 16, each with probability 1/8. The mean is 10.75.

**Public fair value is still about 10.75.**
- At quote 7 I quoted 4 / 16. No informed trader would trade there, because no settlement value is below 4 or above 16.
- So "no trade" tells us nothing new.

**How the quote earns money:**
- Noise traders value the contract at about N(10.75, 6.5).
- Informed traders take my price only when it is wrong compared with the true value.

**Ask side:**
- Ask 16: no informed trader buys. Noise buys with probability about 0.21 and I make 5.25, so expected profit is about 0.5 × 0.21 × 5.25 ≈ 0.55.
- Asking lower adds a loss to the informed trader holding 16, and a quote just under 12 is clearly negative. So 16 is about optimal.

**Bid side:**
- Bid 4: no informed trader sells, since the value 4 is not below 4. Noise sells with probability about 0.15 and I make 6.75, so expected profit is about 0.51.
- Bidding 4.5 or 5 gives up more to the informed trader holding 4 than it gains, and comes out about even or slightly worse.
- Buying here takes me to +3, which is allowed.

{"bid": 4, "ask": 16}

Die 1 is the only unknown, so the settlement value is 4 + die 1. The trading history implies die 1 is almost certainly 0 or 1, which puts fair value at about 4.5. I set each side to maximise expected profit against noise traders while keeping informed traders from trading against me.

**Inference from the history**
- **Quote 1:** a counterparty sold at 10.9. An informed trader sells there only if the total is 4, 5 or 7. A noise trader sells there only about 12% of the time.
- **Quote 2:** a counterparty sold at 5.5. An informed trader sells there only if the total is 4 or 5. A noise trader sells there only about 5% of the time.
- **Quotes 4–6:** none traded. That also rules out totals of 7 and above for an informed trader. In particular, quote 6 at 3.9 / 6.5 did not trade, and an informed trader would have bought at 6.5 if the total were 7.
- **Quotes 7–8:** none traded at 4 / 16. Every possible settlement value lies between 4 and 16, so these quotes tell us nothing.

The posterior is therefore concentrated on a total of 4 or 5, and fair value is about 4.5–4.6.

**Ask**
- Settlement is at most about 5, so an informed trader will not buy at an ask above 5.
- Only noise traders buy, and their valuation is roughly Normal(4.55, 6.5).
- Expected profit is the margin times the chance a noise trader's valuation is above the ask. This is largest when the ask is about 0.75 standard deviations above fair value, around 9.4.
- Selling also cuts my +2 long, which is fine.

**Bid**
- An informed trader would only sell if the bid were above 4.
- Against noise traders alone, the best bid is about 4.9 below fair value, roughly −0.3. I round this to 0.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 9.4}

game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 11.
- Die 2 (4 faces, loaded): 2 (prob 2/5), 2 (prob 1/10), 6 (prob 1/5), 8 (prob 3/10).
- Die 3 (4 faces, each equally likely): 7, 7, 8, 10.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
Expected settlement value is 19.6, the sum of the three dice means:
- Die 1 averages 7.
- Die 2 averages 2×0.5 + 6×0.2 + 8×0.3 = 4.6.
- Die 3 averages 8.

Uncertainty is large. The standard deviation of the sum is about 3.6, the same size as the noise traders' noise. That means informed traders, who make up 35% of arrivals, have a big edge over my quotes.

For a half-spread s, I compared profit from noise traders against losses to informed traders. Expected profit peaks when s is about one standard deviation, roughly 3.6. So I quote symmetrically around 19.6 with that half-spread.

{"bid": 16.0, "ask": 23.2}

The unconditional expected value is 7 + 4.6 + 8 = 19.6. A buyer at 22 suggests a higher value. About 23% of outcomes settle above 22, and roughly 35% of counterparties are informed. Updating on that buy moves my fair value estimate to about 21.2. I'm short one unit, so I lean the quote slightly up and keep a wide spread against informed traders.

{"bid": 19.4, "ask": 23.2}

Die 1 is revealed as 8, so the fair value is 8 + E[die 2] + E[die 3] = 8 + 4.6 + 8 = **20.6**.

The settlement value can only take a few values: 17 (25%), 18 (12.5%), 20 (12.5%), 21 (10%), 22 (5%), 23 (15%), 24 (12.5%) and 26 (7.5%). So informed traders bunch at specific prices, and I chose each side to maximise expected profit per quote.

**Ask side.** Each candidate ask earns from noise buyers and loses to informed buyers who know the value is above it.

| Ask | Net expected profit |
|---|---|
| 22.6 | about 0.21 |
| 23.1 | about 0.28 |
| 23.6 | about 0.32 |
| 24.1 | about 0.33 |

The curve is flat around 24.

**Bid side.**

| Bid | Net expected profit |
|---|---|
| 18.0 | about 0.31 |
| 17.5 | about 0.35 |
| 17.0 | about 0.37 |

At 17.0 informed sellers never trade with me, because no value is below 17. That also suits my short position of -1, since it leans toward buying back.

{"bid": 17.0, "ask": 24.0}

Fair value is about 21.8, so I'm quoting a wide spread around it: bid 19.8, ask 23.6.

**Die values and prior.** Die 1 is revealed as 8.
- Die 2 lands on 2 with probability 0.5, on 6 with 0.2 and on 8 with 0.3, so its mean is 4.6.
- Die 3 lands on 7 with probability 0.5, on 8 with 0.25 and on 10 with 0.25, so its mean is 8.
- Before using the trade history, the expected settlement is 8 + 4.6 + 8 = 20.6.

**Updating on the history.**
- At quote 2 someone bought at 22. This is more likely when the settlement is above 22, which happens when die 2 is 8, or die 2 is 6 and die 3 is 10.
- At quote 4 nobody traded at 17/24. This makes a settlement of 26 less likely, because an informed trader would have bought at 24.
- Weighting the possible outcomes (17, 18, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 26) by these two observations gives an updated fair value of about 21.8.

**Quote.**
- Settlement takes only a few discrete values, and informed traders arrive with probability 0.35, so I keep the spread wide around 21.8.
- At a bid of 19.8, an informed trader sells only if the value is 17 or 18.
- At an ask of 23.6, an informed trader buys only if the value is 24 or 26.
- I'm short 1, so I lean the quote slightly upward.

{"bid": 19.8, "ask": 23.6}

Fair value given die 1 = 8 and the two no-trade quotes is about 20.8.

**Prior.** With die 1 = 8, the settlement is 8 + die 2 + die 3.
- Die 2 has mean 4.6. It shows 2 with probability 0.5, 6 with 0.2 and 8 with 0.3.
- Die 3 has mean 8. It shows 7 with probability 0.5, 8 with 0.25 and 10 with 0.25.
- The prior is therefore 20.6. The possible totals and their chances are:

| Total | 17 | 18 | 20 | 21 | 22 | 23 | 24 | 26 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Prior probability | 0.25 | 0.125 | 0.125 | 0.10 | 0.05 | 0.15 | 0.125 | 0.075 |

**Update on no trades at quotes 4 (17/24) and 5 (19.8/23.6).**
- Quote 4 is weak evidence: an informed trader would only have traded if the total were 26.
- Quote 5 matters more. A no-trade is about 0.60 likely if the total is between 20 and 23, but only about 0.25 likely if it is 17, 18, 24 or 26.
- This moves the posterior mean up slightly, to about 20.8.

**Quote.**
- I am short 1, so I skew slightly upward.
- Bid 19.4: informed traders sell only on 17 or 18, which averages about 17.3. Noise traders sell often enough below 19.4 to more than cover that.
- Ask 22.4: informed traders buy on 23, 24 or 26, a modest loss of about 1. Noise trades above 22.4 earn about 1.6 each.

{"bid": 19.4, "ask": 22.4}

**Fair value.** Die 1 = 8 and die 2 = 6, so 14 is already known. Die 3 is 7, 7, 8 or 10, each equally likely. So the settlement value is 21 (prob 1/2), 22 (prob 1/4) or 24 (prob 1/4). The mean is 22. There have been no trades this stage, so the public fair value is 22.

**Ask side.**
- An informed trader buys only if the settlement value is above my ask. So for any ask of 24 or higher, informed traders never buy.
- A noise trader's valuation is 22 plus noise with standard deviation 3.6. My expected profit from noise trades is 0.65 × P(noise > a − 22) × (a − 22).
- This peaks near a = 24.7, at about +0.40 per quote.
- Asks between 22 and 24 do worse. They lose to informed buyers when the value is 24, and the higher-ask optimum is better anyway.

**Bid side.**
- An informed trader sells only if the settlement value is below my bid. So for any bid of 21 or lower, informed traders never sell.
- The noise-trader calculation mirrors the ask side, so the optimum is near 22 − 2.7 = 19.3.

**Position.** I am short 1, and I have room to trade on both sides, so the limits don't constrain this quote.

{"bid": 19.3, "ask": 24.7}

With dice 1 and 2 revealed (8 + 6 = 14), only die 3 is unknown.

**Possible settlement values**
- Die 3 shows 7, 7, 8 or 10, so the sum is 21, 21, 22 or 24.
- Fair value is (21 + 21 + 22 + 24) / 4 = **22**.
- The no-trade at quote 7 (19.3 / 24.7) tells us nothing new. Every possible value lies inside that spread, so informed traders would not have traded at any outcome.

**Ask side.** An informed trader buys only if the value is above my ask. If I set the ask at 24 or higher, informed traders never buy. {"bid": 5.0, "ask": 17.0}

Fair value is about 11.8. Wide quotes of roughly 5.5 / 16.5 maximise expected edge here.

- Die 1 averages 5 and die 2 averages 6.5, so the prior expected sum is 11.5.

- Quote 1 (5 / 17) got no trade. That rules out an informed trader with a value below 5 (probability about 0.125) or above 17 (probability about 0.075).
- The low tail is heavier, so the no-trade update nudges fair value up to about 11.8.

**Ask side**
I compared the gain from noise buyers above the ask (about ½·P(noise > ask)·(ask − fair)) with the loss to informed traders (½·E[(V − ask)⁺]).

| Ask | Net edge |
|---|---|
| 15 | about +0.30 |
| 16 | about +0.54 |
| 17 | about +0.60 |
| 18 | about +0.57 |

The best ask is around 16.5 to 17.

**Bid side**
I did the same comparison below fair value.

| Bid | Net edge |
|---|---|
| 7 | about +0.18 |
| 6 | about +0.27 |
| 5 | about +0.29 |
| 4 | about +0.29 |

The best bid is around 5 to 5.5.
