Die 2 is revealed as 10, so the settlement value is 10 plus die 1. Die 1 averages 40/8 = 5, so the public fair value is 15. The possible settlement values are 12, 13, 14, 14, 16, 16, 17, 18.

**Informed traders:** they never trade with me if my ask is above 18 and my bid is below 12. Quoting outside that range means they cannot pick me off.

**Noise traders:** their valuation is 15 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 4.7. My expected profit on the ask is P(valuation > a) × (a − 15). Checking candidate asks (profit shown before halving for the 0.5 chance of a noise trader):
- An ask of 18 gives about 0.785.
- An ask of 18.5 gives about 0.798, the best.
- An ask of 19 gives about 0.789.

The bid side is symmetric, so the best bid is 11.5. Both sides sit outside the informed range, so neither side can lose to an informed trader.

{"bid": 11.5, "ask": 18.5}

Die 2 is revealed as 10. Die 1's faces (2, 3, 4, 4, 6, 6, 7, 8) average 5. So the settlement value is 12, 13, 14, 14, 16, 16, 17 or 18, each with probability 1/8. The fair value is 15.

**What the last quote told us.** Quote 3 was 11.5 / 18.5 and nobody traded. An informed trader only trades if the true value is above 18.5 or below 11.5, and no possible value is. So the lack of a trade tells us nothing, and the public fair value stays at 15.

**Where to put the ask.**
- **Against informed traders:** if the ask is above 18, an informed trader never buys, so they cannot cost us anything. At an ask of 17.1, they buy when the value is 18, which costs about 0.06 in expected profit.
- **Against noise traders:** their valuation is about 15 plus or minus 4.7. With the ask d above 15, they buy with probability equal to the chance their noise exceeds d. Our expected profit from them is 0.5 × d × that probability.
- This is largest at d ≈ 3.5:
  - an ask of 18.5 gives about 0.399;
  - an ask of 19 gives about 0.395;
  - an ask of 17.1 gives about 0.287 once the informed-trader loss is included.

**Where to put the bid.** The bid works the same way, mirrored around 15. A bid of 11.5 is below the lowest possible value (12), so informed traders never sell to us. Noise traders sell to us with the same expected profit as on the ask side.

So I quote 11.5 / 18.5.

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A standard 52-card deck is shuffled. Card values: Ace = 1, 2-10 face value, Jack = 11, Queen = 12, King = 13. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
The expected sum of 3 cards is 3 × 7 = 21. The standard deviation, with the finite-deck correction, is √(3·14·49/51) ≈ 6.35.

Noise traders' valuations spread around 21 with sd 6.4, and informed traders' valuations spread around 21 with sd 6.35. These are nearly the same width.

So I place each side k standard deviations from 21, where k maximises 2k(1−Φ(k)) − φ(k). That gives k ≈ 1.2, so each side sits about 7.6 from 21. At that width the expected profit on each side is positive.

{"bid": 13.4, "ask": 28.6}

The contract is the sum of 3 cards. Each card averages 7, so the expected sum is 21. The standard deviation of the sum is about 6.35.

The last quote of 13.4 / 28.6 did not trade. That quote was symmetric around 21, so the public fair value stays at 21.

The informed traders' valuations (about N(21, 6.35)) and the noise traders' valuations (N(21, 6.4)) have almost the same spread. So I can work out one side's profit with a half-spread of d = xσ:

- Gain from noise traders: σ·x·(1−Φ(x))
- Loss to informed traders: σ·[φ(x) − x(1−Φ(x))]
- Net: σ·[2x(1−Φ(x)) − φ(x)]

This net profit is largest at about x ≈ 1.2, which gives d ≈ 7.7. The quote is therefore about 21 ± 7.7.

{"bid": 13.3, "ask": 28.7}

Card 1 is a 9, so the fair value is 9 plus the expected value of two more cards drawn from the remaining 51.

**Fair value**
- The full deck sums to 4 × 91 = 364, so the remaining 51 cards sum to 355.
- The average remaining card is 355 / 51 ≈ 6.96.
- Fair value ≈ 9 + 2 × 6.96 ≈ 22.9.

**Uncertainty in settlement**
- The two unseen cards have a combined standard deviation of about 5.2.
- Noise traders' valuations scatter around fair value with a standard deviation of 6.4.

**Choosing the half-spread h** (profit per side = noise-trader gain minus informed-trader loss, each weighted by 0.5)

| h | Expected profit per side |
|---|---|
| 4 | ≈ 0.20 |
| 6 | ≈ 0.36 |
| 7 | ≈ 0.37 |
| 8 | ≈ 0.35 |

The best half-spread is about 7, so I quote roughly 22.9 ± 7.

{"bid": 15.9, "ask": 29.9}

Card 1 is a 9. The other 51 cards sum to 364 − 9 = 355, which averages about 6.96 per card. So the fair value is about 9 + 2 × 6.96 ≈ 22.9.

The two hidden cards have a standard deviation of about 5.3. The informed trader's valuation is therefore spread roughly N(0, 5.3) around fair. The noise trader's valuation is spread N(0, 6.4) around fair.

I compared the expected profit per side for different half-spreads:

| Half-spread | Expected profit per side |
|---|---|
| 4 | about 0.19 |
| 6 | about 0.35 |
| 7 | about 0.37 (best) |
| 8 | about 0.35 |

Profit peaks at a half-spread of about 7, so I'll quote fair ± 7. The previous quote at a similar width did not trade, which tells us little.

{"bid": 16.0, "ask": 29.9}

Card 3's expected value is lower than the plain average because the trade at quote 4 tells us something about it. I'll bid 15 and ask 25.5.

**Expected value of card 3**
- Before any trading: the 50 unseen cards sum to 364 − 14 = 350, so card 3 averages 7.0.
- At quote 4, after card 1 (9) was revealed, a counterparty sold to me at 16.
  - An informed seller sells only if 9 + card 2 + card 3 < 16. With card 2 now known to be 5, that means card 3 is an ace.
  - A noise trader sold with probability about 14% (public fair value about 23, noise SD 6.4).
- So the chance of that sale was about 0.57 if card 3 is an ace and about 0.07 otherwise.
- Updating on that, P(card 3 is an ace) ≈ 0.42.
- Otherwise card 3 averages about 7.5 (346 / 46 for the non-ace cards).
- Expected card 3 ≈ 4.8, so fair value ≈ 18.8.
- The settlement is 15 with probability about 0.42, and otherwise spread roughly evenly over 16 to 27.

**Quote choice**
- **Bid 15:** an informed trader holding a 15 will not sell into it, because it needs a valuation strictly below the bid. Noise sellers still hit it about 28% of the time, worth roughly +0.5 in expectation.
- **Ask:** the expected profit for each ask, net of losses to informed buyers, was:

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 22 | about 0.13 |
| 24 | about 0.40 |
| 25 | about 0.44 |
| 26 | about 0.44 |
| 27 | about 0.41 |

  The best region is 25 to 26, so I'll ask 25.5.

{"bid": 15, "ask": 25.5}

The quote 5 buy at 25.5 points to a high card 3, so I set fair value near 23.2 and placed the bid and ask where expected profit is highest.

**Fair value before quote 5:** Cards 1 and 2 are 9 and 5, which sum to 14. The 50 cards left in the deck have values summing to 350, so card 3 averages 7. That gives a fair value of 21.

**Updating on the buy at 25.5:**
- An informed trader buys only if card 3 is 12 or 13 (Q or K). That is 8 of the 50 remaining cards.
- A noise trader values the contract at fair value plus noise with standard deviation 6.4. It buys above 25.5 with probability about 24%.
- If card 3 is Q or K, the chance of that buy was 0.5 × 1 + 0.5 × 0.24 = 0.62. For any other card it was 0.5 × 0.24 = 0.12.
- Weighting by card counts, Q/K and the other 42 cards each end up with about half the probability.
- Q/K average 12.5 and the other cards average about 5.95. So card 3 is expected to be about 9.2, and fair value is about 23.2.

**Ask:**

| Ask | Expected profit | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| 26 | about 0.34 | An informed trader buys whenever the settlement is 27 |
| 28 | about 0.55 | Above every possible settlement, so only noise traders buy |
| 29 | about 0.53 | Fewer noise traders buy |

28 is best.

**Bid:**

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 18 | about 0.40 |
| 16 to 17 | about 0.44 to 0.45 |

Lower bids lose less to informed traders when card 3 is low. 16.5 is near the peak.

{"bid": 16.5, "ask": 28.0}

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A standard 52-card deck is shuffled. Card values: Ace = 1, 2-10 face value, Jack = 11, Queen = 12, King = 13. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
Before any cards are revealed, the expected sum of three cards is 3 × 7 = 21. Because the cards are dealt without replacement, the standard deviation of the sum is about 6.35. That is almost the same as the noise traders' spread of 6.4.

So informed and noise counterparties draw valuations from nearly the same distribution around 21. Suppose I quote 21 ± kσ, where σ is that standard deviation:
- The expected gain per side, net of losses to informed traders, is proportional to 2k(1 − Φ(k)) − φ(k). Here Φ and φ are the normal distribution and density functions.
- This is largest at about k ≈ 1.2, which gives a half-spread of about 7.6.

That puts the bid at 21 − 7.6 = 13.4 and the ask at 21 + 7.6 = 28.6.

{"bid": 13.4, "ask": 28.6}

A seller hit my bid at 13.4. That makes it more likely the sum is low, so the public fair value has dropped.

**Fair value before trading:** three cards drawn without replacement have mean 21 and standard deviation about 6.35.

**Updated fair value after the sale:**
- An informed trader sells only if the sum is below 13.4. That has roughly a 12% chance.
- A noise trader sells if 21 plus noise falls below 13.4. That also has roughly a 12% chance.
- The informed and noise explanations are about equally likely. If informed, the expected sum is about 10.5; if noise, the prior mean of 21 still applies.
- The updated fair value is therefore about 15.7, with a two-humped distribution.

**Ask:** noise traders now centre on 15.7, but in the high-value case informed traders still expect about 21. That makes a tight ask costly. Expected profit is highest with an ask near 25 to 27.

**Bid:** in the low-value case the sum is probably below 13. A bid near 12 roughly breaks even. A bid of about 8 to 9 earns the most, and since I'm already long 1, I lean slightly lower.

{"bid": 8.5, "ask": 25.0}

Fair value is about 13.5, so I'll quote a bid of 10.0 and an ask of 17.5, leaning slightly low.

**Value from public information alone**
- Card 1 is a 4, so 51 cards remain, summing to 360.
- Their average is about 7.06, so the two unrevealed cards are expected to sum to about 14.1.
- Unconditional fair value is therefore about 18.1.

**What the trading history adds**
- At quote 1, someone sold to me at 13.4. An informed trader sells there only if the total is below 13.4. That means the two unknown cards sum to 9 or less.
- At quote 2, nobody traded at 8.5 / 25. An informed trader stays out only if the total is between 8.5 and 25.
- Weighting each range of the two-card sum by how likely these two outcomes are, the probabilities shift as follows:

| Two-card sum | Posterior probability |
|---|---|
| 5 to 9 | about 63% |
| 10 to 21 | about 30% |
| 4 or less | about 5% |
| 22 or more | about 1% |

- Posterior fair value is about 13.5.

**Choosing the quote**
- **Ask at 17.5:** noise traders buy fairly often, and I gain about 3.5 on each. Informed traders buy only when the total is high, roughly 20% of the time. The expected value is mildly positive.
- **Bid at 10:** informed traders sell there only if the two unknown cards sum to about 5 or less, which is about 8% likely. Noise traders sell about 29% of the time, at a gain of about 3.5. The expected value is about +0.4, better than bidding 11.
- My current position is +1, which is a further reason to lean slightly low.

{"bid": 10.0, "ask": 17.5}

The public fair value is now about 13, which is well below the unconditional ~18.1, so I'll quote bid 10.3 / ask 15.2 around it.

**Prior after the reveal.** Card 1 is 4. The other two cards come from the remaining 51 cards, which average 360/51 ≈ 7.06. So the expected sum is 4 + 14.1 ≈ 18.1, with a standard deviation of about 5.2.

**What the trading history says.**
- **Quote 1:** someone sold at 13.4. A noise trader rarely does that when fair value is about 21 (roughly a 12% chance). So this is strong evidence that the sum is below 13.4.
- **Quote 2:** no trade at 8.5 / 25. This is weak evidence that the sum is between 8.5 and 25.
- **Quote 3:** no trade at 10 / 17.5. This is moderate evidence that the sum is between 10 and 17.5.

**Posterior.** Combining these with the prior puts most of the weight on a sum of about 10 to 13.4. The posterior mean is about 12.9, so the public fair value is around 13.

**Quote.**
- I bid below fair value and ask above it, with a fairly wide ask. An informed trader with a sum between 10 and 13 should stay out, while I still catch noise flow.
- I'm already long 1, so a slight downward skew is fine.

{"bid": 10.3, "ask": 15.2}

The contract settles at 11 plus the value of card 3, which is unknown.

**Fair value**
- Removing the 4 and the 7 leaves 50 cards.
- Those 50 cards have values summing to 364 − 11 = 353, so their mean is 353 / 50 = 7.06.
- Fair value is 11 + 7.06 ≈ 18.06.
- Card 3 is close to uniform on 1–13, so the settlement lies between 12 and 24.

**Choosing the quotes**
- A quote at or beyond the possible range cannot lose to an informed trader, who knows the settlement exactly.
- Noise traders value the contract at about 18.06 ± 6.4, so roughly 17–18% of them still cross a quote at 12 or 24.
- Each of those trades earns about 6 per unit.
- I checked quotes slightly inside the range. The extra noise trades they attract roughly offset what informed traders take, so expected profit stays at about 0.52 per side.
- Being long 1 doesn't change this, because the position limits are far away.

{"bid": 12.0, "ask": 24.0}

Card 3 settles the contract. All other public information is already known, so I quote around its expected value.

**Fair value**
- Cards 1 and 2 total 4 + 7 = 11.
- The full deck sums to 4 × 91 = 364. Removing the two revealed cards leaves 353 across 50 cards.
- So card 3 has an expected value of 353 / 50 = 7.06, and fair value is 11 + 7.06 = 18.06.
- Settlement can only be between 12 and 24.
- Quote 5 (12 / 24) produced no trade, so it adds no information.

**Ask side**
- At an ask of 24, an informed trader never buys, because settlement cannot exceed 24.
- A noise trader buys with probability P(Z > 5.94 / 6.4) ≈ 0.18, giving an expected gain of about 1.05.
- Lowering the ask to 23.5 makes an informed buy possible when card 3 is a King. That costs about 0.04 in expected value. The extra noise-trader edge does not cover it, so the net is lower.

**Bid side**
- At a bid of 12, an informed trader never sells, because settlement cannot fall below 12.
- A noise trader sells with probability about 0.17, giving an expected gain of about 1.04.
- Raising the bid to 12.5 or 13 lowers the net (about 1.03 and 1.01).

My position is +1, so either trade stays within the limits.

game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 2, 2, 6, 8, 9, 11.
- Die 2 (4 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 11, 11.
- Die 3 (6 faces, each equally likely): 3, 4, 5, 7, 7, 12.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
The expected settlement is 6.33 + 6.25 + 6.33 ≈ 18.9, with a standard deviation of about 6.5. I traded off profit from noise traders against losses to informed traders, and that comes out best with each side about 9 to 10 away from fair.

{"bid": 9.5, "ask": 28.4}

Expected settlement is about 18.9: the three dice average about 6.33, 6.25 and 6.33. The standard deviation is about 6.5.

I'm setting the bid and ask so the expected gain from noise traders minus the expected loss to informed traders is as large as possible on each side. Under a normal approximation, that best distance is about 9 to 10 from fair value. I've held the spread wide because die 2 lands on 11 half the time, which gives the distribution a heavy upper tail.

Quote 1 at 9.5 / 28.4 got no trade, so I'm tightening slightly to 10.0 / 28.0.

{"bid": 10.0, "ask": 28.0}

The contract's expected value is about **18.9**, so I'll quote a symmetric spread of roughly ±9.5 around it: **bid 9.5, ask 28.4**.

**Expected value**
- Die 1: 38/6 = 6.33
- Die 2: 25/4 = 6.25
- Die 3: 38/6 = 6.33
- Sum: about 18.92, with a standard deviation of about 6.5. The settlement value can range from 6 to 34.

**Choosing the half-spread (h)**
For each side, I compared what noise traders pay me (about h × probability their noise exceeds h) against what informed traders take from me (their expected gain beyond my price). I treated the dice sum as roughly normal with SD 6.5, and the noise as SD 9.8.

| Half-spread h | Gain from noise traders | Loss to informed traders | Net per side (×0.5) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | 1.62 | 0.63 | ≈0.99 |
| 8 | 1.66 | 0.35 | ≈1.31 |
| 10 | 1.54 | 0.18 | ≈1.36 |
| 12 | 1.32 | 0.09 | ≈1.23 |

The best half-spread is around 9.5–10. I'm keeping the quotes close to the first two, since nothing has traded and the public fair value hasn't moved.

{"bid": 9.5, "ask": 28.4}

Die 3 = 7, so the maximum possible total is now 11 + 11 + 7 = 29. Expected value from the dice alone is 19.6.

**What the stage-1 trade tells us.** Someone bought at my ask of 28.4.
- An informed trader would only do that if the total is 29, which needs die 1 = 11 and die 2 = 11. That has prior probability 1/12.
- A noise trader buys at 28.4 about 17% of the time.
- Updating on that buy gives P(total = 29) ≈ 0.39.
- So the posterior fair value is about 22.7.

**Ask.** At 29, an informed trader never buys, because valuations of exactly 29 do not trade. Noise traders buy about 26% of the time, at roughly 6.3 above fair value. Moving the ask down to 27.1 does worse, because informed traders holding 29 would then buy.

**Bid.** I weighed the gain from noise sellers against losses to informed sellers whose totals are below the bid. That net value peaks around a bid of 12, at about +0.65 per quote.

{"bid": 12, "ask": 29}

My estimate of fair value is about 16. Die 3 = 7 is now public, so the settlement is 7 + Die 1 + Die 2. I combined the four quotes so far to estimate where Die 1 + Die 2 lies.

**What the trades tell me**
- **Quote 4 (they sold at my bid of 12):** An informed seller means the total is below 12. That only happens when Die 1 = 2 and Die 2 = 1 or 2, giving totals of 10 or 11. A noise trader sells there only about 22% of the time, so this trade pushes weight strongly toward 10–11.
- **Quote 3 (they bought at 28.4):** An informed buyer means the total is 29, which needs Die 1 = 11 and Die 2 = 11. But quotes 1 and 2 had similar asks with no trade, which counts against a total of 29.

**Posterior over the total (approximate)**
- About 51% that the total is 10 or 11.
- About 42% that it is spread from 14 to 27.
- About 7% that it is 29.
- Fair value is therefore about 16, and the distribution is spread widely.

**Choosing the quote**
- **Bid:** If I bid above 10, informed traders holding a total of 10 or 11 would sell to me at a loss to me. A bid around 9 or 9.5 avoids that and still catches noise sellers. Expected edge is about +0.8 per quote.
- **Ask:** Around 26–27, noise buyers still trade often enough. Only totals of 27 or 29 can then hurt me through informed buyers. Expected edge is about +0.65 per quote.

{"bid": 9.2, "ask": 26.6}

Bid 9.0 and ask 26.9: the bid sits below every remaining outcome and the ask mostly avoids informed buyers.

**What's left.** With die 3 = 7, the sum is 7 + die 1 + die 2. Before using the trading history, the outcomes run from 10 to 29 with a mean of about 19.6.

**What the trades tell me.** I updated on each trade (or no trade), assuming half the counterparties know the true value.
- **Quote 3:** someone bought at 28.4. That favours the only outcome above 28.4, which is 29.
- **Quote 4:** someone sold at 12. That strongly favours outcomes of 10 or 11.
- **Quote 5:** nobody traded at 9.2 / 26.6. That counts mildly against outcomes of 27 or more.

**Result.** The estimate is bimodal:
- about 53% on 10–11;
- about 11% on 29;
- the rest spread through the middle.

The fair value is about 16.

**Bid.** No outcome is below 10, so a bid under 10 is never hit by an informed seller. Only noise traders sell, and I gain about 7 from fair value each time. I expect about 0.8 per quote with a bid around 9. A bid near 12 does worse, because informed traders with 10 or 11 would hit it.

**Ask.** An informed buyer hits 26.9 only when the sum is 27 or 29, which is about 13% likely. I lose roughly 1.9 on average then. Noise buyers pay about 11 above fair value, so the expected gain is about 0.6 per quote.

{"bid": 9.0, "ask": 26.9}

The settlement value is now 9 + die 2, because die 3 = 7 and die 1 = 2 are revealed. So it can only be 10, 11, 20 or 20.

**Estimating the value from the trading history:**
- At quote 4, a counterparty sold to me at 12.
- An informed trader would sell at 12 only if the value is 10 or 11.
- A noise trader would sell at 12 only about 22% of the time, because public fair value was about 19.6 then.
- This shifts the odds toward a low die 2: about 85% for a value of 10 or 11, and about 15% for 20.
- The no-trade quotes tell me nothing, since every possible value fell between my bid and ask.
- Public fair value is therefore about 11.95.

**Choosing the quotes:**
- **Bid:** Any bid below 10 means informed traders never sell to me, so only noise traders hit it. The best trade-off between edge and fill rate is about 7.4 below fair value, so I bid 4.6.
- **Ask:** At 20.0, informed traders never buy, because the value is never above 20. Noise traders still buy about 20% of the time, with about 8 of edge each time.

{"bid": 4.6, "ask": 20.0}

Die 3 = 7 and die 1 = 2, so the settlement value is 9 + die 2. Die 2 is 1, 2, 11 or 11, so settlement is 10, 11, 20 or 20, and fair value is 9 + 6.25 = 15.25.

**Avoiding informed traders.** The informed counterparty only trades if its valuation is strictly beyond my price.
- With a bid below 10, informed traders holding 10 or 11 will not sell to me.
- With an ask at or above 20, an informed trader holding 20 will not buy from me.

So inside the band from about 10 to 20, I face only noise traders.

**Pricing against noise traders.** Noise traders value the contract at 15.25 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 9.8. Expected profit on each side is the edge times the chance the noise trader crosses it. For a normal distribution, this peaks when the edge is about 0.75 standard deviations, which is about 7.35.

- Ask: 15.25 + 7.35 = 22.6, which is above 20, so informed buyers never trade.
- Bid: 15.25 − 7.35 = 7.9, which is below 10, so informed sellers never trade.

{"bid": 7.9, "ask": 22.6}

With no inventory and one quote left, the best quote is again a wide bid of 7.9 and ask of 22.6.

**Fair value.** Die 3 = 7 and die 1 = 2, so the known part is 9. Die 2 is 1, 2, 11 or 11, so the contract settles at 10, 11, 20 or 20. Quotes 7 and 8 drew no trades, which tells us nothing. An informed trader's value of 10, 11 or 20 would not have crossed either quote. The public fair value is therefore 9 + 6.25 = 15.25.

**Ask side.** Any ask below 20 sells to informed traders holding 20, which costs money. At an ask of 20 or above, only noise traders buy. Expected profit from the ask is 0.5 × P(noise > a) × (a − 15.25), which peaks at about 0.83 near a = 22.6.

**Bid side.** Any bid at or below 10 avoids informed sellers, since the lowest possible value is 10. Expected profit from noise sellers peaks at about 0.83 near b = 7.9. A bid of 10 earns about 0.78. Bidding above 10 lets informed sellers in and earns less.

{"bid": 7.9, "ask": 22.6}

{"bid": 6.5, "ask": 24.5}

The public fair value is now about 12.8, well below the prior mean of 18.9, because the two sells at low bids pulled the estimate down.

**Prior mean.** Die 1 averages 6.33, die 2 averages 6.25 and die 3 averages 6.33, so the sum averages about 18.9.

The settlement value is the sum of three cards drawn without replacement.

**Fair value**
- One card has mean 7 and variance (13² − 1)/12 = 14.
- For three cards, the mean of the sum is 3 × 7 = 21.
- Drawing without replacement shrinks the variance: 3 × 14 × 49/51 ≈ 40.4. That gives a standard deviation of about 6.35.

**Choosing the spread**
- Treat the settlement value and noise-trader valuations as roughly normal around 21, both with a standard deviation of about 6.4.
- Write x for the half-spread divided by 6.4. The expected profit per side is then about 6.4 × [x·Q(x) − 0.35·φ(x)], where Q is the normal upper tail and φ is the normal density.
- This is largest near x ≈ 1, so the half-spread should be about 6.4.
- That puts the quotes at about 14.6 and 27.4. I'll use 14.6 / 27.4.

{"bid": 14.6, "ask": 27.4}

With nothing revealed, the expected sum of three cards is 21. The standard deviation is about 6.35, close to the noise traders' 6.4.

For a half-spread h, the profit per side is:
0.65 · h · P(noise > h) − 0.35 · E[(V − 21 − h)⁺]

Evaluating this:

| h | Expected profit per side |
|---|---|
| ≈3.2 | ≈0.20 |
| ≈4.8 | ≈0.41 |
| ≈6.4 | ≈0.47 (maximum) |
| ≈8.0 | ≈0.44 |

So a half-spread of about 6.4 around 21 is close to optimal. The two quotes without a trade don't change the fair value, so I'll keep the same quote.

{"bid": 14.6, "ask": 27.4}

**Uncertainty.** The sum of the two unseen cards has a standard deviation of about 5.2.

| Half-spread | Net expected profit per side |
|---|---|
| 4 | about 0.46 |
| 5 | about 0.54 |
| 6 | about 0.56 |

The curve is flat between 5 and 6, so I use about 5.5.

{"bid": 10.7, "ask": 21.7}

  - At ±10 to ±12, I make a small profit.

- **Expected value:** the 15 cards sum to 119, so one card averages 7.93. Three cards average 3 × 7.93 ≈ 23.8.

| h | Net expected profit |
|---|---|
| 2 | −0.20 |
| 4 | +0.31 |
| 5 | +0.34 |
| 6 | +0.31 |

The best half-spread is about 5, which gives a bid of 11.5 and an ask of 21.5.

**Bid:** At 7, informed traders never sell to me, because no value is below 7.

- Without using the trading history, card 2 is drawn from the 15 remaining cards and averages about 8.67. That gives a settlement value of about 10.67.

|---|---|

| 9 | ~21% |
| 7 | ~8% |
| 10 | ~6% |
| higher | ~4% |

- what I earn from noise traders who cross my quote, and
- what I lose to informed traders when the value falls outside my quote.

game.description: A custom deck of 13 cards is shuffled: 4 cards worth 2, 3 cards worth 10, 4 cards worth 13, 2 cards worth 14. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.

info.raw:
Fair value before any reveal is about 27.2 (mean card ≈ 9.08 × 3).

**Distribution of the sum.** I enumerated all 286 three-card hands:
- The sum ranges from 6 to 41, with standard deviation ≈ 7.8.
- It is lumpy: there is a cluster around 25–29 and an upper cluster at 33–41.

**Ask.** A tight ask loses to informed traders whenever the sum lands in the 33–41 cluster.
- At an ask of 38, the expected loss to informed traders is about 0.14 per arrival.
- The expected gain from noise traders is about 0.34.
- That gives a positive edge of about 0.1 per arrival, the best of the asks I checked.

**Bid.** By the same calculation on the downside, a bid around 16 roughly breaks even or makes a small profit. It sits below the 17–18 hands but above the rare 6 and 14 sums.

{"bid": 16, "ask": 38}

The buy at 38 is strong evidence of a high sum, so my estimate rises to about 36. I'll quote the ask at 41 and keep the bid low, around 22.

**Prior.** The average card is 118/13 ≈ 9.08, so the expected 3-card sum is about 27.2. The standard deviation of the sum is about 7.8.

**What the trade at 38 tells us.**
- An informed trader buys at 38 only if the true sum is above 38. That requires {13,13,13}, {14,13,13} or {14,14,13}. These are 20 of the 286 possible hands, so about 7%, and the average sum among them is 40.
- A noise trader buys only if its valuation lands above 38. That needs noise about 1.86 standard deviations above 27.2, which happens about 3% of the time.

Half of all counterparties are informed, and noise traders' valuations only vary by 5.4 around fair value. So a tight quote would mostly trade against informed counterparties and lose money. A rough normal-approximation check gives:

**Uncertainty.** One card has variance 83.2 − 7.8² = 22.36. Three cards drawn without replacement have variance 3 × 22.36 × 7/9 ≈ 52.2, so the standard deviation is about **7.2**.

**Spread.** Half the counterparties know the true sum, so a tight spread mostly loses money to them. Using a normal approximation for one side at 23.4 ± h:
- At h = 5, expected profit per side is about −0.08, a loss.
- At h = 8, it is about +0.04.
- At h = 10, it is about +0.02.

info.raw:
Expected value: die 1 shows at least 7 with probability 4/6 = 2/3, and die 2 does with probability 0.5. So E[value] = 10 × (2/3 + 1/2) ≈ 11.67.

The settlement value can only be 0, 10 or 20:
- 0 with probability 1/6
- 10 with probability 1/2
- 20 with probability 1/3

**Ask side.** An informed trader only buys when the value is 20, as long as my ask is between 10 and 20. That costs me 0.35 × (1/3) × (20 − ask).
- Noise traders pay me (ask − 11.67) when their valuation is above the ask.
- Expected profit is about 0.68 at an ask of 17, about 1.0 at 19, and about 1.07 at 20.
- At 20 the informed buyer no longer trades, so I place the ask there.

**Bid side.** An informed trader sells to me when the value is 0 (probability 1/6). Noise traders sell when their valuation is below the bid.
- Expected profit is about −0.11 at a bid of 10, 0.80 at 5, and about 0.93 at 2.
- It is roughly flat from 1 to 3, so I bid 2.

{"bid": 2, "ask": 20}

The fair value has dropped to about 7.6 after the sale at 2, and the best quote is a bid of 0 and an ask of 20.

- Die 1 shows at least 7 with probability 4/6 = 2/3 (faces 7, 8, 10, 12).
- Die 2 shows at least 7 with probability 1/2 (faces 8 and 9).
- So the settlement value is 0 with probability 1/6, 10 with probability 1/2, and 20 with probability 1/3.
- The prior mean is about 11.67.

- An informed trader sells at 2 only if the value is 0.
- A noise trader sells if its valuation is below 2. That happens with probability Φ((2 − 11.67)/10) ≈ 0.167.
- So the chance of a sale given each value is:
  - value 0: 0.35 + 0.65 × 0.167 ≈ 0.458
  - value 10 or 20: 0.65 × 0.167 ≈ 0.108
- Weighting the prior by these gives a posterior of about 0.458 (value 0), 0.325 (value 10) and 0.217 (value 20).
- The new public fair value is about 7.6.

**Choosing the bid.**
- Any bid above 0 is hit by an informed seller when the value is 0, which costs me the full bid.
- At a bid of 0, informed traders never sell to me.
- Noise traders then sell with probability about 0.22, so the expected profit is about 0.65 × 7.6 × 0.22 ≈ +1.1.

**Choosing the ask.**
- Any ask below 20 is lifted by an informed buyer when the value is 20.
- At an ask of 15, the expected profit is about +1.10 from noise traders minus about 0.38 lost to informed buyers, so about +0.72.

info.raw:
Quote: bid 1.0, ask 9.1. The contract is worth about 3.55 on average, but trading close to that loses to informed counterparties, so both sides sit just inside the lowest and second-highest card values.

**Settlement distribution.** The contract pays the minimum of 3 cards drawn from 12. There are 220 possible hands.

| Minimum | Hands | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 55 | 0.25 |
| 3 | 130 | 0.591 |
| 9 | 31 | 0.141 |
| 14 | 4 | 0.018 |

The expected value is 780 / 220 ≈ 3.55.

**Ask side.**
- Any ask between 3 and 9 sells to every informed trader holding a 9 or 14. That loss is larger than what noise traders pay, so expected profit is about zero or negative.
- Just above 9, only a value of 14 hurts me. Noise traders occasionally pay well above fair value.
- At an ask of 9.1 the expected profit is slightly positive: about 0.13 from noise traders against about 0.09 lost to informed traders, before halving.

**Bid side.**
- Any bid above 3 buys from informed traders holding a 1 or a 3, which is very costly.
- At a bid of 1.0, an informed trader whose value is 1 is not below my bid, so informed traders never sell to me.
- Noise traders still sell to me about 18% of the time, each with an edge of about 2.5. That gives expected profit of roughly 0.46 from noise traders, or about 0.23 after weighting by the 50% chance a counterparty is noise.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9.1}

Fair value is about 3.4. I'll bid 1.0 and ask 9.0 to stay just at the card values, so the informed trader never trades against me except when the min is 14.

**Fair value before trading.** The minimum of 3 cards drawn from {1×1, 3×4, 9×3, 14×4} has this distribution:
- P(min = 1) = 55/220 ≈ 0.25
- P(min = 3) = 130/220 ≈ 0.59
- P(min = 9) = 31/220 ≈ 0.14
- P(min = 14) = 4/220 ≈ 0.02

The expected value is about 3.55.

**Effect of quote 1.** There was no trade at 1 / 9.1. An informed trader would only have traded if the value were 14, so that outcome becomes about half as likely. Fair value moves to roughly 3.4.

**Bid side.**
- **Bid at 1.0:** An informed trader holding a value of 1 does not sell, because 1 is not below 1. A noise trader sells about 19% of the time, and each sale gains me about 2.4.
- **Bid above 1:** Every informed trader holding a value of 1 would sell to me. That loss is larger than the extra noise flow.

**Ask side.**
- **Ask at 9.0:** An informed trader only buys if the value is 14, which is rare. A noise trader occasionally buys, and each purchase gains me about 5.6.
- **Ask below 9:** Every informed trader holding a value of 9 would buy from me. Asking 8, for example, gives a lower expected profit than 9.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9.0}

Card 1 is a 9, so the settlement is min(9, card 2, card 3). The other two cards come from the 11 left: one 1, four 3s, two 9s and four 14s.

**Settlement distribution**
- P(min = 1) = 10/55 ≈ 0.18
- P(min = 3) = 30/55 ≈ 0.55
- P(min = 9) = 15/55 ≈ 0.27
- Fair value = 235/55 ≈ 4.27

**Ask side**
- Any ask below 9 sells to informed traders whenever the value is 9. That loses more than the noise buyers pay us.
- An ask of 9 avoids informed buyers entirely, because a value of 9 is not above 9.
- At 9 the expected profit from noise buyers is about 0.11. That is about the best available on this side.

**Bid side**
- Any bid above 1 buys from informed sellers when the value is 1.
- A bid of 1 avoids that loss, because a value of 1 is not below 1.
- At 1 the expected profit from noise sellers is about 0.20, the best on this side.

{"bid": 1, "ask": 9}

The first card is a 9, so the settlement value can only be 1, 3 or 9. It is 1 if the 1 is dealt, otherwise 3 if any 3 is dealt, otherwise 9.

**Remaining deck (11 cards):** one 1, four 3s, two 9s, four 14s. Two more cards are dealt, giving 55 possible pairs.

| Settlement | Condition | Pairs | Probability |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | the 1 is dealt | 10 | 2/11 |
| 3 | at least one 3, no 1 | 30 | 6/11 |
| 9 | both cards are 9 or 14 | 15 | 3/11 |

The fair value is (2 + 18 + 27)/11 ≈ **4.27**. No trades so far, and an informed trader would not have traded at 1/9 anyway, so the history tells us nothing more.

**Ask:** Any ask below 9 gets bought by informed traders whenever the value is 9 (3/11 of the time). That loss is bigger than the noise-trader profit; for example, ask 6 has expected value of about −0.35. At an ask of exactly 9, informed traders never buy, and noise traders occasionally buy at a profit of about 4.7.

**Bid:** Any bid above 3 is hit by informed traders whenever the value is 1 or 3, which is a heavy loss. Between 1 and 3, the bid is hit by informed traders when the value is 1. Comparing bids, a bid of 1 does best: informed traders never sell, and it has the best noise-trader edge (about 0.40 per unit, versus about 0.38 at 1.2 and 0.29 at 2).

{"bid": 1, "ask": 9}

Card 2 is the only card worth 1, so the minimum, and the settlement value, is certainly **1**.

**Informed traders:** they value the contract at exactly 1. If my bid is below 1 and my ask is above 1, they never trade with me.

**Noise traders:** their valuation is 1 + N(0, 2.8). If I quote at a distance x from 1, my expected profit on each side is x·Φ(−x/2.8).

**Best distance:** maximising that requires Φ(−z) = z·φ(z), where z = x/2.8. This gives z ≈ 0.75, so x ≈ 2.1.

That puts the bid at 1 − 2.1 = −1.1 and the ask at 1 + 2.1 = 3.1. One trade moves my position by at most one unit, so the ±3 limit is not a concern.

{"bid": -1.1, "ask": 3.1}

Card 2 is a 1, which is the lowest card in the deck. So the minimum of the dealt cards is certainly 1, and the contract settles at exactly 1.

**Informed traders:** they value the contract at exactly 1. With my bid at or below 1 and my ask at or above 1, they never trade at a loss to me.

**Noise traders:** they value it at 1 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 2.8. On each side my expected profit is d × P(Z > d/2.8), where d is the distance from fair value. This is maximised at d/σ ≈ 0.75, so d ≈ 2.1.

**Position:** I am long 1, so either a buy or a sell keeps me within the ±3 limit.

That gives a bid of 1 − 2.1 = −1.1 and an ask of 1 + 2.1 = 3.1.

game.title: Dice/cards max
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (4 faces, each equally likely): 2, 4, 8, 8.
- Die 2 (4 faces, each equally likely): 4, 6, 7, 12.
- Die 3 (6 faces, loaded): 0 (prob 1/5), 1 (prob 1/5), 2 (prob 1/5), 6 (prob 1/10), 9 (prob 1/10), 12 (prob 1/5).
game.contract: The contract settles at the largest of the dice.

info.raw:
Expected settlement value is about 9.09:

- **Max of dice 1 and 2:** it is 4 with probability 2/16, 6 with 2/16, 7 with 2/16, 8 with 6/16 and 12 with 4/16. Its mean is 8.125.
- **Die 3 is 0, 1 or 2 (probability 0.6):** die 3 never matters, so the expected max is 8.125.
- **Die 3 is 6 (0.1):** the expected max is 8.375.
- **Die 3 is 9 (0.1):** the expected max is 9.75.
- **Die 3 is 12 (0.2):** the max is 12.
- **Fair value** is 0.6×8.125 + 0.1×8.375 + 0.1×9.75 + 0.2×12 ≈ 9.09.

The settlement is 12 with probability 40%, so it is heavily skewed upward. An informed trader often buys at a large edge, so I set the ask a little wider above fair than the bid is below it. The spread also has to cover the 20% chance of facing an informed trader, given noise traders' 2.6 standard deviation.

{"bid": 7.9, "ask": 10.4}

Expected settlement is about 9.09. I'm quoting slightly tighter than last time around that value.

**Distribution of the max of dice 1 and 2**

| Value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 4 | 2/16 |
| 6 | 2/16 |
| 7 | 2/16 |
| 8 | 6/16 |
| 12 | 4/16 |

**Expected max for each die 3 outcome**

| Die 3 | Probability | Expected max |
|---|---|---|
| 0, 1 or 2 | 0.6 | 8.125 |
| 6 | 0.1 | 8.375 |
| 9 | 0.1 | 9.75 |
| 12 | 0.2 | 12 |

The weighted average is 0.6 × 8.125 + 0.1 × 8.375 + 0.1 × 9.75 + 0.2 × 12 ≈ **9.09**.

Last quote's no-trade gives almost no information. The settlement value has a wide spread, so informed counterparties are a real risk. That calls for a moderately wide quote centred near 9.1, a bit tighter than the last one (7.9 / 10.4).

{"bid": 8.0, "ask": 10.2}

With die 3 = 1 revealed, the settlement is the larger of die 1 and die 2. Over the 16 equally likely pairs, the settlement distribution is:

| Value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 4 | 2/16 |
| 6 | 2/16 |
| 7 | 2/16 |
| 8 | 6/16 |
| 12 | 4/16 |

The expected value is 130/16 ≈ 8.1. The earlier sell at 8 nudges public fair value slightly lower, to about 8.0.

**Ask side:** An informed trader only buys if the value is 12, which has probability 0.25. Noise traders have standard deviation 2.6. My rough expected profit by ask level:
- 9.3: about 0.16
- 10.0: about 0.23
- 10.5: about 0.25

So the best ask is around 10.2–10.5.

**Bid side:** Informed traders sell if the value is below my bid. The jumps at 6 and 7 make bids near 7–7.5 costly. My rough expected profit by bid level:
- 7.5: about 0.03
- 6.5: about 0.25
- 6.0: about 0.30
- 5.5: about 0.30

So the best bid is around 6.0.

I'm long 1, so I lean the ask slightly lower to make a sale a bit more likely.

{"bid": 6.0, "ask": 10.2}

Die 3 = 1, so the contract now settles at the larger of die 1 and die 2.

**Prior fair value.** Die 1 and die 2 give 16 equally likely pairs:
- Die 1 = 2 gives 4, 6, 7, 12.
- Die 1 = 4 gives 4, 6, 7, 12.
- Die 1 = 8 (twice) gives 8, 8, 8, 12.

The mean is 130/16 ≈ 8.13. The settlement is 12 with probability 0.25. Otherwise it averages about 6.83, taking the values 4, 6, 7 and 8.

**Update for the buy at 10.2.**
- If the value is 12, a buy is about 0.37 likely: 0.2 from an informed trader plus about 0.17 from noise.
- If the value is not 12, a buy is about 0.17 likely.
- So the chance of 12 rises to about 0.42, and fair value becomes about 0.42 × 12 + 0.58 × 6.83 ≈ 9.0.

**Choosing the quotes.**
- **Ask:** An informed trader only buys if the value is 12. The expected profit is roughly flat at about 0.3 for asks between 11.5 and 12.
- **Bid:** An informed trader sells if the value is 4, 6 or 7. The expected profit peaks at about 0.28 for bids between 6.5 and 7.

{"bid": 6.8, "ask": 11.6}

**Bid 7.0, ask 11.5.** The value can only be 8 or 12, with expected value 9, and these prices give the best expected profit on each side.

**Settlement value now.** Die 1 = 8 and die 3 = 1, so the contract settles at the larger of 8 and die 2.
- Die 2 rolls 4, 6 or 7 with probability 3/4, so the value is 8.
- Die 2 rolls 12 with probability 1/4, so the value is 12.
- Fair value is 0.75 × 8 + 0.25 × 12 = 9.

**Bid side.** An informed trader never sells to me at a bid of 8 or below: if the value is 8 its valuation is not below my bid, and if it is 12 it would not sell at all. So a bid of 8 or below carries no adverse selection and only faces noise traders, whose valuations are centred on 9.
- Expected profit is about 0.8 × y × P(noise < −y), where y is the distance of my bid below 9.
- This peaks at about y = 0.75 × 2.6 ≈ 1.95, so the bid is about 7.0.
- That gives about 0.35, against 0.28 for a bid of 8.

**Ask side.** An informed trader buys only when the value is 12 and my ask is below 12. That costs me 0.05 × (12 − ask). I compared expected profit at a few asks:

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 11.0 | 0.303 |
| 11.5 | 0.312 |
| 11.6 | 0.310 |
| 12.0 | 0.298 |

The ask of 11.5 comes out best.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 11.5}

Die 3 is 1 and die 1 is 8, so the maximum is at least 8. It goes up to 12 only if die 2 shows 12, which has probability 1/4. Otherwise it stays at 8. That makes the fair value 0.75×8 + 0.25×12 = 9.

**Bid:** An informed trader only sells to me if the true value is below my bid. The value is 8 or 12, so a bid of 8 or less never trades against an informed seller. Among bids at or below 8, expected profit from noise traders is highest at 7, about 0.35.

**Ask:** An ask below 12 loses about 0.05 times (12 minus the ask) to informed buyers when die 2 is 12. Netting that against noise-trader profit, the best ask is about 11.5, worth about 0.31. That is slightly better than asking 12, worth about 0.30.

{"bid": 7, "ask": 11.5}

game.title: Dice/cards max
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (4 faces, each equally likely): 2, 4, 8, 8.
- Die 2 (4 faces, each equally likely): 4, 6, 7, 12.
- Die 3 (6 faces, loaded): 0 (prob 1/5), 1 (prob 1/5), 2 (prob 1/5), 6 (prob 1/10), 9 (prob 1/10), 12 (prob 1/5).
game.contract: The contract settles at the largest of the dice.

info.raw:
Expected max of the three dice (the public fair value) is about **9.09**. It comes from the max's distribution: P(4)=0.075, P(6)=0.1, P(7)=0.0875, P(8)=0.2625, P(9)=0.075, P(12)=0.4.

To set the quotes, I weighed the profit from noise traders (fair value plus N(0, 2.6) noise) against the loss to informed traders (probability 0.2), who know the settlement value.

- **Ask:** There is a 40% chance the value is 12, so selling much below 12 loses heavily to informed buyers. Expected profit peaks around 11.5–11.9, at about +0.30 per quote.
- **Bid:** Informed sellers only hurt when the value is 4, 6 or 7. Expected profit peaks around 6.9–7.0, at about +0.29 per quote.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 11.5}

Before any reveal, the fair value of the contract is about 9.09, the expected maximum of the three dice.

**Step 1: largest of dice 1 and 2.**

| Value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 4 | 0.125 |
| 6 | 0.125 |
| 7 | 0.125 |
| 8 | 0.375 |
| 12 | 0.25 |

**Step 2: combine with die 3.**

| Die 3 result | Probability | Expected maximum |
|---|---|---|
| 0, 1 or 2 | 0.6 | 8.125 |
| 6 | 0.1 | 8.375 |
| 9 | 0.1 | 9.75 |
| 12 | 0.2 | 12 |

Weighting these gives an expected maximum of about **9.09**.

**Risk to the ask.** There is a 40% chance the settlement is 12, which happens whenever die 2 or die 3 shows 12. An informed buyer is therefore a large risk on the ask side, so I skew the ask somewhat wider.

**Last quote.** The previous quote of 7 / 11.5 drew no trade. That tells us little, since that outcome is common for noise traders anyway.

{"bid": 7.8, "ask": 10.8}

Die 3 = 6 is now public, so I quote around its fair value and set each side for the best expected profit.

**Fair value.** The contract is max(die 1, die 2, 6). The 16 equally likely (die 1, die 2) pairs give:
- 6 with probability 4/16
- 7 with probability 2/16
- 8 with probability 6/16
- 12 with probability 4/16

The expected value is 134/16 = 8.375.

**Ask.** The noise trader's valuation is 8.375 plus noise with standard deviation 2.6. The informed trader buys only when the value is 12. The expected profit from the ask peaks near 10.5–11, at about 0.28 per quote.

**Bid.** The informed trader sells only when the value is below the bid. A bid at or near 6 limits informed losses to the value-6 case (25% chance), and only if the bid is above 6. The expected profit from the bid peaks around 6.0–6.3, at about 0.34 per quote.

{"bid": 6.1, "ask": 10.7}

Fair value is about 8.4 now that die 3 = 6 sets a floor of 6. I'll quote a 6.3 bid and a 10.8 ask.

**Settlement distribution given die 3 = 6**
- Die 1 is effectively 6 or 8, each with probability 1/2.
- Die 2 is effectively 6 (prob 1/2), 7 (1/4) or 12 (1/4).
- The maximum is 6 with prob 1/4, 7 with 1/8, 8 with 3/8 and 12 with 1/4. The mean is 8.375.
- Quote 3 (6.1 / 10.7) got no trade. That makes a settlement of 6 or 12 slightly less likely, so fair value stays around 8.4.

**Ask side**
- An informed buyer is only a danger if the value is 12, which has probability 1/4.
- Asks between about 10.5 and 11 give the highest expected profit, about 0.28 per quote, against noise traders.

**Bid side**
- An informed seller is only a danger if the value is 6 or 7.
- A bid just above 6 gives an expected profit of about 0.34. Since a 6 now looks a little less likely, I can bid slightly higher.

{"bid": 6.3, "ask": 10.8}

**Quote: bid 7.9, ask 12.0.** I set these from the possible settlement values and an updated estimate of how likely each one is.

**Possible settlement values.** Die 3 is 6 and die 1 is 8. The maximum is therefore 8 unless die 2 shows 12. Die 2 shows 12 with prior probability 1/4, so settlement is either 8 or 12.

**What the earlier trade tells us.** The stage‑2 buy at 10.8 makes 12 more likely.
- In stage 2, the public fair value was about 8.375.
- An informed buyer at 10.8 only buys if settlement is 12.
- A noise trader buys at 10.8 with probability about 0.175.
- Updating on that buy raises P(settle = 12) from 0.25 to about 0.45.
- That gives a fair value of about 9.8.

**Ask.** At or below 12, an informed trader only buys from me when settlement is 12, which loses me money. Against that, noise traders buy at a profit to me. Expected profit per quote rises to about 0.35 at an ask of 12.0 and stays about the same at 12.1 before falling at higher asks.

**Bid.** With the bid at 8 or below, informed traders never sell to me, because settlement is never below 8. Expected profit from noise sellers is about 0.35 for bids between 7.8 and 8.0, and 7.9 sits in that range.

{"bid": 7.9, "ask": 12.0}

Settlement is max(8, die 2). That is 12 if die 2 is 12, and 8 otherwise.

**Value of the contract**
- The prior chance that die 2 is 12 is 1/4.
- The buy at 10.8 in stage 2 raises that chance, because an informed trader would buy there only if die 2 were 12.
- The earlier quotes with no trade lower it again.
- My estimate is about a 30–35% chance of 12. That puts fair value near 9.3.

**Bid**
- The value can never be below 8, so a bid of 8.0 never trades with an informed seller.
- Noise sellers at 8 give an expected edge of about 1.3 per unit.

**Ask**
- An informed trader buys only when the value is 12.
- Weighing the edge from noise buyers against that loss, the best ask is about 11.7.

{"bid": 8.0, "ask": 11.7}

game.title: Dice/cards min
game.description: A custom deck of 12 cards is shuffled: 1 card worth 1, 4 cards worth 3, 3 cards worth 9, 4 cards worth 14. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the smallest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
Settlement is the minimum of 3 cards drawn without replacement from {1, 3×4, 9×3, 14×4}.

**Settlement distribution** (out of C(12,3) = 220 hands):
- P(min = 1) = 55/220 ≈ 0.25
- P(min = 3) = 130/220 ≈ 0.59
- P(min = 9) = 31/220 ≈ 0.14
- P(min = 14) = 4/220 ≈ 0.02

E[min] ≈ **3.55**.

**Bid side.** Any bid above 3 gets hit by informed traders whenever the value is 1 or 3. That happens about 84% of the time, so those bids are clearly bad. A bid between 1 and 3 still loses to informed sellers when the value is 1. A bid at exactly 1.0 gets no informed sells, because the counterparty only sells if its valuation is strictly below my bid. Noise traders still sell there about 18% of the time, for an edge of about 2.5 each. This was the best bid I checked, worth about +0.23 in expectation.

**Ask side.** Below 9, informed buyers pick me off whenever the value is 9 or 14 (about 16% of the time). From about 7 up to 9 the expected value is close to zero. Just above 9, only a value of 14 hurts me, and that is about 2% likely. Noise traders still buy sometimes, so 9.1 comes out slightly positive.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9.1}

No trade at 1 / 9.1 slightly lowers fair value to about 3.44, so I'll keep the bid at 1.0 and tighten the ask to 9.0.

**Prior fair value.** Using counts out of C(12,3) = 220, the smallest card is distributed as:

| Smallest card | Count | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 55 | 0.25 |
| 3 | 130 | 0.59 |
| 9 | 31 | 0.14 |
| 14 | 4 | 0.02 |

That gives an expected value of 780/220 ≈ 3.55.

**Update from quote 1.** At 1 / 9.1, an informed trader would trade only if the value were 14. So no trade makes 14 less likely, and fair value drops to about 3.44.

**Bid.** Any bid above 1 lets an informed trader holding value 1 sell to me. At exactly 1.0 that can't happen, and noise traders sell about 19% of the time at roughly 2.4 below fair value. This came out best among the bids I checked, at about +0.23 per quote.

**Ask.** At 9.0, an informed trader holding value 9 won't buy, and only the small remaining chance of 14 hurts me. Noise traders buy about 2.4% of the time, so the expected edge is small but positive. An ask of 8.5 is about the same.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9.0}

Card 1 is a 9, so the settlement is min(9, card 2, card 3). The remaining 11 cards are one 1, four 3s, two 9s and four 14s.

**Settlement distribution**
- P(min = 1) = 1 − C(10,2)/C(11,2) = 10/55
- P(min = 3) = 30/55
- P(min = 9) = 15/55
- Fair value = (10·1 + 30·3 + 15·9)/55 ≈ 4.27

An informed trader values the contract at exactly 1, 3 or 9. A noise trader values it at about 4.27 ± 2.8.

**Ask:** At 9.0, an informed trader never buys, because a valuation of 9 is not above 9. A noise trader buys about 4.5% of the time and I gain about 4.7 per trade, so the expected gain is about +0.11. Any ask between 3 and 9 exposes me to the 27% chance the value is 9, and those asks all score lower.

**Bid:** At 1.0, an informed trader never sells, because a valuation of 1 is not below 1. A noise trader sells about 12% of the time and I gain about 3.3 per trade, so the expected gain is about +0.20. Bids between 1 and 3 add informed losses when the value is 1. They come out worse: about 0.18 at 1.5 and 0.15 at 2.

{"bid": 1, "ask": 9}

The fair value is about 4.27. I'll quote a bid of 1 and an ask of 9.

**Fair value after card 1 = 9.** The 11 cards left are one 1, four 3s, two 9s and four 14s. Two more cards are dealt, and the contract settles at the smallest of the three.
- P(min = 1) = 1 − (10/11)(9/10) = 2/11
- P(min = 3) = (9/11)·[1 − (6/10)(5/9)] = 6/11
- P(min = 9) = 3/11
- Expected settlement = (2 + 18 + 27)/11 ≈ 4.27

**Ask side.** An informed trader buys only when it knows the value is 9 and my ask is below 9. Any ask under 9 therefore loses money to them.
- At an ask of 9, informed traders never buy.
- A noise trader buys at 9 with probability about 4.6%, for an expected gain of about 0.11.
- Asks between 7 and 8.5 do worse, because the losses to informed buyers outweigh the extra noise trades.

**Bid side.** An informed trader sells only when it knows the value is 1 and my bid is above 1. Any bid over 1 therefore loses money to them.
- At a bid of 1, informed traders never sell.
- A noise trader sells at 1 with probability about 12%, for an expected gain of about 0.20.
- Bids of 1.5 or 2 do worse, because the losses to informed sellers outweigh the extra noise trades.

{"bid": 1, "ask": 9}

The fair value is 5.8. I'll quote a bid of 3.0 and an ask of 9.0.

**What the third card can do.** Ten cards remain: one 1, four 3s, two 9s and three 14s. With 9 and 14 already showing, the minimum depends only on card 3:
- If card 3 is 1, the contract settles at 1 (probability 0.1).
- If card 3 is 3, it settles at 3 (probability 0.4).
- If card 3 is 9 or 14, it settles at 9 (probability 0.5).

The expected value is 0.1×1 + 0.4×3 + 0.5×9 = 5.8. No trades so far, and my wide quotes could not have revealed anything, so the public fair value is 5.8.

**Ask.** An informed trader buys only if the true value is above my ask.
- At exactly 9, no informed trader buys, because the value is never above 9.
- Noise traders still buy about 12.7% of the time at a 3.2 edge, worth about +0.20 per quote.
- Any ask just below 9 is lifted by informed traders when the value is 9, which costs more than it gains.
- A higher ask, such as 10, keeps the safety but cuts the noise profit to about 0.14.

So 9.0 is the best ask.

**Bid.** An informed trader sells only if the true value is below my bid.
- At exactly 3, the only informed sale is when the value is 1, costing about 0.10.
- Noise traders sell about 15.9% of the time at a 2.8 edge, worth about +0.22.
- The net is about +0.12, the best of the bids I checked:

| Bid | Net expected profit |
|---|---|
| 1 | 0.10 |
| 2 | 0.12 |
| 2.5 | 0.12 |
| 3.0 | 0.12 (highest) |
| 3.1 | 0.10 |

So 3.0 is the best bid.

{"bid": 3, "ask": 9}

The fair value is 5.8. I'm quoting bid 3 and ask 9.

**Settlement distribution.** The 10 unseen cards are: one 1, four 3s, two 9s and three 14s. The contract pays min(9, 14, card 3):
- 1 with probability 0.1
- 3 with probability 0.4
- 9 with probability 0.5

That gives a fair value of 0.1 + 1.2 + 4.5 = 5.8.

**Ask side.**
- **At 9:** an informed trader never buys, because a value of 9 is not above 9. A noise trader buys with probability P(Z > 1.14) ≈ 0.127, earning 3.2. Expected value ≈ 0.20.
- **Below 9:** the informed trader buys whenever the value is 9, which costs more than the extra noise trades earn. At an ask of 8 the expected value is about 0.
- **Above 9:** at 9.5 the expected value is ≈ 0.17, and at 10 it is ≈ 0.14.

So 9 is the best ask.

**Bid side.**
- **At 3:** an informed trader sells only when the value is 1, costing 0.5 × 0.1 × 2 = 0.1. A noise trader sells with probability P(Z < −1) ≈ 0.159, earning 2.8, which is worth ≈ 0.22. Expected value ≈ 0.12.
- **At 3.5:** the informed trader also sells when the value is 3, and the expected value drops to ≈ 0.01.
- **Lower bids:** 2 gives ≈ 0.12 and 1 gives ≈ 0.10, so they are slightly worse.

So 3 is the best bid.

{"bid": 3, "ask": 9}

game.title: Dice/cards min
game.description: A custom deck of 8 cards is shuffled: 1 card worth 2, 2 cards worth 9, 4 cards worth 13, 1 card worth 14. 2 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the smallest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
The fair value is about 8.68, so I quote bid 4.0 and ask 13.0, each placed near its profit-maximising point.

**Fair value: expected minimum of the 2 dealt cards.** There are C(8,2) = 28 equally likely pairs.

| Minimum | Pairs | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | Any pair containing the 2: 7 | 0.25 |
| 9 | 9-9 (1) plus 9 with a 13 or 14 (10): 11 | 0.393 |
| 13 | Pairs from the 13s and 14: 10 | 0.357 |

Expected value = (7·2 + 11·9 + 10·13) / 28 = 243 / 28 ≈ 8.68.

**Ask side.**
- A noise trader buys if its valuation exceeds my ask, which happens with probability P(Z > (a − 8.68)/6.3).
- An informed trader buys only when the value is 13 (probability 0.357), costing me 13 − a. If the ask were below 9, it would also buy when the value is 9.
- Expected profit = 0.8·P_noise·(a − 8.68) − 0.2·0.357·(13 − a).
- This flattens out around a = 13 to 13.5, at about 0.85 per quote. I use 13.0.

**Bid side.**
- An informed trader sells when the value is 2 (probability 0.25), costing me b − 2.
- Expected profit = 0.8·P_noise·(8.68 − b) − 0.2·0.25·(b − 2).
- This peaks around b = 3 to 4, at about 0.78. I use 4.0.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 13.0}

After the first trade (someone sold to me at 4), my updated fair value is about **7.2**. I'll quote a bid of 2.5 and an ask of 12.5.

**Prior for the minimum.** There are 28 equally likely pairs of cards.
- The minimum is 2 in 7 pairs (any pair containing the 2).
- The minimum is 9 in 11 pairs (the two 9s together, or one 9 with a 13 or 14).
- The minimum is 13 in 10 pairs (two 13s, or a 13 with the 14).
- The prior expected value is 243/28 ≈ 8.68.

**Update from the sale at 4.**
- An informed trader sells at 4 only if the value is 2.
- A noise trader sells if 8.68 plus noise is below 4. That happens with probability Φ(−4.68/6.3), about 0.229.
- A sale is therefore about 2.1 times as likely when the value is 2 (0.383 versus 0.183).
- Updated probabilities: value 2 ≈ 0.41, value 9 ≈ 0.31, value 13 ≈ 0.28.
- New fair value ≈ **7.24**.

**Choosing each side.**
- **Ask:** An informed trader buys only if the value is 13 (probability 0.28). Expected profit rises with the ask and is roughly flat between 12.5 and 13, at about 0.82–0.83. I'll use 12.5.
- **Bid:** An informed trader sells if the value is 2 (probability 0.41). Expected profit peaks with the bid around 2–2.5, at about 0.82–0.85. I'll use 2.5.
- My position is +1, so inventory limits don't constrain either side.

{"bid": 2.5, "ask": 12.5}

Card 1 is the only 2 in the deck, so the minimum of the two cards is certainly 2. The settlement value is therefore known to be exactly 2, and the public fair value is 2.

- **Informed traders** value the contract at 2. They will never trade against a quote that is outside 2 on either side.
- **Noise traders** value it at 2 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 6.3.
- **Choosing the spread:** the expected edge per side is proportional to x·P(noise > x), where x is the distance from 2. This is largest at about x ≈ 0.75σ ≈ 4.7.
- **Quote:** that gives a bid of about -2.7 and an ask of about 6.7. My position of +1 leaves room to trade on either side.

{"bid": -2.7, "ask": 6.7}

game.title: Dice/cards min
game.description: A custom deck of 8 cards is shuffled: 1 card worth 2, 2 cards worth 9, 4 cards worth 13, 1 card worth 14. 2 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the smallest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
The settlement value is the smaller of two cards drawn from {2, 9, 9, 13, 13, 13, 13, 14}. There are 28 equally likely pairs:
- **Settles at 2** (pair includes the 2): 7 pairs, probability 0.25.
- **Settles at 9** (no 2, at least one 9): 11 pairs, probability about 0.39.
- **Settles at 13** (both cards from the 13s and the 14): 10 pairs, probability about 0.36.

So the fair value is 243/28, about **8.68**.

**Ask side.** An informed trader buys only when the value is 13. Expected profit per quote is:
0.8 × (a − 8.68) × P(noise trader's valuation > a) − 0.2 × 0.357 × (13 − a), with the second term only applying when a < 13.

This rises up to about a ≈ 13–14 and peaks around **13.5**, at roughly 0.86 per quote.

**Bid side.** An informed trader sells only when the value is 2, which costs 0.2 × 0.25 × (b − 2). Expected profit is best around **b ≈ 3.3**, at roughly 0.78 per quote.

{"bid": 3.3, "ask": 13.5}

No update to fair value from the first trade. An informed trader never pays 13.5, because the maximum possible minimum is 13. So that buy came from a noise trader, and noise trades carry no information.

**Settlement distribution (minimum of 2 cards, 28 equally likely pairs):**
- Minimum is 2: 7 of 28 pairs.
- Minimum is 9: 11 of 28 pairs.
- Minimum is 13: 10 of 28 pairs.
- Fair value = (7×2 + 11×9 + 10×13) / 28 = 243/28 ≈ 8.68.

**Quote choice:**
- **Ask:** at 13.0 or above, no informed trader ever buys from me. The expected edge from noise traders is about the same anywhere from 13 to 14, so I keep the ask at 13.5.
- **Bid:** any bid above 2 gets picked off by informed sellers when the minimum is 2. Expected profit is highest with the bid around 2.9–3.0, at about 0.79 per quote. Since I'm short 1, buying back would be slightly welcome.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 13.5}

Card 1 is a 13, so the fair value is the expected minimum given the 7 cards left (2, 9, 9, 13, 13, 13, 14):
- The settlement is 2 with probability 1/7, 9 with probability 2/7, and 13 with probability 4/7.

Fair value after the first trade is about 4.15. Since I'm short 1, I lean the quote slightly toward buying.

- **Prior fair value:** with no cards revealed, the expected smallest card is 2 + 2731/1540 ≈ 3.77.
- **Two kinds of outcome:** the smallest card is 5 or more with probability 286/1540 ≈ 0.19, and in that case it averages about 7.19. Otherwise it is 2, 3 or 4 and averages about 3.0.
- **Effect of the buy at 4.6:**
  - If the smallest card is 5 or more, an informed trader always buys. A noise trader buys with probability P(Z > (4.6 − 3.77)/2.3) ≈ 0.36. The chance of a buy is then 0.2 + 0.8 × 0.36 ≈ 0.49.
  - If the smallest card is below 5, only a noise trader buys, so the chance is 0.8 × 0.36 ≈ 0.29.
  - The probability that the smallest card is 5 or more therefore rises to about 0.28.
- **Updated fair value:** 0.28 × 7.19 + 0.72 × 3.0 ≈ 4.15.

The spread is fairly wide because informed traders gain a lot on the side where the smallest card is high.

{"bid": 3.5, "ask": 5.2}

Card 1 is 13, so the contract settles at min(13, card 2, card 3). Card 2 and card 3 come from the 21 cards still in the deck.

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 2 | 39/210 |
| 3 | 51/210 |
| 4 | 54/210 |
| 5 | 38/210 |
| 12 | 13/210 |
| 13 | 15/210 |

The fair value is 988/210 ≈ 4.7. The two buys in stage 1 nudge it up a little, to about 4.7–5. There is roughly a 13% chance the settlement is 12 or 13.

**Position:** I am short 2, which hurts in that 13% high case.

**Bid at 3.0:**
- Informed traders only sell to me when the value is 2, so their expected cost is small.
- Noise traders sell often enough that the expected edge is about +0.27 per quote.
- A buy here also reduces my risky short.

**Ask at 6.8:**
- Selling another unit adds tail risk, since an informed trader buys whenever the value is 12 or 13.
- A wide ask means I sell only to noise traders with high valuations, and the expected edge is still slightly positive, about +0.14.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 6.8}

Quoting a bid of 4.3. My ask is pulled because I'm at -3.

**Prior fair value given card 1 = 13.** The settlement is min(13, c2, c3), where c2 and c3 come from the 21 cards left. Thirteen of those are low cards (2, 3, 4 or 5) and eight are high (12, 13 or 15).

- The chance that both c2 and c3 are 12 or higher is C(8,2)/C(21,2) = 28/210 ≈ 0.13. In that case the settlement is about 12.5.
- Otherwise the settlement averages about 3.5.
- That gives an expected value of about 4.7.

**Update for the stage-2 buy at 6.8.**
- An informed trader buys at 6.8 only if the value is high.
- A noise trader buys at 6.8 about 18% of the time.
- Applying that likelihood raises the chance of a high settlement to roughly 27%.
- Fair value becomes about 6.0. The stage-1 buys push it a little higher, roughly 6.0–6.2.

**Choosing the bid.**
- Noise sellers would give me about 1.7 of edge per unit.
- Informed sellers only hit my bid when the value is low, mostly 2 or 3, so they cost me money.
- Comparing bids between 4 and 5, a bid around 4.3 gives the best expected profit, about 0.2 per quote. It also gives me a chance to cover part of my short.

{"bid": 4.3, "ask": null}

I'm at the short limit of -3, so only a bid is allowed. I'll bid **7.2**, a small positive-edge bid.

**Prior on settlement.** With cards 13 and 15 revealed, 20 cards remain. The settlement is card 3 if it is below 13, otherwise 13. That gives:
- 2 with 2 cards, 3 with 3, 4 with 4, 5 with 4, 12 with 2, and 13 with 5 (the remaining 13s and 15s).
- The prior expected value is 6.9.

**Updating on the trade history.**
- At quote 3, someone bought at my ask of 6.8. An informed trader only buys there if the value is 12 or 13, so this points toward high values.
- At quote 4, nobody sold at my bid of 4.3. An informed trader would have sold if the value was 4 or less, so this points slightly away from low values.
- Using rough likelihoods for noise and informed traders, the posterior expected value is about 9.6.
- The posterior is bimodal: about 36% chance the value is 5 or less (average about 3.9), and about 64% chance it is 12 or 13.

**Choosing the bid.**
- Noise traders who sell to me are buying from me below the expected value, which is profitable for me.
- An informed trader sells to me only when the value is 5 or less, which costs me.
- Expected profit as a function of the bid:
  - 6: about +0.02
  - 7: about +0.05
  - 7.3: about +0.05 (peak)
  - 8: about +0.02
- I'm shading slightly to 7.2 because my fair-value estimate is uncertain.

{"bid": 7.2, "ask": null}

With cards 13 and 15 revealed, the contract settles at card 3 if card 3 is below 13, otherwise at 13. Card 3 comes from the 20 cards left: 2×2, 3×3, 4×4, 4×5, 2×12, 3×13, 2×15. That gives an expected settlement value of 138 / 20 = **6.9**.

I'm short 3, so I can only post a bid. For each bid I weighed two effects:
- **Noise traders:** they sell to me when their valuation, about Normal(6.9, 2.3), is below my bid. I gain 6.9 minus the bid each time.
- **Informed trader:** they sell only when the true value is below my bid, so those fills lose money. That happens whenever card 3 is a 2, 3, 4 or 5.

| Bid | Noise gain | Informed loss | Expected profit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4.0 | 0.241 | 0.070 | 0.171 |
| 4.2 | 0.259 | 0.088 | 0.171 |
| 4.4 | 0.277 | 0.106 | 0.171 |
| 5.0 | 0.310 | 0.160 | 0.150 |
| 5.5 | 0.303 | 0.225 | 0.078 |
| 6.0 | 0.250 | 0.290 | −0.040 |

Expected profit is flat at its highest, about 0.17, for bids between 4.0 and 4.4. It falls once the bid reaches 5, because the informed trader then also sells when card 3 is a 4 or 5. I'll bid 4.2.

game.title: Dice/cards min
game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (8 faces, each equally likely): 0, 0, 2, 2, 3, 5, 5, 10.
- Die 2 (4 faces, loaded): 0 (prob 1/10), 3 (prob 3/10), 4 (prob 1/5), 5 (prob 2/5).
game.contract: The contract settles at the smallest of the dice.

info.raw:
The fair value is the expected minimum of the two dice, which is about **2.175**.

Distribution of the minimum (V):

| V | Probability |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0.325 |
| 2 | 0.225 |
| 3 | 0.225 |
| 4 | 0.075 |
| 5 | 0.15 |

**Choosing the ask.** I compared the expected loss to informed buyers with the expected gain from noise buyers at several prices:

| Ask | Net expected edge |
|---|---|
| 3.1 | ≈ +0.06 |
| 3.5 | ≈ +0.11 |
| 4.0 | ≈ +0.13 |
| 4.5 | ≈ +0.12 |

The best ask is around 4.0–4.2.

**Choosing the bid.** About a third of the probability sits at 0, so any bid well above 0 loses heavily to informed sellers.

| Bid | Net expected edge |
|---|---|
| 1.0 | ≈ +0.08 |
| 0.5 | ≈ +0.135 |
| 0.1 | ≈ +0.157 |
| 0.0 | ≈ +0.16 |

The best bid is around 0.0–0.1.

{"bid": 0.1, "ask": 4.1}

Quote for step 2: bid 0.5, ask 3.8, about 1.8 below and 1.5 above my fair value of 2.33.

**Prior fair value.** The contract settles at the smaller of the two dice.
- If die 2 shows 3, the expected minimum is 2.0.
- If die 2 shows 4, it is 2.375.
- If die 2 shows 5, it is 2.75.
- If die 2 shows 0, it is 0.

Weighting by die 2's odds gives E[min] = 2.175.

**Possible settlement values before quote 1:**

| Value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0.325 |
| 2 | 0.225 |
| 3 | 0.225 |
| 4 | 0.075 |
| 5 | 0.15 |

**Update from the no-trade at 0.1 / 4.1.**
- An informed trader would have sold if the value were 0 and bought if it were 5. So a no-trade makes 0 and 5 less likely.
- A noise trader would not have traded with probability about 0.73.
- So a no-trade has likelihood about 0.48 if the value is 0 or 5, and about 0.83 if it is 2, 3 or 4.
- The posterior fair value is about **2.33**.
- The posterior chance that the value is 0 is about 0.23, that it is 4 about 0.09, and that it is 5 about 0.11.

**Choosing the quote.** I weighed the gain from noise trades against losses to informed traders on each side:
- **Ask:** An ask near 3.7–3.8 earns about 1.4 per noise buy. Informed buyers only come in when the value is 4 or 5, which is about a 20% chance. The expected gain is roughly +0.14. An ask of 3.1 is worse, at about +0.07, because informed traders would buy whenever the value is 4 or 5 and the loss per trade is larger.
- **Bid:** A bid of 0.5 earns about 1.8 per noise sell. When the value is 0, an informed seller costs me only 0.5. The expected gain is about +0.14, better than a bid of 1.0 at about +0.12.

{"bid": 0.5, "ask": 3.8}

With die 2 revealed as 5, the contract settles at min(die 1, 5).

**Settlement distribution:**
- 0 with probability 1/4
- 2 with probability 1/4
- 3 with probability 1/8
- 5 with probability 3/8

The fair value is 22/8 = 2.75.

**Ask side:** The settlement can never be above 5. An informed trader only buys if its valuation is strictly above my ask, so at an ask of 5.0 it never buys. Only noise traders can lift that offer, at 2.25 above fair. Expected value is about 0.65 × P(noise > 5) × 2.25 ≈ +0.15. This is the best ask I checked; 4.9 gives about +0.149 and 5.1 about +0.146.

**Bid side:** Below 2, an informed trader sells to me only when the value is 0. That costs about 0.0875 × bid in expectation. Noise traders also sell below fair. A bid around 0.4 to 0.5 gives about +0.11, the best I found.

{"bid": 0.5, "ask": 5.0}

Die 2 is 5, so the contract settles at min(die 1, 5). That gives these equally likely values: 0, 0, 2, 2, 3, 5, 5, 5. The plain average is 2.75.

At quote 3 my quote was 0.5 / 5 and nobody traded. An informed trader holding a value of 0 would have sold at 0.5, so the lack of a trade makes 0 less likely. Updating on that gives:
- P(0) ≈ 0.17
- P(2) ≈ 0.28
- P(3) ≈ 0.14
- P(5) ≈ 0.42
- Public fair value ≈ 3.06

**Ask.** An ask of 5.0 can never be lifted by an informed trader, because a value of 5 is not above 5. Noise traders still buy there, for an expected profit of about 0.18. Any ask below 5 gets hit by informed traders holding 5, which loses money. Higher asks get fewer noise buyers and earn less.

**Bid.** Somewhere between 0 and 2, only an informed trader holding 0 sells to me. A bid around 1.1 best balances profit from noise sellers against that loss, for about 0.11 expected profit.

{"bid": 1.1, "ask": 5.0}
