game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 2/5, P(heads) = 0.7 with probability 3/5. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 7 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Expected settlement before any reveals:

- Expected P(heads) = 0.4·0.5 + 0.6·0.7 = 0.62.
- Expected value = 10 · 7 · 0.62 ≈ 43.4.
- The settlement standard deviation is about 14.
- Settlement only takes multiples of 10.

Where I put the quotes:

- **Ask at 50.0.** An informed trader buys only when the value is 60 or more, which has probability about 0.22. A noise trader buys about 27% of the time, and I earn about 6.6 on each of those trades.
- **Bid at 37.0.** An informed trader sells only when the value is 30 or less, which has probability about 0.28. That loss is offset by edge against noise traders.

{"bid": 37.0, "ask": 50.0}

Revealed flips are 0, 1, 1, so the fair value is about 45.1. I'm quoting roughly ±5 around that, skewed slightly up because I'm short one unit.

**Which coin.** The chance of seeing tails, heads, heads differs by coin:
- If P(heads) = 0.5, the chance is 0.125.
- If P(heads) = 0.7, the chance is 0.3 × 0.49 = 0.147.

Weighting by the priors (2/5 and 3/5) gives a 0.638 chance that the coin is the 0.7 coin. So the expected chance of heads on each remaining flip is 0.5 × 0.362 + 0.7 × 0.638 ≈ 0.628.

**Fair value.** We have 2 heads so far. The 4 remaining flips should add about 4 × 0.628 ≈ 2.51 heads. That makes about 4.51 expected heads, so the contract is worth about 45.1. The buy at 49.4 earlier was before any flips were revealed, so it tells us little now.

**Spread.** About 4 units of value are still uncertain. An informed counterparty knows the exact settlement value, so I quote roughly ±5 around fair value to protect against them. I nudge both prices up slightly because I'm short one unit.

{"bid": 40.5, "ask": 50.8}

Fair value is about 52.6 after updating on the revealed flips and on both buys at my ask. I'll quote 47.5 / 57, slightly skewed up because I'm short 2 and the risk is to the upside.

**Revealed flips (0, 1, 1):**
- Likelihood under p = 0.5 is 0.125; under p = 0.7 it is 0.147.
- With the 2/5 and 3/5 prior, P(p = 0.7) ≈ 0.638, so the expected chance of heads is about 0.628.
- With 2 heads so far and 4 flips left, that alone gives a fair value of about 45.1.

**Trade history:** Both trades were buys at my ask.
- Quote 3 was a buy at 50.8. An informed buyer only does that if the contract settles at 60. A noise trader does it about 30% of the time. That makes 60 about 2.8× more likely.
- Quote 2 was a buy at 49.4. An informed buyer does that if it settles at 50 or more. That makes 50 or 60 about 2.8× more likely.

**Posterior over settlement:**

| Settlement | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | ~1% | 5% | 11% | 35% | 49% |

The expected value is about 52.6.

**Quote:**
- An ask of 57 sits below 60, so an informed trader only lifts it when the contract settles at 60. That loss is capped at 3.
- A noise trader still buys at 57 about 34% of the time.
- A bid of 47.5 is only hit by an informed trader when settlement is 40 or lower, which is about 16% likely.

{"bid": 47.5, "ask": 57}

Using Bayes on the revealed flips (0, 1, 1, 1), the probability that the coin is the 0.7 one is now about 0.71. That puts the expected number of heads in the last three flips at about 1.93. The public fair value is therefore about 49.3.

The settlement can only be 30, 40, 50 or 60, with probabilities of roughly 5.5%, 24%, 42% and 28%.

**Ask at 60.** No informed trader buys there, because the best possible settlement is 60 and they buy only if their value is strictly above my ask. Noise traders still buy about 16.5% of the time, at roughly 10.7 above fair value. Expected profit on this side is about 1.15, the best of the asks I tested.

**Bid at 40.** Informed traders sell only when the settlement will be 30, a loss of about 0.19. Noise traders sell about 20% of the time, at roughly 9.3 below fair value. Expected profit on this side is about 1.0, better than bidding at 38 or 42.

I am short 2, which is well within the limits, so inventory does not change this quote.

{"bid": 40, "ask": 60}

With 3 heads in the first 4 flips, there is about a 71% chance the coin is the 0.7 coin. The 0.7 coin makes 3 heads in 4 flips much likelier than the fair coin does (0.103 vs 0.0625). That gives an expected heads probability of about 0.642 for each remaining flip. The fair value is 30 + 3 × 0.642 × 10 ≈ 49.3. I ignored any information in the trading history when working this out.

The remaining 3 flips can only add 0 to 3 heads, so settlement can only be 30, 40, 50 or 60:

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 30 | about 0.055 |
| 40 | about 0.243 |
| 50 | about 0.422 |
| 60 | about 0.280 |

An informed trader only hurts me if the value is strictly beyond my price. So quotes just inside 40 and 60 lose almost nothing to informed traders and still collect noise-trader edge of about 10 per trade.

- **Ask at 59.9:** expected value is about +1.15 per quote, with essentially no informed losses (it only loses if the value is 60, by 0.1).
- **Bid at 40:** expected value is about +1.0 per quote, losing only to the small chance the value is 30.

{"bid": 40, "ask": 59.9}

Six flips are revealed and 5 of them are heads.

**Which coin is it?**
- The chance of seeing 5 heads and 1 tail with the fair coin (0.5) is 1/64, about 0.0156.
- With the biased coin (0.7) it is 0.7⁵ × 0.3, about 0.0504.
- Weighting by the starting odds (2/5 fair, 3/5 biased) gives a 0.83 chance the coin is the 0.7 coin.

**Fair value**
- The chance that flip 7 is heads is 0.5 × 0.17 + 0.7 × 0.83, about 0.666.
- The contract settles at either 50 or 60.
- So the fair value is about 50 + 6.66 = 56.66.

**Choosing the ask**
- An informed trader buys whenever the true value (60 or 50) is above my ask. Any ask between 50 and 60 loses to the informed trader about 67% of the time.
- If the ask is 60 or higher, the informed trader never buys. Then only noise traders, valuing at about N(56.66, 11), trade on that side.
- I tried asks from 60 to 66. Expected profit was highest at about 65, roughly 1.2 per quote.

**Choosing the bid**
- If the bid is 50 or lower, the informed trader never sells to me.
- For noise traders, expected profit is about 1.21 at a bid of 48 to 49, which is the highest of the bids I tried.
- A bid of 51 does worse, because the informed trader would then sell to me when the value is 50.

**Position check**
- I am short 3, so either trade keeps me inside the ±5 limit.
- Buying at 48.5 would also reduce my short exposure.

{"bid": 48.5, "ask": 65}

Five of the six revealed flips are heads, so I update on the coin's bias.

**Posterior on the coin:**
- Likelihood of the flips under a fair coin: 0.5⁶ = 0.0156. Times the 2/5 prior gives 0.00625.
- Likelihood under the 0.7 coin: 0.7⁵ × 0.3 = 0.0504. Times the 3/5 prior gives 0.0303.
- So P(0.7 coin) ≈ 0.829.

**Flip 7 and fair value:**
- P(flip 7 is heads) ≈ 0.171 × 0.5 + 0.829 × 0.7 ≈ 0.666.
- Settlement is either 50 or 60, so fair value ≈ 56.66.

**Ask:**
- Any ask below 60 is hit by informed traders whenever the value is 60, which gives up edge.
- Quoting the ask above 60 trades only with noise traders.
- I maximise x(1−Φ(x/11)), where x is the distance from fair value. This gives x ≈ 8.3, so the ask is about 65.

**Bid:**
- Any bid above 50 is hit by informed traders whenever the value is 50.
- Below 50 only noise traders sell to me. The same optimisation puts the bid about 8.3 below fair value, at about 48.4.

**Position:** I'm short 3 against a −5 limit, so selling one more unit is allowed.

{"bid": 48.4, "ask": 65}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 7/10, P(heads) = 0.7 with probability 3/10. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 5 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Fair value with nothing revealed is 16.8. The chance of heads per flip is 0.7×0.5 + 0.3×0.7 = 0.56, so expected heads are 6 × 0.56 = 3.36, and the contract pays 5 per head.

The settlement can only be a multiple of 5 (0, 5, …, 30). That changes how I should place quotes. A bid just above a possible value, such as 15.1, loses to informed sellers whenever the value is 15 or less. That happens about 54% of the time.

Weighing the loss to informed traders against the gain from noise traders (fair value plus noise with standard deviation 9.9):
- **Bid:** expected profit is highest around 8–9, at roughly +0.67 per quote. Informed traders then sell only when the value is 5 or less.
- **Ask:** expected profit is highest just above 25, at roughly +0.72 per quote. Informed traders then buy only when the value is 30.

{"bid": 8.5, "ask": 25.1}

Quote 1 produced no trade, which tells us little. The public fair value stays near 16.8, so I'll keep a wide quote around it.

**Fair value**
- Expected chance of heads is 0.7 × 0.5 + 0.3 × 0.7 = 0.56.
- Expected heads over 6 flips is 3.36, so the contract is worth about 16.8.
- The settlement can only be 0, 5, 10, …, 30.

**Settlement probabilities**
- 5 or more heads (value 25 or 30): about 0.20.
- 6 heads (value 30): about 0.046.
- 1 or fewer heads (value 0 or 5): about 0.08.
- 0 heads (value 0): about 0.011.

**Choosing the quotes**
For each candidate price I compared two things. One is the expected gain from noise traders who cross my quote. The other is the expected loss to informed traders who know the true value.
- On the ask side, the expected edge is about 1.44 for asks between 24.9 and 26. This is because only the 6-heads outcome (30) beats an ask above 25.
- On the bid side, the expected edge is about 1.3 for bids between 8 and 9. Only the 0-heads outcome (0) and 1-head outcome (5) lie below such a bid.

I'll quote a bid of 9.0 and an ask of 25.0.

{"bid": 9.0, "ask": 25.0}

With no trades yet, the fair value is still about 16.8, and quoting roughly 8 points either side looks best.

**Fair value.** Nothing has been revealed and no one has traded, so the public fair value is unchanged.
- The expected chance of heads is 0.7 × 0.5 + 0.3 × 0.7 = 0.56.
- Over 6 flips that is 3.36 expected heads, worth 3.36 × 5 = 16.8.

**Ask side.** The settlement value moves in steps of 5. An informed trader only buys if the value is above my ask, so 25 or 30 when I ask about 24–25.
- P(value ≥ 25) ≈ 0.20 and P(value = 30) ≈ 0.046.
- At ask 25.1, noise traders buy about 20% of the time at a profit of 8.3. Informed traders only hurt me when the value is 30. Net expected value is about +0.7 per quote.
- At ask 20.1, the gains from noise traders are cancelled by losses when the value is 25. Net expected value is about 0.
- So I keep the ask near 25.

**Bid side.** An informed trader only sells if the value is below my bid, so 0 or 5 when I bid about 9.
- P(value ≤ 5) ≈ 0.08.
- Bids between 8.5 and 10 give a net expected value of about +0.6 to +0.66 per quote.
- So I keep the bid near 9.

{"bid": 9, "ask": 25}

Fair value is 19.4.

- **Value:** after flip 1 = 1, P(biased coin) = 0.21/0.56 = 0.375. E[P(heads)] = 0.575, so expected heads = 1 + 5 × 0.575 = 3.875. Fair value = 5 × 3.875 = 19.375.
- **Ask:** settlement moves in steps of 5. An ask at 24.9 means an informed trader buys only when the value is 25 or 30, which has probability about 0.315 and average value about 26.3. Noise buyers at 24.9 are profitable enough to outweigh that, for an expected edge of about +0.57. An ask near 20 would lose money to informed traders.
- **Bid:** a bid at 14.9 means an informed trader sells only when the value is 10 or below, which has probability about 0.13 and average value about 9.2. Expected edge is about +0.36. A bid near 20 would be clearly negative.

{"bid": 14.9, "ask": 24.9}

I quote just outside the possible settlement levels, so informed traders rarely trade against me and noise traders still trade at a good edge.

**Fair value.** Flip 1 came up heads, so I update the chance that this is the biased coin:
- P(biased) = 0.21 / (0.21 + 0.35) = 0.375.
- Expected P(heads) for a future flip = 0.625 × 0.5 + 0.375 × 0.7 = 0.575.
- Expected value = 5 × (1 + 5 × 0.575) ≈ 19.4.
- The four quotes with no trade tell us almost nothing new, so 19.4 stands.

**Settlement distribution.** The contract can only settle at 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 or 30. Their probabilities, mixing the two coin types for the 5 unknown flips, are about 2%, 11%, 24%, 31%, 23% and 8%.

**Ask side.** For each ask I weighed the loss to informed buyers against the gain from noise buyers (noise standard deviation 9.9).
- Ask 25.1: expected profit about 0.60.
- Ask 27: about 0.72.
- Ask 29: about 0.76, the best of those tried. Only a settlement of 30 hurts me, and that loss is only 1.
- Ask 29.9: about 0.76, no better.

**Bid side.** The same trade-off applies to sellers.
- Bid 14.9: about 0.36. Informed sellers hold value 10 or below, which costs too much.
- Bid 9.9: about 0.75.
- Bid 10.1: about 0.76, the best. Only a settlement of 5 hurts me, and that loss is small.

{"bid": 10.1, "ask": 29}

Fair value is about 18.5. The quotes are wide around that, and both sit just outside the values an informed trader is likely to hold, so they mostly trade with noise traders.

**Coin posterior after flip 1 = heads.**
- P(biased coin) = 0.21 / 0.56 = 0.375.
- Expected P(heads) is 0.575, so the 5 unseen flips give about 2.9 more heads.
- That puts the value at about 19.4 before using the trading history.

**What the lack of trades tells us.**
- At quote 4 (14.9 / 24.9), an informed trader would only stay out if the value were 15 or 20.
- At quote 5 (10.1 / 29), an informed trader would only stay out if the value were 15, 20 or 25.
- Both no-trades raise the weight on those middle values.

**Updated settlement distribution.**

| Value | 5 | 10 | 15 | 20 | 25 | 30 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 0.3% | 1.8% | 38% | 48% | 10% | 1.4% |

The fair value comes out at about 18.5.

**Choosing the quotes.**
- Values of 15 and 20 carry about 86% of the weight.
- The ask should sit above 25 so that an informed trader holding 25 won't buy.
- The bid should sit well below 15 so that only the unlikely values of 10 or 5 would sell to me.
- Within those limits, expected profit from noise traders is roughly flat at about 0.8 per quote for a bid between 10 and 12 and an ask between 25 and 27.

{"bid": 11.5, "ask": 25.5}

Fair value from the revealed flips is about 20.8. I'll quote around it, keeping both sides outside the values an informed trader could know (15 to 25).

**Which coin.** Flips 1–4 show 3 heads.
- Fair coin likelihood: 0.5⁴ = 0.0625.
- Biased coin likelihood: 0.7³·0.3 = 0.1029.
- With the 7/10 and 3/10 prior, P(biased) ≈ 0.414.
- So P(heads) for the remaining flips ≈ 0.583.

**Settlement value.** Settlement is 5 × (3 + X), where X is the number of heads in flips 5 and 6.

| X | Probability | Settlement |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | ≈ 0.184 | 15 |
| 1 | ≈ 0.467 | 20 |
| 2 | ≈ 0.349 | 25 |

Fair value ≈ 20.8.

**Ask.**
- An ask below 25 gets bought by every informed trader whenever the value is 25 (probability 0.35), so it loses money.
- Above 25, only noise traders buy. Expected profit is 0.5 × P(noise > a) × (a − 20.83).
- This is highest at about a ≈ 28, giving roughly 0.84 per quote.

**Bid.**
- A bid above 15 gets sold to by informed traders whenever the value is 15.
- Below 15, only noise traders sell, and expected profit peaks at about b ≈ 13.5, giving roughly 0.84 per quote.
- A tighter bid such as 19 earns only about 0.39 from noise traders and loses about 0.37 to informed traders, so it is worse.

{"bid": 13.5, "ask": 28.3}

Fair value is about 20.83, so I'm bidding 13.6 and asking 28.0.

**Fair value**
- The revealed flips show 3 heads and 1 tail.
- The chance of seeing that with the fair coin is 0.5⁴ = 0.0625. With the biased coin it is 0.7³ × 0.3 = 0.1029.
- Weighting by the 7/10 and 3/10 priors, the chance the coin is biased is about 0.414.
- That makes the chance of heads on each remaining flip about 0.583.
- Fair value is 5 × (3 + 2 × 0.583) ≈ 20.83.

**What it can settle at**
- 15 (no more heads) with probability about 0.18.
- 20 (one more head) with probability about 0.47.
- 25 (two more heads) with probability about 0.35.

**Choosing the quotes**
- An informed trader only buys above my ask if settlement is 25. So any ask of 25 or higher is never hit by an informed buyer.
- An informed trader only sells below my bid if settlement is 15. So any bid of 15 or lower is never hit by an informed seller.
- Below those limits, only noise traders trade with me. For each side I maximise (probability a noise trader trades) × (edge over fair value):
  - The ask's expected profit peaks around 28.
  - The bid's expected profit peaks around 13.6.

{"bid": 13.6, "ask": 28.0}

Bid 13.6, ask 28.1. Fair value is about 20.83, and both quotes sit outside the range where an informed trader would hit me.

**Probability of a biased coin.** The revealed flips show 3 heads in 4.
- Chance of that result with a fair coin: 0.5⁴ = 0.0625.
- Chance with the biased coin: 0.7³ × 0.3 = 0.1029.
- Weighting by the starting odds gives P(biased) = (0.3 × 0.1029) / (0.3 × 0.1029 + 0.7 × 0.0625) ≈ 0.414.

**Expected value.** The chance of heads on each remaining flip is 0.5 + 0.2 × 0.414 ≈ 0.583. Two flips remain, so expected heads are 3 + 2 × 0.583 ≈ 4.17. Fair value is 5 × 4.17 ≈ 20.83.

**Possible settlements.** With 3 to 5 total heads, the contract settles at 15, 20 or 25.
- P(15) ≈ 0.18
- P(20) ≈ 0.47
- P(25) ≈ 0.35

**Choosing the quotes.**

- Expected profit from noise trades is (chance of a trade) × (distance from fair value). On the ask side this peaks near 28. On the bid side it is fairly flat between about 13 and 14.

The expected settlement value is about 16.8. The informed trader's value can only be a multiple of 5 (0, 5, …, 30). So I place my quotes just outside multiples of 5, chosen so informed losses stay small compared with what I earn from noise traders.

**Ask side.** Each figure below is expected profit per quote, with probability 0.5 that the counterparty is informed.
- At an ask of 20.1, I lose about 0.61 to informed buyers (true value 25 or 30). I gain about 0.61 from noise traders, so it roughly breaks even.
- At an ask of 25.1, I lose only about 0.11 to informed buyers (true value 30). I gain about 0.83 from noise traders, which is clearly better.

**Bid side.**

- At a bid of 9.9, I lose about 0.22 to informed sellers (true value 5 or less). I gain about 0.84 from noise traders, so it is clearly positive.

So I quote a bid of 9.9 and an ask of 25.1.

{"bid": 9.9, "ask": 25.1}

{"bid": 9.9, "ask": 25.1}

{"bid": 10.1, "ask": 27.5}

{"bid": 8, "ask": 23}

Position limits are not a concern with only two quotes left.

{"bid": 8.2, "ask": 23.2}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.2 with probability 1/5, P(heads) = 0.7 with probability 3/10, P(heads) = 0.9 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 5 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 5 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Fair value with no information: the expected heads probability is 0.2·0.2 + 0.3·0.7 + 0.5·0.9 = 0.70. Over 5 flips that is 3.5 heads, so the contract is worth 17.5. The settlement standard deviation is about 7.8.

I quote 4 points either side of 17.5:
- **Ask at 21.5:** an informed buyer only takes it when the value is 25, about 35% of the time, losing me 3.5 each. A noise trader buys about 37% of the time, earning me about 4. Net, the ask is worth about +0.94.
- **Bid at 13.5:** an informed seller only hits it when the value is 10 or less, about 24% of the time, losing me about 6. A noise trader sells about 37% of the time, earning me about 4. Net, the bid is worth about +0.89.

Both sides have positive expected value.

{"bid": 13.5, "ask": 21.5}

No trade on quote 1 hints mildly that the settlement is 15 or 20, but the fair value stays at about 17.5, so I'll keep the same quote.

**Fair value.** The expected chance of heads is 0.2·0.2 + 0.3·0.7 + 0.5·0.9 = 0.70. Over 5 flips that is 3.5 expected heads, so the contract is worth about 5 × 3.5 = 17.5.

**What the first quote tells me.**
- At 13.5 / 21.5, an informed trader would only have stayed out if the settlement were 15 or 20.
- That lowers the chance of the extremes (a settlement of 25 or of 10 and below).
- Both tails lose weight, so the fair value stays close to 17.5.

**Spread.** A spread of about ±4 around fair value earns about 4 per noise trade, and noise traders trade at roughly a 37% rate on each side. The main adverse risk is an informed buyer when the settlement is 25. That costs 3.5 per unit, and the chance is about 0.2 × 0.34, which is small. So this spread stays profitable, and I'll repeat the quote.

{"bid": 13.5, "ask": 21.5}

Fair value is about 9.33, and I'm quoting 5.3 bid / 13.5 ask, roughly ±4 around it.

**Fair value after flip 1 = tails**
- Prior chances for the three coins are 0.2, 0.3 and 0.5 (P(heads) of 0.2, 0.7 and 0.9). The chances of tails on each are 0.8, 0.3 and 0.1.
- Multiplying gives 0.16, 0.09 and 0.05, so the updated chances are about 0.533, 0.30 and 0.167.
- The expected chance of heads is now about 0.467.
- Four flips remain, so expected heads are about 1.87 and fair value is 5 × 1.87 ≈ 9.33.
- The two quotes with no trade tell us almost nothing new.

**Uncertainty and spread**
- The settlement value has a standard deviation of about 7. That is wide relative to the noise traders' spread of 12.
- An informed counterparty would pick us off on a tight spread. A half-spread of about 4 still lets a fair share of noise traders deal with us while charging informed traders for the risk.

{"bid": 5.3, "ask": 13.5}

Fair value is about 9.3, so I'm quoting roughly 9.3 ± 3.8.

**Posterior on the coin after flip 1 = tails:**
- Weight for P(heads) = 0.2: 0.2 × 0.8 = 0.16
- Weight for P(heads) = 0.7: 0.3 × 0.3 = 0.09
- Weight for P(heads) = 0.9: 0.5 × 0.1 = 0.05
- These sum to 0.30, giving posterior probabilities of 0.533, 0.300 and 0.167.

**Fair value:**
- Expected P(heads) = 0.533 × 0.2 + 0.3 × 0.7 + 0.167 × 0.9 ≈ 0.467.
- Four flips remain, so expected remaining heads ≈ 4 × 0.467 ≈ 1.87.
- Flip 1 was tails and adds nothing, so fair value ≈ 5 × 1.87 ≈ 9.3.

**Quote:**
- The last quote's no-trade carries little information, so I keep fair value at about 9.3.
- The settlement value is bimodal, with weight near 0 (low-bias coin) and near 15–20 (high-bias coins).
- That makes informed traders dangerous on both sides. Against noise traders with standard deviation 12, a spread of about ±3.8 around fair value is reasonable.

{"bid": 5.5, "ask": 13.1}

**Fair value after two tails**

1. The prior on the coin is 0.2 / 0.3 / 0.5 for p = 0.2 / 0.7 / 0.9.
2. The chance of two tails under each coin is 0.64, 0.09 and 0.01.
3. Multiplying gives weights 0.128, 0.027 and 0.005, so the posterior is about 0.80 / 0.169 / 0.031.
4. The expected chance of heads is now about 0.306.
5. The three remaining flips give about 0.92 expected heads, so fair value is about **4.6**.

**Settlement distribution**

- About 41% of the time the contract settles at 0.
- About 25% of the time there are two or more more heads, so it settles at 10 or more.
- The rest of the time it settles at 5.

**Quote choice**

- Noise traders' valuations spread widely (standard deviation 12), so fairly wide quotes still trade often and earn a good edge.
- With the ask around 10, an informed trader only buys when the contract settles at 10 or 15, and loses me little then.
- With the bid near 0, an informed trader almost never gets a good deal selling to me.
- I am short 1, so I lean the quotes slightly upward.

{"bid": 0.5, "ask": 10.0}

Fair value is about 3.6, and with noise this wide the best quotes sit about 9 either side of it.

**Fair value**
- After two tails, the coin is most likely the 0.2 one. The posterior is 0.2 coin 0.80, 0.7 coin 0.169, 0.9 coin 0.031.
- That gives E[p] ≈ 0.306. Expected heads in the last 3 flips is about 0.92, so the value is about 4.6.
- The sell at my 0.5 bid is mild evidence that the value is 0, because an informed trader only sells there if there are no heads. Updating on it gives P(value = 0) ≈ 0.54.
- So the public fair value is about 3.6.

**Quote placement**
- Noise traders' valuations spread with standard deviation 12. Against that, the profit-maximising distance from fair value is about 9 on each side.
- Bid side: a bid at or below 0 can never be hit by an informed trader, because the value cannot be negative. The best bid is about −5.
- Ask side: an informed trader only buys above about 12.5 if the value is 15, which has probability about 0.07. The best ask is about 12.5–13.

Each side is worth about +1.6 in expectation. My position is 0, so the position limits don't bind.

{"bid": -5, "ask": 12.6}

Settlement is either 10 or 15. Two heads are already revealed, and flip 5 is the only unknown flip.

**Which coin is it?** Each coin's weight is its prior times the chance of the observed 2 heads and 2 tails, p²(1−p)²:
- p = 0.2: 0.2 × 0.0256 = 0.00512
- p = 0.7: 0.3 × 0.0441 = 0.01323
- p = 0.9: 0.5 × 0.0081 = 0.00405

Normalising gives posteriors of about 0.229, 0.591 and 0.181.

**Fair value.** The chance that flip 5 is heads is 0.229×0.2 + 0.591×0.7 + 0.181×0.9 ≈ 0.622. So the fair value is 10 + 5 × 0.622 ≈ 13.1.

**Choosing the quotes.**
- An informed trader only trades if my bid is above 10 or my ask is below 15. Quoting outside that range means only noise traders can hit me.
- Against noise (standard deviation 12), the expected profit from a quote at distance x from fair is x·(1−Φ(x/12)). This peaks near x ≈ 0.75 × 12 ≈ 9, giving about 1.6 per side.
- That is better than quoting at 10 or 15, which would give about 1.0 and 0.66 per side.
- My position limits are not binding, so I quote the same distance on both sides: bid 13.1 − 9 = 4.1 and ask 13.1 + 9 = 22.1.

{"bid": 4.1, "ask": 22.1}

Bid 4.1 and ask 22.1, about 9 either side of the public fair value of 13.1.

**Fair value.** The revealed flips are 0, 0, 1, 1. Updating the three coins on that sequence:

| Coin | Prior × likelihood | Posterior |
|---|---|---|
| p = 0.2 | 0.2 × 0.0256 = 0.00512 | 0.229 |
| p = 0.7 | 0.3 × 0.0441 = 0.01323 | 0.591 |
| p = 0.9 | 0.5 × 0.0081 = 0.00405 | 0.181 |

- The expected chance that flip 5 is heads is 0.622.
- Settlement is 10 if flip 5 is tails or 15 if it is heads.
- So fair value = 10 + 5 × 0.622 ≈ 13.11.

**Informed traders.** They only ever trade at 10 or 15. A bid at or below 10 is never hit by them, and an ask at or above 15 is never lifted by them.

**Noise traders.** Their valuation is 13.11 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 12. For a quote at distance d from fair value, the expected gain is P(trade) × d. This is largest at about 0.75 standard deviations, which is about 9 points. That gives:
- a bid near 13.11 − 9 ≈ 4.1
- an ask near 13.11 + 9 ≈ 22.1

Both prices are outside the range where informed traders act. Each side earns about 1.6 in expectation. Tighter quotes, such as a bid at 10 or an ask at 15, earn less (about 1.0 and 0.66). My position limits allow either trade.

{"bid": 4.1, "ask": 22.1}

{"bid": 13.0, "ask": 28.0}

Fair value is about 21, possibly slightly higher. I'm quoting bid 18.5 and ask 24, set a little high because I'm short one unit.

- **Bid 18.5:** an informed trader sells only when the value is 15 or less. Noise traders sell often enough to make this side profitable.

{"bid": 18.5, "ask": 24}

The fair value is about 22.6, so I'm quoting a wide spread around it: bid 15.5, ask 29.5.

**Quote placement**

- I'm short 2, so I make buying slightly more attractive and keep the ask a little closer.

{"bid": 15.5, "ask": 29.5}

Fair value is about 22.6, and settlement can be at most 25.

**Posterior on the coin after two heads.** The priors are 0.2, 0.3 and 0.5. The likelihoods of two heads are 0.04, 0.49 and 0.81. So the posterior is about 0.014, 0.263 and 0.723.

**Fair value.** The expected P(heads) is about 0.8375. That gives 2 + 3 × 0.8375 ≈ 4.51 expected heads, so fair value is about 22.56.

**Settlement distribution:**

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 10 | 0.015 |
| 15 | 0.075 |
| 20 | 0.293 |
| 25 | 0.617 |

**Ask side.** Any sale at 25 or above can never lose against an informed trader. For noise traders, the ask that maximises expected edge times fill probability sits about 0.5–0.75σ above fair value. Since I'm short 2 and can only go to −3, I'll set the ask a bit higher, around 28.

**Bid side.** I compared expected profit across bids, counting both noise and informed sellers:

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 19 | ≈1.0 |
| 17 | ≈1.38 |
| 16 | ≈1.50 |
| 15 | ≈1.6 |

The curve flattens below 16. Buying back also cuts my short exposure, so I'll bid around 16.

{"bid": 16, "ask": 28}

With four heads revealed the coin is very likely biased towards heads. The fair value is about 24.3, so I'm quoting wide: bid 15.5, ask 33.5.

**Posterior on the coin after 4 heads**

| Coin P(heads) | Prior × likelihood | Posterior |
|---|---|---|
| 0.2 | 0.2 × 0.2⁴ = 0.00032 | ≈ 0.001 |
| 0.7 | 0.3 × 0.7⁴ = 0.07203 | ≈ 0.18 |
| 0.9 | 0.5 × 0.9⁴ = 0.32805 | ≈ 0.82 |

- The chance flip 5 is heads is about 0.864.
- The contract settles at 20 or 25, so the fair value is 20 + 5 × 0.864 ≈ 24.32.

**Ask side**
- Any ask at or above 25 is never hit by an informed trader.
- For a noise trader, the expected profit is 0.8 × P(noise > a − 24.32) × (a − 24.32).
- This peaks when the ask is about 9 above fair, giving about 1.63 per quote at an ask of about 33–34.

**Bid side**
- Any bid at or below 20 is never hit by an informed trader.
- For a noise trader, the expected profit is 0.8 × P(noise < b − 24.32) × (24.32 − b).
- This peaks at a bid of about 15–16, also giving about 1.63.

**Position**
- I'm short 2, so either fill keeps me within the ±3 limit.
- With these quotes neither side loses money to an informed trader.

{"bid": 15.5, "ask": 33.5}

Quote bid 15.3 and ask 33.4, centred on a fair value of about 24.3.

**Fair value.** Four heads have been revealed, so settlement is either 20 (flip 5 is tails) or 25 (flip 5 is heads). Bayes' rule over the three coins gives these unnormalised weights:

| Coin P(heads) | Prior × P(4 heads) | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| 0.2 | 0.2 × 0.2⁴ | 0.00032 |
| 0.7 | 0.3 × 0.7⁴ | 0.0720 |
| 0.9 | 0.5 × 0.9⁴ | 0.3281 |

The weights sum to about 0.4004. Weighting each coin's heads probability by its weight gives P(flip 5 = heads) ≈ 0.864. So the expected settlement value is 20 + 5 × 0.864 ≈ 24.3.

**Informed traders.**
- If the value is 25, an informed trader buys only when my ask is below 25.
- If the value is 20, an informed trader sells only when my bid is above 20.
- So an ask at or above 25 and a bid at or below 20 cannot lose to informed traders.

**Noise traders.** Their valuation is roughly Normal(24.3, 12). The expected gain on each side is roughly P(trade) × distance from fair value. This is largest at about 0.75 standard deviations from fair value, which is about 9 points. That puts the ask near 33.3 and the bid near 15.3. Both are safely outside the informed-trader range.

My position is -2, so selling one more unit would take me to -3, which is still allowed.

{"bid": 15.3, "ask": 33.4}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.4 with probability 3/5, P(heads) = 0.8 with probability 2/5. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Prior fair value is 6 × (0.6·0.4 + 0.4·0.8) = 3.36, with a standard deviation of about 1.62. With a 20% chance of an informed trader, I set each side to balance the edge earned from noise traders against losses to informed ones.

- **Ask at 4.9:** an informed trader only buys if the outcome is 5 or 6 heads. That costs about 0.03 per quote, while noise buyers earn about 0.21.
- **Bid at 2.0:** an informed trader only sells if the outcome is 0 or 1 heads. That costs about 0.03, while noise sellers earn about 0.21.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 4.9}

Before any flips are revealed, the expected chance of heads is 0.6 × 0.4 + 0.4 × 0.8 = 0.56. Over 6 flips that gives an expected settlement of about 3.36 heads, with a standard deviation of roughly 1.6.

- **Last quote:** the no-trade at 2 / 4.9 tells us little, so I keep the fair value near 3.36.
- **Spread:** I quote about ±1 around fair value, which earns on noise traders.
- **Integer settlement:** because the count is a whole number, an ask of 4.4 means informed traders only buy when the count is 5 or 6. A bid of 2.4 means they only sell when it is 2 or less.

{"bid": 2.4, "ask": 4.4}

Fair value is about 2.5, so I'm quoting a bid of 1.7 and an ask of 3.4, centred slightly above fair to lean against my short position.

**Coin after flip 1 = 0 (tails).**
- Likelihood of tails is 0.6 for the 0.4 coin and 0.2 for the 0.8 coin.
- Prior weights become 0.6 × 0.6 = 0.36 and 0.4 × 0.2 = 0.08.
- So the 0.8 coin has probability 0.08 / 0.44 ≈ 0.18.

**Updating on the stage 1 buy at 4.4.** A buy there is a little more likely under the 0.8 coin.
- A noise trader buys with probability about 0.26 under either coin, which contributes 0.8 × 0.26 ≈ 0.206.
- An informed trader buys only if settlement is at least 5, which now needs flips 2–6 all heads.
  - Under the 0.4 coin that is 0.01, so the total buy probability is about 0.208.
  - Under the 0.8 coin it is about 0.33, so the total is about 0.272.
- This lifts the 0.8 coin to about 0.22.
- The buy also slightly raises the expected heads within each coin: about 2.03 for the 0.4 coin and 4.24 for the 0.8 coin.
- Fair value ≈ 0.78 × 2.03 + 0.22 × 4.24 ≈ 2.5.

**Quote.** Noise traders' valuations have a standard deviation of 1.6, and the settlement is uncertain enough that informed traders matter. I am therefore quoting a moderately wide spread around 2.5.

{"bid": 1.7, "ask": 3.4}

Public fair value is about 2.1, so I'm quoting a wide market around it: bid 1.3, ask 3.0.

**Starting estimate from the revealed flip.** Flip 1 = 0 (tails) shifts belief toward the 0.4 coin.
- Before the reveal, the 0.4 coin had probability 0.6 and the 0.8 coin had 0.4.
- The chance of tails is 0.6 with the 0.4 coin and 0.2 with the 0.8 coin.
- After seeing tails, the 0.4 coin has probability about 0.818 and the 0.8 coin about 0.182.
- The expected chance of heads on each remaining flip is about 0.473.
- Five flips remain, so the expected total is about 5 × 0.473 ≈ 2.36 heads.

**Adjusting for the sell at 1.7 in quote 3.**
- A noise trader with valuation centred on 2.36 sells at 1.7 with probability about 0.8 × 0.34 ≈ 0.27, whatever the true value.
- An informed trader sells only if the final count is at most 1, which has probability about 0.277.
- Weighting the outcomes by these chances lowers the expected settlement to about 2.1.

**Setting the quote.**
- The possible settlement values are spread widely, and 20% of counterparties know the answer.
- So I keep a wide spread around 2.1, leaning slightly toward caution on the bid.

{"bid": 1.3, "ask": 3.0}

With four tails revealed, the coin is almost certainly the 0.4 coin, and fair value is about 0.81. I'm quoting bid -0.2 and ask 2.0.

**Fair value.** I updated the coin probabilities on the four revealed tails:
- 0.4 coin: 0.6 × 0.6⁴ ≈ 0.0778.
- 0.8 coin: 0.4 × 0.2⁴ = 0.00064.
- So P(0.8 coin) ≈ 0.8%, and the expected heads probability is about 0.403.
- With 0 heads so far and 2 flips left, the expected settlement is about 2 × 0.403 ≈ 0.81.
- Settlement is 0, 1 or 2, with probabilities of roughly 0.36, 0.48 and 0.16.

**Ask.** I traded off profit from noise buyers against losses to informed buyers. An informed trader buys above my ask only if the settlement is 2. An ask of 2.0 loses nothing to informed traders. It earns about 0.8 × P(noise valuation > 2.0) × (2.0 − 0.81) ≈ 0.22 per quote, which is roughly the best of the asks I tried.

**Bid.** An informed seller with settlement 0 sells only if my bid is above 0. A bid at or below 0 therefore loses nothing to informed traders. Noise sellers have valuations centred on 0.81 with standard deviation 1.6, so a fair number fall below zero. A bid between -0.2 and -0.3 earns about 0.22 per quote; I chose -0.2.

**Position.** I'm short 1, so either a buy or a sell keeps me well within the ±3 limit.

{"bid": -0.2, "ask": 2.0}

This is the final quote, so I priced it against the expected settlement value and the risk of trading with an informed counterparty. My current position (short 1) does not change where I should quote.

**Which coin is it?** Flips 1–4 were all tails, which is strong evidence for the 0.4 coin.
- Fair coin (0.4): prior 3/5 × 0.6⁴ = 0.07776.
- Biased coin (0.8): prior 2/5 × 0.2⁴ = 0.00064.
- So P(0.8 coin) ≈ 0.008, and the expected P(heads) is about 0.403.

**Settlement value.** The revealed flips contribute 0 heads, so the value is the heads in flips 5 and 6.
- Expected value ≈ 2 × 0.403 ≈ 0.81.
- Chance of each outcome: 0 heads ≈ 0.36, 1 head ≈ 0.48, 2 heads ≈ 0.16.

**Choosing the ask.** I compared expected profit for each price. Noise traders buy when their valuation is above the ask, and I earn the ask minus 0.81. An informed trader buys only when the true value is above the ask.

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 1.5 | 0.168 |
| 1.9 | 0.213 |
| 2.0 | 0.217 |
| 2.2 | 0.214 |

At 2.0 an informed trader never profits from buying, since the value cannot exceed 2.

**Choosing the bid.** A bid at or below 0 is never hit by an informed trader, since the value cannot be below 0. Below that, I only trade with noise traders.

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0.198 |
| -0.4 | 0.218 |
| -0.6 | 0.213 |

So the best quote is a bid of -0.4 and an ask of 2.0.

{"bid": -0.4, "ask": 2.0}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.4 with probability 3/5, P(heads) = 0.8 with probability 2/5. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Fair value is about 3.36 heads. The coin is 0.4-heads with probability 0.6 and 0.8-heads with probability 0.4, so the average heads probability is 0.56, and 6 × 0.56 = 3.36.

- **Uncertainty:** the settlement value has a standard deviation of about 1.62, roughly the same as the noise traders' spread of 1.6.
- **Ask:** a 20% informed trader only buys when it knows the result is at least 5 heads. At 4.9 that risk is small, and the noise traders above 4.9 still give an expected profit of about 0.18 per quote.
- **Bid:** by the same reasoning, a bid of 2.0 only gets hit by informed traders when the result is 0 or 1 heads. That also gives about 0.18 per quote.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 4.9}

Fair value is now about 2.97. I'm quoting bid 1.9 and ask 3.9.

**Prior.** P(heads) averages 0.6×0.4 + 0.4×0.8 = 0.56, so expected heads before any trading was 6 × 0.56 = 3.36.

**What the sale at 2 tells us.**
- An informed counterparty sells at 2 only if the true count is 0 or 1. Before trading, that had probability about 0.141.
- A noise trader sells if 3.36 plus noise falls below 2. That happens with probability Φ(−0.85) ≈ 0.198.
- So the chance of a sale was 0.2 + 0.8×0.198 = 0.358 when heads ≤ 1, and 0.8×0.198 = 0.158 otherwise.
- Updating on that likelihood lowers the public fair value to about **2.97**.

**Quote.**
- The settlement value is widely spread and informed traders are 20% of flow, so I want a spread of about ±1 around fair value.
- I'm long one unit, so I lean the quote slightly lower to make selling a little easier than buying more.

{"bid": 1.9, "ask": 3.9}

Fair value is about 3.8. Given flip 1 = 1, the chance the coin is the 0.8 coin is 4/7, so the expected number of heads is 1 + 5 × 4.4/7 ≈ 4.14. The two earlier trades pull this down:

- **Quote 1:** someone sold to me at 2. Only a counterparty valuing the contract below 2 would sell there, which makes very low outcomes slightly more likely.
- **Quote 2:** no trade at 1.9 / 3.9. This makes outcomes of 2 or 3 heads more likely.

Weighting each possible outcome by how likely those two trades were under it brings the expected number of heads down to about 3.8.

I am long 1, so I set my quotes a little below centre to make selling slightly more likely than buying. I keep about 0.85 on each side to cover losses to informed traders.

{"bid": 2.8, "ask": 4.5}

Fair value is about 4.4.

1. **Revealed flip.** Before flip 1, there was a 0.4 chance the coin is the 0.8 coin. A head on flip 1 raises that to 0.32 / 0.56 ≈ 0.571.
2. **Expected heads.** The expected heads probability per flip is now about 0.629. That makes the expected settlement 1 + 5 × 0.629 ≈ 4.14.
3. **Trade history.** In stage 2 someone bought at 4.5.
   - An informed trader would only do that if the settlement is 5 or 6, which has probability about 0.46 with an average of about 5.42.
   - A noise trader buys above 4.5 about 41% of the time.
   - Updating on this buy moves the fair value up to about 4.4.
   - The stage-1 sale at 2 pulls it down very slightly, because a settlement of 1 is unlikely.

So the fair value is about 4.4. I quote symmetrically around it, about 0.8 each side, to cover the risk of trading against an informed counterparty.

{"bid": 3.6, "ask": 5.2}

Fair value is about **4.31**. I'm quoting a bid of 3.0 and an ask of 5.5, which roughly maximise expected profit on each side.

**Which coin is it?** The revealed flips are 1, 1, 1, 0.
- For the 0.4 coin, the chance of these flips is 0.4³ × 0.6 = 0.0384. Weighted by its prior of 3/5, that gives 0.02304.
- For the 0.8 coin, the chance is 0.8³ × 0.2 = 0.1024. Weighted by its prior of 2/5, that gives 0.04096.
- So the chance it is the 0.8 coin is 0.04096 / 0.064 = 0.64.

**Expected value.** Each remaining flip comes up heads with chance 0.64 × 0.8 + 0.36 × 0.4 = 0.656. Two flips remain, so fair value is 3 + 2 × 0.656 = **4.312**.

The contract can only settle at 3, 4 or 5:

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 3 | 0.155 |
| 4 | 0.378 |
| 5 | 0.467 |

**Ask side.** An informed trader can only buy above me if settlement exceeds my ask. With an ask of 5.0 or more, informed buyers never trade with me. I only gain from noise traders, roughly 0.8 × P(noise buys) × (ask − 4.312). This is largest at about 5.5, worth about 0.22 per quote.

**Bid side.** Informed traders sell only when settlement is 3, and that loss disappears once my bid is 3.0 or lower. The noise-trader gain is largest around 3.0–3.1, worth about 0.215.

My position is +1, well within the limits, so it doesn't change the quote.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 5.5}

This is the last quote. I can stay within the position limit (+1) on either side, so I'll set each side to maximise expected profit.

**Posterior on the coin** (revealed flips: 1, 1, 1, 0)
- Weight for the 0.8 coin: 0.4 × 0.8³ × 0.2 = 0.04096
- Weight for the 0.4 coin: 0.6 × 0.4³ × 0.6 = 0.02304
- So P(0.8 coin) = 0.04096 / 0.064 = 0.64, and P(0.4 coin) = 0.36.
- Expected heads per remaining flip: 0.64 × 0.8 + 0.36 × 0.4 = 0.656.

**Settlement distribution**
Three heads are already revealed, so settlement is 3 plus heads in flips 5 and 6.

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 3 | 0.155 |
| 4 | 0.378 |
| 5 | 0.467 |

Fair value is 3 + 2 × 0.656 ≈ 4.31. This ignores any small information in the trading history.

**Ask**
- An informed trader buys at ask a only if settlement exceeds a, so any ask of 5 or above has no informed-trade loss.
- A noise trader buys with probability 1 − Φ((a − 4.31) / 1.6) and I earn a − 4.31 per trade.
- Expected profit 0.8 × P(buy) × (a − 4.31) peaks near a = 5.6, at about 0.217.

**Bid**
- An informed trader sells at bid b only if settlement is below b, so a bid of 3 or below has no informed-trade loss.
- A noise trader sells with probability Φ((b − 4.31) / 1.6) and I earn 4.31 − b per trade.
- At b = 3.0 the expected profit is about 0.216. Bids above 3 add informed-trade losses, which reduce it to about 0.204 at b = 3.3.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 5.6}

game.title: Urn of unknown mix
game.description: An urn holds 10 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 10. 3 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of red balls originally in the urn.

info.raw:
With no draws revealed yet, the number of red balls is equally likely to be anything from 0 to 10. That puts fair value at 5, with wide uncertainty.

Informed traders (35% of arrivals) know the exact count. They will hit any quote that sits inside the range of possible values. Noise traders only add ±2.4 around 5, so a wide spread is needed to keep informed losses below noise profits.

Expected profit per side, for a half-spread h around 5:

| Half-spread h | Expected profit per side |
|---|---|
| 2 | +0.07 |
| 2.5 | +0.10 |
| 3 | +0.11 (best) |
| 3.5 | +0.10 |

At h = 3 the quotes are a bid of 2 and an ask of 8.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 8.0}

Before quote 2 I updated the fair value to about 7.16, from a prior mean of 5. The trade at 8 was a buy, and only a few red-ball counts make a buy that high likely.

**Updating on the buy at 8**
- If the true count R is 9 or 10, an informed trader would buy at 8. Probability of a buy from that source: 0.35.
- A noise trader values the contract at 5 + N(0, 2.4). They buy only if the noise exceeds +3, which has probability ≈ 0.106. Their contribution to the buy probability is 0.65 × 0.106 ≈ 0.069.
- So the chance of a buy is about 0.069 if R ≤ 8 and about 0.419 if R is 9 or 10.
- Weighting R = 0…10 by these probabilities gives:
  - each of R = 9 and R = 10: probability ≈ 0.288.
  - each of R = 0…8: probability ≈ 0.047.
  - expected R: about **7.16**.

**Choosing the ask**
- At 10.0, an informed trader never buys, because R cannot exceed 10. Noise traders buy about 12% of the time, with an edge of about 2.84.
- Expected profit is about +0.22, roughly the best of the asks I checked.
- Going from −1 to −2 is within the position limit.

**Choosing the bid**
- I would lose to informed sellers whenever R is low, and the remaining probability on low R is still meaningful.
- Expected profit is about +0.03 at a bid of 4.0 or 4.5. It turns negative above about 5.5.
- I'll bid 4.0.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 10.0}

Two pieces of public information move the fair value: the blue first draw and the trades so far.

**The blue first draw.** Before the draw, every red count R from 0 to 10 is equally likely. A blue first draw is more likely when there are fewer reds, so each R is weighted by (10−R). That gives a mean of exactly 3.

**Quote 1: a buy at 8.**
- An informed trader would buy at 8 only if R is 9 or 10.
- A noise trader (valuation about 5 + N(0, 2.4)) would buy at 8 about 11% of the time.
- So the buy is about 0.42 likely if R is 9 or 10, and about 0.07 likely otherwise.

**Quote 2: no trade at 4 / 10.**
- An informed trader would not trade if R is 4 or more.
- A noise trader would not trade about 64% of the time.
- So no trade is about 0.77 likely if R is 4 or more, and about 0.42 likely if R is below 4.

**Result.** Combining these likelihoods with the (10−R) weights gives a public fair value of about 4.26. The distribution is skewed, with a noticeable chance that R = 9.

**Quote.** I'll centre the quote near 4.3 with roughly ±1.7 width. That catches noise traders while limiting losses to informed traders. Since I'm short 1, I'll lean the quote slightly upward so I'm a little more likely to buy back.

{"bid": 2.7, "ask": 6.0}

The posterior mean of the red count is about 2.9, so I'm quoting a bid of 1.0 and an ask of 5.6.

**Starting point.** Before any trades, the 0–10 prior combined with draw 1 being blue gives weights proportional to (10 − R). That puts the mean at 3.

**Updating on the trades.** Each trade changes how likely each red count is:
- **Quote 1 (they bought at 8):** an informed trader only buys there if R ≥ 9, so this pushes weight onto R = 9.
- **Quote 2 (no trade at 4 / 10):** this mildly favours R ≥ 4.
- **Quote 3 (they sold at 2.7):** an informed trader sells there if R ≤ 2, so this strongly favours R = 0, 1 or 2.

**Resulting distribution.** The posterior has two humps. About 61% of the weight sits on R = 0–2, and a separate pocket sits at R = 9. The mean comes out at about 2.9.

**Choosing each side.** For each candidate price I weighed the expected gain from noise traders against the expected loss to informed traders.
- **Bid:** around 1.0 an informed seller only appears when R = 0, which keeps that risk small. Noise traders still sell often, so the expected edge is about +0.19 per quote. Higher bids such as 1.5 or 2 lose too much to informed sellers when R is 0 or 1.
- **Ask:** about 5.5–6 is best, with an expected edge of about +0.08. Lower asks lose to the R = 9 pocket.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 5.6}

Fair value is 5. Before any trades, after a blue draw and then a red draw, the chance of each red count R is proportional to R(10−R). That spread is symmetric around 5, with a standard deviation of about 2.2. The trades so far roughly cancel out, so they don't move it.

**Choosing the ask.** I compared expected profit per quote at several ask prices, counting the gain from noise traders and the loss to informed traders:

| Ask | Net expected profit |
|---|---|
| 6.5 | about 0.14 |
| 7.0 | about 0.19 |
| 7.5 | about 0.20 |
| 8.0 | about 0.19 |

**Choosing the bid.** The posterior is symmetric around 5, so the best bid mirrors the ask at 2.5.

My position limit is not binding at −1, and the objective is expected profit, so I don't skew the quotes for inventory.

{"bid": 2.5, "ask": 7.5}

Weighing the reveals and the trade history, I estimate the contract is worth about 8.2. My quotes are bid 6.8 and ask 9.1.

**Draws alone.** Draw 1 was blue and draw 2 was red. That makes the probability of each red count proportional to R(10−R), which centres on 5.

**Trade history.** Each trade is about 35% likely to come from an informed counterparty. I weighted each red count by how likely the trades were if it were true:
- The buy at 8 in quote 1 points to R = 9.
- The no-trade at 4/10 in quote 2 points to R ≥ 4.
- The sell at 2.7 in quote 3 points to R ≤ 2.
- The buy at 5.6 in quote 4 points to R ≥ 6.
- The buy at 7.5 in quote 5 points to R ≥ 8.

Combined, R = 9 has about 65% probability and R = 8 about 19%. The estimated fair value is about 8.2.

**Ask.** R is at most 9, so an ask of 9.1 is never hit by an informed trader. A noise trader still buys at that price about 36% of the time, earning about 0.9 per sale.

**Bid.** A bid near 6.8 balances buying from noise traders below fair value against the small chance (about 7%) that R is 6 or less. It also lets me reduce my short position of −2.

{"bid": 6.8, "ask": 9.1}

Quote: bid 4.0, ask 8.3.

**Fair value.** With a uniform prior and the draws blue, red, red, the posterior weight on R red balls is proportional to (10−R)·R·(R−1). That gives a posterior mean of R = 6.2 and a standard deviation of about 1.8.

**Ask.** Expected profit per quote is the noise-trader edge minus the expected loss to informed traders, who buy only when R is above the ask:

| Ask | Net edge |
|---|---|
| 7.5 | 0.16 |
| 8.0 | 0.23 |
| 8.3–8.5 | about 0.235 (the peak) |

**Bid.** The same calculation for the bid peaks at around 0.22 for bids between 3.9 and 4.1. I'm short 1, so I'm happy to buy back. I'll use 4.0.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 8.3}

Quote bid **4.0** and ask **8.4**. This is the last quote, so I just pick the pair with the highest expected profit. My current short position doesn't change that.

**Posterior on the number of red balls (R).** The draws came out blue, red, red. The chance of that sequence is proportional to R(R−1)(10−R).

| R | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | .024 | .064 | .109 | .152 | .182 | .191 | .170 | .109 |

The weights sum to 660, which puts the fair value at **6.2**. That matches a uniform-prior update: 2 drawn reds plus 7 × 0.6 = 6.2.

**Ask.** Each quote earns from noise traders and loses to informed traders whose true value is beyond my price. At an ask of 8.3–8.5, noise buyers bring in about 0.26 and informed buyers cost about 0.02–0.03 (only R = 9 is above the ask). That nets roughly 0.23, which is the best ask I found.

**Bid.** The bid works the same way on the other side. At 4.0, noise sellers bring in about 0.26 and informed sellers cost about 0.04 (when R = 2 or 3). That nets roughly 0.22, again the best I found.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 8.4}

game.title: Urn of unknown mix
game.description: An urn holds 10 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 10. 3 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of red balls originally in the urn.

info.raw:
With the prior alone, the red-ball count is uniform on 0 to 10, so fair value is 5. I picked a symmetric spread by trading off two things: the expected gain from noise traders against the expected loss to informed traders.

For an ask at 5 + d, the net expected profit is 0.65 × P(noise > d) × d minus 0.35 × E[(V − ask)⁺].

| Ask | Net expected profit |
|---|---|
| 7.0 | ≈ 0.072 |
| 7.5 | ≈ 0.099 |
| 7.9 | ≈ 0.109 |
| 8.0 | ≈ 0.110 |
| 8.5 | ≈ 0.101 |

The best is around an ask of 8, so I quote 3 either side of 5. By symmetry, the bid at 2 earns the same.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 8.0}

After one trade, the market's fair value is about 2.83, down from a prior of 5. I'm quoting bid 0.5 and ask 6 to stay just above break-even on each side.

**Updating the fair value.** Before any trade, the red count was equally likely to be 0 through 10, so the fair value was 5.
- An informed trader would sell at my bid of 2 only if the true value is 0 or 1.
- A noise trader would sell if its valuation fell below 2. That is about 1.25 standard deviations below 5, so it happens with probability about 0.106.
- Combining these, values 0 and 1 now carry about 0.288 probability each. Values 2 to 10 carry about 0.047 each.
- The new fair value is about 2.83.

**Choosing the ask.** Informed buyers take my ask when the value is above it, so I lose on those trades. Noise buyers pay above fair value, so I gain on those.

| Ask | Informed loss | Noise gain | Net per quote |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 0.25 | 0.26 | +0.01 |
| 6 | 0.17 | 0.19 | +0.03 |
| 7 | 0.10 | 0.11 | +0.01 |

An ask of 6 has the best expected profit, and selling also reduces my long position.

**Choosing the bid.** Low bids are only hit by informed sellers when the value is 0. Noise sellers still hit them fairly often because the fair value is now only 2.83.

| Bid | Net per quote |
|---|---|
| 1.0 | +0.16 |
| 0.5 | +0.20 |
| 0.3 | +0.21 |

The edge is fairly flat around 0.2 to 0.5. I'm choosing 0.5, at the high end of that range, to keep a reasonable chance of a trade. I'm already long one unit, so I don't want to bid aggressively.

{"bid": 0.5, "ask": 6}

Given draw 1 was red and the earlier trades, I estimate the settlement value at about 8.1. My quote is centred there, with the spread skewed to protect against the most likely high outcomes.

**Prior.** The number of red balls R is uniform over 0 to 10.

**Trade 1: they sold at my bid of 2.**
- At that point the public fair value was 5.
- An informed counterparty sells at 2 only if R is 0 or 1.
- A noise trader sells at 2 with probability 0.65 × P(noise < −3) = 0.65 × 0.106 ≈ 0.069.
- So the likelihood is about 0.42 for R = 0 or 1, and about 0.069 for R = 2 to 10.

**Trade 2: they bought at my ask of 6.**
- After trade 1 the public fair value was about 2.84.
- A noise trader buys at 6 with probability 0.65 × P(noise > 3.16) = 0.65 × 0.094 ≈ 0.061.
- An informed counterparty buys at 6 only if R is 7 or more.
- So the likelihood is about 0.41 for R = 7 to 10, and about 0.061 for R up to 6.

**Draw 1 = red.** The chance of drawing red first is proportional to R, so I multiply each weight by R.

**Posterior.**
- About 90% of the weight now sits on R = 7 to 10.
- The posterior mean is about 8.1.

**Quote.** I bid 7.0 and ask 9.2.
- An informed counterparty would only sell to me at 7.0 if R is 6 or less, which is now unlikely.
- At 9.2, an informed counterparty only buys when R = 10, and then I lose 0.8 on the unit.
- Noise traders around 8.1 should trade on both sides, which is where the profit comes from.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 9.2}

Fair value is about 7.5, so I'm quoting a wide market around it: bid 5, ask 10.

**Posterior on red balls R.** Start from a uniform prior on 0 to 10, then apply each piece of public information in turn.

| Step | Evidence | Fair value before the trade | Likelihood of the evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Quote 1 | They sold at my bid of 2 | 5 | 0.42 if R < 2, else 0.069 |
| Quote 2 | They bought at my ask of 6 | about 2.84 | 0.41 if R > 6, else 0.061 |
| Reveal | Draw 1 is red | — | Weight each R by R/10 |
| Quote 3 | They sold at my bid of 7 | about 8.14 | 0.56 if R < 7, else 0.21 |

The resulting posterior is:

| R | Probability |
|---|---|
| 7 | 0.158 |
| 8 | 0.180 |
| 9 | 0.203 |
| 10 | 0.225 |
| 6 or below | 0.235 combined, most of it at R = 1 and R = 6 |

The public fair value is therefore about **7.48**.

**Choosing the ask.** Expected profit per quote is the gain from noise buyers minus the loss to informed buyers.
- Ask 8.5: about +0.07 net.
- Ask 9.5: about +0.22 net.
- Ask 10: about +0.24 net, and informed traders never buy because R cannot exceed 10. This is the best.

**Choosing the bid.**
- Bid 6: about +0.07 net, because there is too much informed selling when R is low.
- Bid 5: about +0.12 net. This is the best.
- Bid 4: about +0.09 net.

I am long 1 unit, so a slightly lower bid is also fine for inventory.

{"bid": 5, "ask": 10}

Given two red draws, the base estimate is 8. The trades so far shift it up to about **8.3**, so I quote a **6.3 bid and a 9.4 ask**.

**Base estimate from the draws.** The red count starts equally likely from 0 to 10. After two reds, each count is weighted by R(R−1). That gives an expected red count of 8.

**Adjusting for the trades so far.** I treated each past trade as weak evidence about who traded and why:
- **Stage 1:** someone sold to me at 2, then someone bought from me at 6. These are more likely if the true count is 7 or more, because the buy at 6 points that way.
- **Quote 3:** someone sold to me at 7. This makes a count of 6 or less somewhat more likely.
- **Quote 4:** nobody traded at 5 / 10. This makes a count of 5 or more more likely.

Taken together, my estimate of fair value rises to about **8.3**.

**Choosing the quote.**
- **Ask:** Only an informed buyer hurts me on the sell side, and only if the count is 10. Noise traders buying above 9.4 give a good expected profit on the trades they make.
- **Bid:** An informed seller only shows up if the count is 6 or below, which is now fairly unlikely. A bid around 6.0–6.5 earns the most per quote against noise sellers.
- **Position:** I am already long one unit, so I lean slightly toward selling. That puts the quote a little below the best-earning levels: 6.3 bid and 9.4 ask.

{"bid": 6.3, "ask": 9.4}

The draws give a fair value of about 8. With my long position of +1, I quote 6.8 / 9.0, skewed slightly toward selling.

**Posterior from the draws.** The prior on red balls R is uniform over 0 to 10. After two red draws, the probability of R is proportional to R(R−1), and these weights sum to 330. The expected value is E[R] = Σ R²(R−1) / 330 = 2640 / 330 = 8. The most likely values are:

| R | Probability |
|---|---|
| 10 | 0.27 |
| 9 | 0.22 |
| 8 | 0.17 |
| 7 | 0.13 |
| ≤6 | 0.21 |

**Trading history.** The trades lean slightly bearish, so the public fair value is probably a little under 8, around 7.8–8:
- A counterparty sold to me at 7 when the fair value was 7.
- Nobody traded inside my 6.3 / 9.4 quote last time.

**Ask at 9.0.**
- An informed trader buys only if R = 10. That costs 1.0 × 0.27 × 0.35 ≈ 0.10.
- A noise trader buys with probability about 0.34, gaining about 1 each time: 0.65 × 0.34 ≈ 0.22.
- So the ask has positive expected value.

**Bid at 6.8.**
- An informed trader sells if R ≤ 6. That costs about 0.12–0.13 in expectation.
- A noise trader sells with probability about 0.30, gaining about 1.2 each time: roughly 0.23–0.25.
- So the bid also has positive expected value.

{"bid": 6.8, "ask": 9.0}

Given three red draws, the posterior on the number of red balls is proportional to r(r−1)(r−2) for r ≥ 3. That puts the fair value at 17028/1980 = 8.6.

The posterior is skewed toward high values:

| Red balls | 10 | 9 | 8 | 7 | 6 or fewer |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 36% | 25% | 17% | 11% | 11% |

For each side I compared what I gain from noise traders against what I lose to informed traders:

- **Ask:** Expected profit rises until the informed losses on r = 10 disappear at an ask of 10. It peaks around 10.4–10.5, at about +0.26.
- **Bid:** Informed traders sell to me only when the true count is below the bid. Expected profit peaks around 6.5, at about +0.22.

I am risk-neutral, so my current long position of +1 does not change the quote.

{"bid": 6.5, "ask": 10.4}

This is the final quote, so I'm pricing directly against the posterior on the number of red balls.

**Posterior after drawing 3 reds out of 3:** P(R) ∝ R(R−1)(R−2) for R = 3…10.
- P(10) ≈ 0.364
- P(9) ≈ 0.255
- P(8) ≈ 0.170
- P(7) ≈ 0.106
- P(6) ≈ 0.061
- P(5) ≈ 0.030
- P(4) ≈ 0.012
- P(3) ≈ 0.003

The fair value is E[R] = 8.6. The earlier trades were at quotes far from this, so I treat them as adding little information.

**Ask side:** The settlement value can't exceed 10. So any ask at or above 10 loses nothing to informed buyers, and the edge comes only from noise buyers.
- The expected profit is 0.65 · P(noise > a) · (a − 8.6).
- It peaks near a ≈ 10.4, at about 0.265 per quote.
- Asks below 10 do worse, because informed buyers lift them whenever R = 10.

**Bid side:** Informed sellers hit the bid only when R < bid, and low values of R are unlikely.
- At b = 6.5, the loss to informed sellers is about 0.04, and the gain from noise sellers is about 0.26.
- The net is about +0.22, the best of the levels I checked (6.0, 6.5, 6.9, 7.0 and 7.5).

{"bid": 6.5, "ask": 10.4}

game.title: Urn of unknown mix
game.description: An urn holds 10 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 10. 3 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of red balls originally in the urn.

info.raw:
Before anything is revealed, the number of red balls is equally likely to be any value from 0 to 10, so fair value is **5**.

To pick the spread, I compared expected profit per side for different half-spreads h. The gain is 0.8 × P(noise trader crosses) × h. The loss to informed traders is 0.2 × the average of max(V − 5 − h, 0) over V = 0 to 10.

| Half-spread h | Gain from noise traders | Loss to informed traders | Net per side |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 0.54 | 0.11 | 0.43 |
| 3 | 0.63 | 0.05 | 0.57 |
| 4 | 0.63 | 0.02 | 0.615 |
| 5 | 0.58 | 0 | 0.58 |

The net profit is highest at about h = 4, so I quote 1 / 9.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9.0}

Fair value is 5. The red count is uniform on 0 to 10, and the last quote's no-trade at 1/9 doesn't shift that, because it was symmetric.

I compared expected profit per quote for different half-spreads around 5. Each figure is noise-trader profit minus losses to informed traders:

| Half-spread | Quote | Expected net per quote |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 3 / 7 | about 0.85 |
| 3 | 2 / 8 | about 1.15 |
| 3.5 | 1.5 / 8.5 | about 1.20 |
| 4 | 1 / 9 | about 1.22 |

The curve is flat between 3.5 and 4. I'll quote 1.5 / 8.5, which gives up almost nothing in expectation and makes a trade more likely.

{"bid": 1.5, "ask": 8.5}

With nothing revealed yet, the fair value is 5: red balls are uniform on 0–10, so the mean is 5 and the standard deviation is about 3.16. The two quotes with no trade don't move it, because they were symmetric.

I compared expected profit per side at different half-spreads:
- **Half-spread 3:** about 0.57 per side.
- **Half-spread 3.5:** about 0.60 per side.
- **Half-spread 3.9–4:** about 0.61 per side. This is the best range, and the curve is fairly flat here.

At a half-spread of 3.9, informed traders only trade against me when the true value is 9 or 10 on the ask side, or 0 or 1 on the bid side. That keeps losses to them small, while noise traders still trade often enough to pay for it.

{"bid": 1.1, "ask": 8.9}

Fair value comes to about 7.2, so I'm quoting a wide spread around it: bid 4.2 and ask 10.0.

**Fair value from the reveal.** Drawing a red ball first makes urns with more red balls more likely, in proportion to the number of red balls R. The expected value is then E[R] = Σ R² / Σ R = 385/55 = 7.0.

**Fair value from trading.** The stage-1 history adds a little more information.
- Quotes 1 and 2 got no trade. An informed trader would have traded at those quotes if R had been near 0 or 10, so this makes the extreme values slightly less likely.
- Quote 3 was a buy at 8.9. An informed trader would only do that if R was 9 or 10, so this makes those values more likely.
- Combining these gives a fair value of about **7.2**.

**Quote choice.** With noise standard deviation 4.7, a wide quote still trades with noise traders fairly often.
- **Ask at 10.0:** an informed trader can never profitably buy, since R is at most 10. Noise traders still buy about 27% of the time, with roughly 2.8 of edge per trade.
- **Bid at 4.2:** an informed trader only sells if R is 4 or less, which has about 16% probability. The expected loss on those trades is small next to the noise-trader edge of about 3.
- Being short 1 unit leaves plenty of room within the position limits on both sides.

{"bid": 4.2, "ask": 10.0}

Fair value is about 7.24. I quote 4.9 / 9.1 around it, wide enough on the bid to limit losses to informed sellers.

**Prior after draw 1 is red.** The chance of seeing red is proportional to R, so P(R) ∝ R/10. That puts the expected number of red balls at 7.

**Quote 3 (they bought at 8.9 when fair value was about 5).**
- If R is 9 or 10, an informed trader would buy. The chance of a buy is 0.2 + 0.8 × P(noise > 8.9) = 0.2 + 0.162 ≈ 0.36.
- Otherwise only a noise trader buys, with chance about 0.16.

**Quote 4 (they sold at 4.2 when fair value was about 7.2).**
- If R is 4 or less, an informed trader would sell. The chance of a sell is 0.2 + 0.8 × P(noise < 4.2) ≈ 0.2 + 0.209 ≈ 0.41.
- Otherwise only a noise trader sells, with chance about 0.21.

**Posterior.** Combining the prior with both trades gives an expected value of about 7.24. Roughly 22% of the probability sits on R ≤ 4, and about 25% sits on R = 10.

**Quote.**
- **Bid 4.9:** an informed seller only hits it when R ≤ 4, and the spread to fair value pays for that risk.
- **Ask 9.1:** an informed buyer only lifts it when R = 10, which costs just 0.9 per trade.
- This gives a spread of about ±2.2 around fair value, against noise with standard deviation 4.7.

{"bid": 4.9, "ask": 9.1}

Fair value given the public information is about 6.9, so I'm quoting around it.

- **Draw 1 is red.** The prior on the number of red balls R becomes proportional to R, which puts E[R] at 7.
- **Stage-1 buy at 8.9.** This makes R = 9 or 10 a bit more likely, since an informed trader would only buy if R were above 8.9.
- **Sell at 4.2 in quote 4.** This makes R ≤ 4 more likely.
- **No trade at 4.9 / 9.1 in quote 5.** This makes R between 5 and 9 more likely.
- **Combined estimate.** Putting these together gives a posterior mean of about 6.9.

The 20% chance of an informed counterparty means I need a fairly wide spread. Last quote's 4.9 / 9.1 drew no trade, so I'll tighten slightly to 5.0 / 8.8 while staying roughly symmetric around 6.9. This tries to earn edge from noise traders while limiting losses to informed ones.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 8.8}

With two red balls drawn, the urn's red count R has posterior weight proportional to R(R−1). That puts fair value at E[R] = 2640/330 = **8**. The distribution is skewed high: P(10) ≈ 27%, P(9) ≈ 22%, P(8) ≈ 17%.

**Ask side.** An informed buyer can never beat an ask at 10 or above, since R is at most 10. Above that level, the only question is how far to step out into the noise traders' distribution (sd 4.7). Expected profit per quote rises to about 0.63 around 11 to 11.5 and is flat beyond that.

**Bid side.** The posterior has little mass below 5, so losses to an informed seller are small. Expected profit is about 0.61 at a bid of 5 and about 0.63 at 4.5, so the curve is flat in that range.

I'll quote a wide two-sided market from my flat position.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 11.0}

Fair value is **8**. I'm quoting **bid 4.5, ask 11.5**.

**Fair value after two red draws.** The prior on the number of red balls R is uniform over 0 to 10. The chance of drawing red twice is R(R−1)/90, so the posterior is proportional to R(R−1). That gives E[R] = (ΣR³ − ΣR²)/(ΣR² − ΣR) = 2640/330 = 8. The trading history adds little, so I take the public fair value as 8.

**Choosing the ask.** An informed buyer only profits if R is above my ask, and R can be at most 10.
- At an ask of 10 or more, informed traders never buy from me.
- Expected profit from noise traders is 0.8 × P(noise > ask − 8) × (ask − 8):

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 11 | 0.628 |
| 11.5 | 0.638 |
| 12 | 0.632 |

- So the ask is about 11.5.

**Choosing the bid.** Each informed trader who sells to me costs the bid minus R.

| Bid | Noise gain | Informed loss | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | — | — | 0.61 |
| 4.5 | 0.638 | 0.012 | 0.626 |
| 4 | — | — | 0.626 |

- So the bid is about 4.5.

My position is flat, so inventory doesn't change these quotes.

{"bid": 4.5, "ask": 11.5}

With two red draws revealed, my fair-value estimate is 8, and I quote 6.5 bid / 9.3 ask around it.

**Fair value.** The prior is uniform on R = 0..10. The chance of drawing 2 reds is R(R−1)/90, so the posterior is proportional to R(R−1).
- The weights sum to 330.
- E[R] = (ΣR³ − ΣR²)/330 = (3025 − 385)/330 = **8**.
- I've ignored any information in the earlier trades. That history is mixed and adds little.

**Informed-trader risk.**
- **Bid side:** with a bid of 6.5, an informed seller appears when R ≤ 6. That has probability 70/330 ≈ 0.21. The average R in that case is about 5, so each such trade loses about 1.5.
- **Ask side:** with an ask of 9.3, an informed buyer appears only when R = 10. That has probability 90/330 ≈ 0.27, but each such trade loses only 0.7.

**Noise traders.** Their valuations have a standard deviation of 4.7 around 8. Quoting about 1.3 to 1.5 away from 8 on each side still captures a lot of their flow.

So I quote a little tighter on the ask, where an informed trade costs less.

{"bid": 6.5, "ask": 9.3}

Three reds in three draws pushes the expected red count to **8.6**, so I'm quoting a wide market around that: bid 5.2, ask 12.0.

**Fair value.** The prior on the number of red balls (R) is uniform over 0..10. Given 3 reds out of 3 draws, the likelihood is proportional to R(R−1)(R−2).
- The posterior weights for R = 3..10 are 6, 24, 60, 120, 210, 336, 504, 720, which sum to 1980.
- The expected value is E[R] = 17028 / 1980 ≈ **8.6**, with a standard deviation of about 1.5.
- R = 10 has probability about 0.36, and R ≤ 6 has probability about 0.11.

**Ask.** Expected profit per quote, from noise trader buys minus informed losses:
- At 9.6: about 0.31.
- At 10.1: about 0.45. Above 10 the informed trader never buys, since R cannot exceed 10.
- At 11: about 0.59.
- At 12: about 0.64, which is roughly the peak.
- At 13.3: about 0.60.

**Bid.** Expected profit per quote:
- At 7: about 0.44. The informed trader sells when R ≤ 6 (probability 0.11).
- At 6: about 0.59.
- At 5: about 0.64. Informed selling is very rare here (R ≤ 4, probability 0.015).
- At 4.5: about 0.63.

My position is +1, so the position limits don't bind. I'll quote close to both optima.

{"bid": 5.2, "ask": 12.0}

With three red balls drawn, the expected red count is about 8.6, and I quote wide around it: bid 5.3, ask 11.9.

**Fair value.** Each value of the red count R from 0 to 10 starts equally likely. Three red draws in a row update each value in proportion to R(R−1)(R−2).

- The resulting probabilities are: R=10 about 0.36, R=9 about 0.25, R=8 about 0.17, R=7 about 0.11, R=6 about 0.06.
- This gives an expected settlement value of about **8.6**.

**Choosing the quotes.** For each candidate price I added the expected profit from noise traders (probability 0.8, valuation 8.6 plus noise with standard deviation 4.7) to the expected loss to informed traders (probability 0.2, who know R).

- **Ask:** No one can value the contract above 10, so an ask above 10 never trades with an informed trader. The noise-trader edge, (ask − 8.6) times the chance of a buy, peaks around an ask of 12.
- **Bid:** An informed trader only sells at a low bid when R is small, and R ≤ 5 now has only about 5% probability. The noise-trader edge peaks around a bid of 5 to 5.5.

My position is +1, well inside the ±4 limit, so I don't need to lean the quotes.

{"bid": 5.3, "ask": 11.9}

This is the last quote, so I set each side to maximise expected profit against the posterior on the number of red balls.

**Posterior after three red draws.** The probability of drawing 3 reds without replacement, given r red balls, is proportional to C(r,3). That makes P(r) ∝ C(r,3) for r = 3 to 10, with weights 1, 4, 10, 20, 35, 56, 84 and 120 (total 330).
- The expected settlement value is 2838/330 ≈ 8.6.
- P(10) ≈ 0.36, P(9) ≈ 0.25 and P(8) ≈ 0.17.

**Ask side.** An informed buyer at an ask of 10 or more never exists, because the value cannot exceed 10. So the ask only trades with noise traders.
- Expected profit is 0.8 × P(noise > ask − 8.6) × (ask − 8.6).
- This is about 0.43 at 10, 0.59 at 11, 0.64 at 12 and 0.62 at 13.
- It peaks near 12.

**Bid side.** Informed sellers only matter when the true value is below the bid, and the chance of a value below 5 is very small.
- Expected profit is about 0.44 at a bid of 7, 0.59 at 6, 0.64 at 5 and 0.60 at 4.
- It peaks near 5.

My position of +1 doesn't constrain either side.

{"bid": 5.1, "ask": 12.1}

info.raw:
With nothing revealed yet, every count of red balls from 0 to 10 is equally likely. So the expected settlement value is 5.

I picked the half-spread h to maximise expected profit per side:

- **Profit from noise traders:** 0.8 × h × P(noise > h), where the noise has standard deviation 4.7.
- **Loss to informed traders:** 0.2 × E[(V − 5 − h)⁺], where V is the true number of red balls.

| h | Noise profit | Informed loss | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 0.536 | 0.109 | 0.427 |
| 3 | 0.629 | 0.055 | 0.574 |
| 3.5 | 0.638 | 0.036 | 0.602 |
| 4 | 0.631 | 0.018 | 0.613 |
| 4.5 | 0.609 | 0.009 | 0.600 |

The net is fairly flat between h = 3.5 and h = 4.5, with the best point near h = 4. I'm quoting about 3.8 either side of 5.

{"bid": 1.2, "ask": 8.8}

Before any draw, every red count from 0 to 10 is equally likely, so the fair value starts at 5. Someone sold to me at 1.2. An informed trader sells there only if the true count is 0 or 1. A noise trader sells with about 21% probability. Updating on that sale brings the public fair value to about **4.2**.

I then checked the expected edge per quote at a few prices. This weighs profit from noise traders against losses to informed ones.

- **Ask side:** the edge peaks around 8 to 9, at about 0.59 per quote. It falls to 0.52 at an ask of 7.
- **Bid side:** the edge is about flat between 0.5 and 1, at about 0.60 to 0.62.

I'm already long 1, so I'll lean slightly toward selling by shading both quotes down a little.

{"bid": 0.8, "ask": 7.8}

The public fair value has dropped to about **3.6**, so I'm quoting **bid 0.3 / ask 7.4**, with the ask slightly lowered to lean against my long position.

**Updating the fair value.** I started from the uniform prior on 0–10, with mean 5. For each trade I weighed how likely it was under each possible red count. A sale at my bid comes from an informed trader whose value is below the bid, or from a noise trader whose valuation falls below the bid.

- **Quote 1:** at fair value 5, a sell at 1.2 had noise-sell probability Φ(−0.81) ≈ 0.21. That raises the weight on 0 or 1 red balls. Fair value fell to about 4.2.
- **Quote 2:** a sell at 0.8 then raised the weight on 0 red. Fair value fell to about **3.6**. The posterior is roughly P(0) ≈ 0.29, P(1) ≈ 0.14, and about 0.064 for each of 2 through 10.

**Choosing the quotes.** I compared expected profit across prices: gains from noise traders minus losses to informed traders.

- **Ask:** expected profit is about 0.56 at 7, peaks around 0.58 between 7.5 and 8, and drops to about 0.24 at 5. Since I'm already long 2, I shade the ask slightly lower to 7.4 to make selling more likely.
- **Bid:** a very low bid still attracts about 22% of noise traders, worth about 0.6–0.64 in expectation, while informed losses are tiny. That is because only a red count of 0 sits below such a bid. I keep it low because my position is near the +4 limit.

{"bid": 0.3, "ask": 7.4}

Posterior fair value is about 6.5. I'm quoting bid 4.0 / ask 8.8, which is wide on both sides and leans toward selling because I'm already long 2.

**Fair value**
- The prior is uniform on R = 0..10, so it starts at 5.
- **Quote 1:** a sale at 1.2 is more likely when R ≤ 1, because an informed trader would sell then. Fair value drops to about 4.2.
- **Quote 2:** a sale at 0.8 adds weight to R = 0. Fair value drops to about 3.57.
